fact_lentivirus_clock.summary: While phylogenies are mirror images, virus splits occurred over thousands of years, while host splits occurred over millions of years. (Page 632)

fact_lentivirus_switching.label: Lentivirus Switching Mechanism
fact_lentivirus_switching.summary: Similarity in immune systems makes it easier for viruses to switch between phylogenetically closely related primate hosts. (Page 632)

arms_races.label: Coevolutionary Arms Races
arms_races.summary: Reciprocal evolutionary pressure where predators evolve better weapons and prey evolve better defenses.

encephalization_quotient.label: Encephalization Quotient (EQ)
encephalization_quotient.summary: A measure of relative intelligence defined as the ratio of actual brain size to expected brain size given body size.

jerison_mammal_study.label: Jerison (1973) Mammal Study
jerison_mammal_study.summary: Analysis of Cenozoic mammals showing an increase in relative brain size for both predators and prey.

fact_predator_prey_eq.label: Carnivore vs Ungulate EQ
fact_predator_prey_eq.summary: Predators typically have larger relative brains than their prey, suggesting a coevolutionary race to increase intelligence for catching/escaping. (Page 633-634)

evolutionary_escalation.label: Evolutionary Escalation
evolutionary_escalation.summary: A general pattern described by Vermeij where life becomes more dangerous over time due to the reciprocal improvement of weapons and defenses.

escalation_vs_progress.label: Escalation vs. Evolutionary Progress
escalation_vs_progress.summary: The distinction between organisms becoming better adapted to an environment versus matching the improvements of an antagonist.

fact_escalation_definition.label: Escalation Definition
fact_escalation_definition.summary: In escalation, later predators are no better at catching contemporary prey than their ancestors were at catching their contemporaries, although they would easily defeat ancestral prey. (Page 634)

mollusk_escalation_evidence.label: Mollusk Escalation Evidence
mollusk_escalation_evidence.summary: Paleontological evidence from marine mollusks supporting the theory of escalation.

fact_shell_repair.label: Shell Repair Frequency
fact_shell_repair.summary: Increased frequency of non-lethal shell repair over time indicates a higher frequency of predatory attacks. (Page 635)

fact_shell_morphology.label: Shell Attachment Trends
fact_shell_morphology.summary: Decrease in loosely attached forms and increase in burrowing or cemented forms indicates a move toward better defense. (Page 635)

fact_aperture_defense.label: Aperture Thickening
fact_aperture_defense.summary: Internal thickening or narrowing of the shell aperture has proportionally increased through time as a defense. (Page 635-636)

taxonomic_survivorship.label: Taxonomic Survivorship
taxonomic_survivorship.summary: The study of the duration of species in the fossil record to understand extinction rates.

van_valen_survivorship.label: Van Valen's Survivorship Curves
van_valen_survivorship.summary: A finding that taxonomic survivorship is approximately log-linear.

fact_log_linear_implication.label: Implication of Log-Linearity
fact_log_linear_implication.summary: Log-linearity means the probability of extinction is independent of the age of the species; species do not evolve to be better at avoiding extinction over time. (Page 637-638)

red_queen_hypothesis.label: Red Queen Hypothesis
red_queen_hypothesis.summary: The theory that species must constantly evolve adaptive improvements just to maintain their relative fitness against evolving competitors/parasites.

red_queen_dynamics.label: Red Queen Dynamics
red_queen_dynamics.summary: A dynamic equilibrium where adaptive improvement is always possible and necessary to avoid extinction.

fact_environmental_deterioration.label: Relative Environmental Deterioration
fact_environmental_deterioration.summary: In the Red Queen mode, a species' environment deteriorates as its competitors evolve new adaptations, leading to a constant probability of extinction. (Page 639)

fact_zero_sum_resources.label: Zero-Sum Resource Competition
fact_zero_sum_resources.summary: Van Valen reasoned that because total resources are approximately constant, one species' adaptive improvement necessarily decreases resources for others, maintaining constant selection pressure. (Page 639)

adaptive_radiation.label: Adaptive Radiation
adaptive_radiation.summary: The rapid diversification of a small number of ancestral species into a larger number of descendant species occupying diverse ecological niches.

radiation_causes.label: Causes of Adaptive Radiation
radiation_causes.summary: Circumstances that trigger rapid diversification of taxa.

fact_colonization_radiation.label: Colonization of New Areas
fact_colonization_radiation.summary: Radiation occurs when species colonize areas with unexploited resources and no competitors (e.g., Galápagos finches). (Page 644-645)

fact_extinction_radiation.label: Extinction of Competitors
fact_extinction_radiation.summary: Vacated ecological space allows surviving groups to radiate (e.g., mammals after the dinosaur extinction). (Page 645)

fact_replacement_radiation.label: Replacement of Competitors
fact_replacement_radiation.summary: A taxon radiates if it is adaptively superior to its competitors, driving them extinct. (Page 645)

fact_breakthrough_radiation.label: Adaptive Breakthroughs
fact_breakthrough_radiation.summary: The evolution of a new adaptation allows a taxon to exploit previously unreachable resources (e.g., colonization of land). (Page 645)

extinction_dynamics.label: Extinction Dynamics
extinction_dynamics.summary: The study of the causes, patterns, and consequences of species extinction in the fossil record.

pseudoextinction.label: Pseudoextinction
pseudoextinction.summary: The appearance of extinction due to artifacts in evidence rather than the death of a lineage.

fact_taxonomic_pseudo.label: Taxonomic Name Change
fact_taxonomic_pseudo.summary: A continuous lineage is subdivided into different species by taxonomists, making the earlier species appear extinct. (Page 647)

fact_phenetic_pseudo.label: Phenetic Higher Taxon Extinction
fact_phenetic_pseudo.summary: A higher taxon (e.g., family) defined phenetically disappears even though some descendants persist (e.g., dinosaurs and birds). (Page 647)

fact_lazarus_taxa.label: Lazarus Taxa
fact_lazarus_taxa.summary: Lineages that disappear from the fossil record temporarily due to lack of sedimentary deposition and then reappear. (Page 647)

mass_extinction.label: Mass Extinction
mass_extinction.summary: Periods of exceptionally high extinction rates across diverse taxa.

big_five_extinctions.label: The Big Five Extinctions
big_five_extinctions.summary: The five largest mass extinction events in Earth's history.

fact_big_five_list.label: Major Extinction Events
fact_big_five_list.summary: Late Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian (largest), Late Triassic, and End-Cretaceous. (Page 649)

kt_boundary_extinction.label: K-T Boundary Extinction
kt_boundary_extinction.summary: The mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous, characterized by the demise of dinosaurs and ammonites.

asteroid_impact_theory.label: Asteroid Impact Theory
asteroid_impact_theory.summary: The hypothesis that a large asteroid collision caused the K-T mass extinction.

fact_iridium_anomaly.label: Iridium Anomaly
fact_iridium_anomaly.summary: Exceptionally high concentrations of iridium at the K-T boundary, an element rare on Earth but common in extraterrestrial objects. (Page 651)

fact_chicxulub_crater.label: Chicxulub Crater
fact_chicxulub_crater.summary: A large impact structure (approx. 180 km diameter) off the Yucatan coast of Mexico dating to the K-T boundary. (Page 652)

fact_impact_mechanisms.label: Impact Destructive Effects
fact_impact_mechanisms.summary: Global dust clouds blocking sunlight, global warming, acid rain, and extreme volcanism. (Page 652)

extinction_causes.label: General Causes of Extinction
extinction_causes.summary: A variety of biological and physical factors that drive species to extinction.

fact_sea_level_extinction.label: Sea Level Changes
fact_sea_level_extinction.summary: Falls in sea level reduce marine habitat, increasing extinction rates. (Page 654-655)

fact_volcanism_extinction.label: Volcanic Eruptions
fact_volcanism_extinction.summary: Large-scale flood-basalt volcanism is associated with several major mass extinctions. (Page 655)

fact_tectonic_extinction.label: Plate Tectonics
fact_tectonic_extinction.summary: Changes in the shape and position of continents influence climate and sea levels, contributing to extinction. (Page 655)

extinction_probability_models.label: Extinction Probability Models
extinction_probability_models.summary: Mathematical models used to explain the distribution of extinction rates.

poisson_distribution_model.label: Poisson Distribution Model
poisson_distribution_model.summary: Suggests extinction probability is constant and variation in rates is due to random chance. (Page 656)

power_law_fractal_model.label: Power Law / Fractal Model
power_law_fractal_model.summary: Suggests extinction rates show self-similarity (fractal pattern), meaning mass extinctions are not distinct events but part of a continuum. (Page 656-657)

fact_ecosystem_connectedness.label: Ecosystem Interdependence Model
fact_ecosystem_connectedness.summary: Extinction rates are fractal because species are interdependent; the loss of one key species can trigger a cascade of extinctions depending on current interconnectivity. (Page 657)

sedimentary_artifact_model.label: Sedimentary Artifact Model
sedimentary_artifact_model.summary: The theory that observed changes in extinction rates are primarily artifacts of the quality and amount of preserved sedimentary rock. (Page 658-660)

fact_peters_foote_finding.label: Peters & Foote Analysis
fact_peters_foote_finding.summary: Much of the variation in extinction rates correlates with the amount of exposed marine sedimentary rock. (Page 660)

species_selection.label: Species Selection
species_selection.summary: A higher-level evolutionary process where certain types of species proliferate because they have lower extinction or higher speciation rates.

developmental_mode_selection.label: Developmental Mode Selection in Snails
developmental_mode_selection.summary: How larval development types influence a species' likelihood of survival and diversification.

planktonic_development.label: Planktonic Development
planktonic_development.summary: Development involving a larval stage that disperses in open water.

fact_planktonic_extinction.label: Planktonic Extinction Rates
fact_planktonic_extinction.summary: Associated with lower extinction rates and wider geographic ranges, reducing vulnerability to local events. (Page 662)

fact_planktonic_speciation.label: Planktonic Speciation Rates
fact_planktonic_speciation.summary: Likely have lower speciation rates because high gene flow prevents allopatric speciation. (Page 663)

direct_development.label: Direct Development
direct_development.summary: Development where offspring grow near or inside the parent without a dispersing larval stage.

fact_direct_extinction.label: Direct Development Extinction Rates
fact_direct_extinction.summary: Associated with higher extinction rates and narrower geographic ranges. (Page 662)

fact_direct_speciation.label: Direct Development Speciation Rates
fact_direct_speciation.summary: Associated with higher speciation rates because localized populations are more prone to allopatric speciation. (Page 663)

niche_persistence.label: Niche Persistence
niche_persistence.summary: The theory that extinction rates are determined by the longevity of the ecological niche occupied by a species.

stickleback_case_study.label: Stickleback Niche Study
stickleback_case_study.summary: Comparing coastal vs. freshwater populations of the three-spined stickleback.

fact_coastal_niche_persistence.label: Coastal vs Freshwater Niche
fact_coastal_niche_persistence.summary: Coastal niches are more persistent, resulting in lower extinction rates for those populations compared to freshwater populations, where habitats are more volatile. (Page 664-665)

fact_species_selection_vs_natural.label: Species Selection vs Natural Selection
fact_species_selection_vs_natural.summary: Species selection operates on the frequency of species types over time, which can lead to macroevolutionary trends that are not driven by natural selection within individual lineages. (Page 665-666)

taxonomic_replacement.label: Taxonomic Replacement
taxonomic_replacement.summary: The process where one higher taxonomic group replaces another in an ecological role.

competitive_replacement.label: Competitive Replacement
competitive_replacement.summary: One group outcompetes another, leading to a simultaneous decline of the first and expansion of the second (Double-wedge pattern).

bryozoan_replacement.label: Bryozoan Replacement Study
bryozoan_replacement.summary: The replacement of Cyclostomata by Cheilostomata.

fact_bryozoan_overgrowth.label: Competitive Overgrowth
fact_bryozoan_overgrowth.summary: Evidence of competition seen in fossils where Cheilostomes grew over and killed Cyclostomes. (Page 671)

independent_replacement.label: Independent Replacement
independent_replacement.summary: One group goes extinct due to external factors (environmental change or mass extinction) and is later replaced by another group that radiates into the vacant space.

dinosaur_mammal_replacement.label: Dinosaur-Mammal Replacement
dinosaur_mammal_replacement.summary: The classic example of independent replacement where mammals radiated after the K-T extinction.

fact_fossil_mammal_dates.label: Fossil Record of Mammals
fact_fossil_mammal_dates.summary: Fossils suggest modern mammal orders appeared in the early Tertiary, after dinosaurs went extinct. (Page 671-672)

fact_molecular_mammal_dates.label: Molecular Clock for Mammals
fact_molecular_mammal_dates.summary: Molecular evidence suggests modern mammal orders originated 90-100 million years ago, meaning they coexisted with dinosaurs for millions of years. (Page 672)

mammal_origins.label: Origins of Modern Mammal Orders
mammal_origins.summary: The investigation into when modern mammal orders originated, highlighting the tension between fossil evidence and molecular dating.

dating_discrepancy.label: Dating Discrepancy
dating_discrepancy.summary: The conflict between traditional fossil appearance dates and molecular clock estimates for mammal origins.

fact_foote_date.label: Foote et al. (1999) Estimate
fact_foote_date.summary: Concluded that mammal orders unlikely originated much before 55 million years ago based on fossil appearance. (p. 674)

fact_molecular_date.label: Molecular Clock Estimate
fact_molecular_date.summary: Suggests the origin of Primata occurred around 90 million years ago. (p. 674)

fossil_record_incompleteness.label: Fossil Record Incompleteness
fossil_record_incompleteness.summary: The phenomenon where the fossil record fails to capture the true age of a taxon due to sampling gaps.

incompleteness_types.label: Types of Incompleteness
incompleteness_types.summary: The two primary ways the fossil record is incomplete: (1) Incompleteness within observed lineages, and (2) Missing whole lineages. (p. 674)

fact_tavare_adjustment.label: Tavaré et al. (2002) Adjustment
fact_tavare_adjustment.summary: Recalculated the origin of Primata to 81 million years ago by accounting for both within-lineage and whole-lineage incompleteness. (p. 674)

eutherian_evidence.label: Eutherian Fossil Evidence
eutherian_evidence.summary: Discoveries of earlier fossils that push back the timeline of placental mammal origins.

fact_ji_fossil.label: Ji et al. (2002) Discovery
fact_ji_fossil.summary: Reported a 125 million-year-old eutherian fossil from the Yixian formation in China, pushing the record back by 50 million years. (p. 674)

mammal_radiation_reconciliation.label: Reconciliation of Evidence
mammal_radiation_reconciliation.summary: The theory that reconciles the molecular date (origin) with the fossil date (proliferation).

fact_lay_low_hypothesis.label: The 'Lay Low' Hypothesis
fact_lay_low_hypothesis.summary: Suggests mammals existed for 40 million years in low numbers, only radiating into dinosaurian niches after the end-Cretaceous extinction. (p. 674)

evolutionary_replacement.label: Evolutionary Replacement
evolutionary_replacement.summary: The process where one taxon replaces another in the ecosystem.

fact_replacement_evidence.label: Evidence for Replacement
fact_replacement_evidence.summary: Evidence is derived from the time course of the rise/fall of taxa and direct competition (e.g., bryozoan overgrowth). (p. 674)

species_diversity_models.label: Global Species Diversity Models
species_diversity_models.summary: Differing mathematical models used to describe how the total number of species on Earth has changed since the Cambrian.

logistic_model.label: Logistic Model (Sepkoski)
logistic_model.summary: Diversity increase characterized by an initial exponential rise followed by a plateau as resource space is filled.

fact_sepkoski_faunas.label: Sepkoski's Three Faunas
fact_sepkoski_faunas.summary: Distinguishes between the Cambrian, Paleozoic, and Modern faunas. (p. 675)

fact_paleozoic_plateau.label: The Paleozoic Plateau
fact_paleozoic_plateau.summary: A period of constant diversity in the Paleozoic, potentially broken by the Permian mass extinction, which allowed the 'Modern' fauna to diversify further. (p. 675)

exponential_model.label: Exponential Model (Benton)
exponential_model.summary: Suggests a steady, noisy exponential increase in diversity across all life forms, including land organisms.

fact_benton_implications.label: Benton's Model Implications
fact_benton_implications.summary: Implies that niches are persistently subdivided into finer units and that mass extinctions were less critical for overall diversity. (p. 675)

plateau_model.label: Prolonged Plateau Model
plateau_model.summary: Recent statistical corrections suggesting diversity remained relatively constant from the Paleozoic to the Oligocene.

fact_ucsb_database.label: UCSB Database Results
fact_ucsb_database.summary: Preliminary findings using statistical corrections for bias suggest diversity has a tighter limit than previously suspected. (p. 676)

paleontological_bias.label: Paleontological Data Biases
paleontological_bias.summary: Factors that distort the observed diversity in the fossil record.

bias_types.label: Primary Biases
bias_types.summary: 1. Amount of rock preserved from different time intervals. 2. Amount of preserved rock actually studied. 3. Geographic and Taxonomic biases. (p. 676)

fact_bryozoan_bias.label: Tropical Bryozoan Bias
fact_bryozoan_bias.summary: Jackson & Johnson (2001) found Pliocene diversity was underestimated because paleontologists studied Europe/North America, which were no longer tropical. (p. 676)

mass_extinction_theory.label: Phases of Mass Extinction Theory
mass_extinction_theory.summary: The evolution of scientific thought regarding the reality and significance of mass extinctions.

phase_1.label: Phase 1: Discovery
phase_1.summary: Early 19th century discovery of main faunal transitions and stages of the fossil record. (p. 677)

phase_2.label: Phase 2: Environmentalism
phase_2.summary: Lyell and Darwin doubted catastrophes, attributing faunal changes to environmental and sedimentary conditions. (p. 677)

phase_3.label: Phase 3: Catastrophism
phase_3.summary: The 1980s view that mass extinctions were real, distinct events (e.g., asteroid impact) that cleared space for new radiations. (p. 677)

fact_asteroid_theory.label: Asteroid Impact Theory
fact_asteroid_theory.summary: Alvarez et al. found iridium anomalies at the K-T boundary, suggesting a 12km asteroid caused the extinction. (p. 678)

phase_4.label: Phase 4: Unified/Fractal View
phase_4.summary: Recent research suggests extinction rates are 'fractal', meaning the same causes operate at all times, and 'mass' extinctions may be statistical artifacts. (p. 677)

macroevolutionary_mechanisms.label: General Macroevolutionary Mechanisms
macroevolutionary_mechanisms.summary: The overarching processes that drive large-scale evolutionary change.

radiation_triggers.label: Triggers of Radiation
radiation_triggers.summary: 1. Colonization of new areas. 2. Extinction of competitors. 3. Adaptive breakthroughs. (p. 678)

extinction_power_law.label: Power Law of Extinction
extinction_power_law.summary: The theory that the distribution of extinction rates fits a power law, suggesting no distinct 'cause' for mass extinctions vs. background extinctions. (p. 678)

foundations.label: Foundations of Evolution
foundations.summary: Basic definitions and the fundamental logic of evolutionary change.

def_evolution.label: Definition of Evolution
def_evolution.summary: The process of biological change over generations.

fact_evo_definition.label: Evolution Definition
fact_evo_definition.summary: Evolution is defined as a change in the gene pool of a population over time. (Intro p.1)

fact_gene_definition.label: Gene Definition
fact_gene_definition.summary: A gene is a hereditary unit that can be passed on unaltered for many generations. (Intro p.1)

def_gene_pool.label: Definition of Gene Pool
def_gene_pool.summary: The collective genetic information of a population.

fact_gene_pool_definition.label: Gene Pool Definition
fact_gene_pool_definition.summary: The gene pool is the set of all genes in a species or population. (Intro p.1)

evo_scales.label: Scales of Evolution
evo_scales.summary: Categorization of evolutionary change based on magnitude and time.

microevolution.label: Microevolution
microevolution.summary: Small-scale evolutionary changes within a population.

fact_micro_def.label: Microevolution Definition
fact_micro_def.summary: Microevolution consists of small changes in gene frequencies within a population over a short period. (Intro p.1)

fact_biston_example.label: Biston betularia Case Study
fact_biston_example.summary: Observation of industrial melanism where dark-colored moths increased from <2% to 95% in industrialized areas due to bird predation on lighter moths against sooty backgrounds. (Intro p.1)

fact_macro_def.label: Macroevolution Definition
fact_macro_def.summary: Macroevolution involves larger changes, such as the formation of new species. (Intro p.1)

hardy_weinberg.label: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
hardy_weinberg.summary: A principle stating that genetic variation in a population will remain constant from one generation to the next in the absence of disturbing factors.

fact_hw_assumptions.label: HW Assumptions
fact_hw_assumptions.summary: Assumes no mutation, no migration, large population size, random mating, and no selection. (Index p.741)

bottleneck_effect.label: Bottleneck Effect
bottleneck_effect.summary: Sharp reduction in the size of a population due to environmental events, reducing genetic diversity. (Index p.749)

gene_flow.label: Gene Flow
gene_flow.summary: The transfer of genetic material from one population to another.

fact_migration_effect.label: Migration and Gene Flow
fact_migration_effect.summary: Migration can unify gene frequencies between populations or maintain genetic differences. (Index p.743)

speciation.label: Speciation
speciation.summary: The process by which new biological species arise.

fact_allopatric_def.label: Allopatric Process
fact_allopatric_def.summary: Occurs via geographic separation and population divergence. (Index p.736)

fact_sympatric_def.label: Sympatric Process
fact_sympatric_def.summary: Speciation occurring without geographic isolation. (Index p.749)

fact_parapatric_def.label: Parapatric Process
fact_parapatric_def.summary: Involves hybrid zones and stepped clines. (Index p.747)

fact_prezygotic_mechanisms.label: Prezygotic Barriers
fact_prezygotic_mechanisms.summary: Includes behavioral (courtship), temporal, and mechanical isolation. (Index p.747)

fact_postzygotic_mechanisms.label: Postzygotic Barriers
fact_postzygotic_mechanisms.summary: Includes hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown. (Index p.743)

fact_kimura_neutral.label: Kimura's Contribution
fact_kimura_neutral.summary: Proposed by Motoo Kimura, stating that most mutations are neutral rather than adaptive. (Index p.745)

fact_clock_mechanism.label: Clock Mechanism
fact_clock_mechanism.summary: Based on the relatively constant rate of amino acid or nucleotide substitutions over time. (Index p.744)

fact_synonymous_def.label: Synonymous Substitution
fact_synonymous_def.summary: A change in DNA that does not change the amino acid sequence of the protein. (Index p.750)

fact_nonsynonymous_def.label: Non-synonymous Substitution
fact_nonsynonymous_def.summary: A change in DNA that alters the amino acid sequence. (Index p.750)

phylogenetics.label: Phylogenetics and Systematics
phylogenetics.summary: The study of evolutionary relationships among biological entities.

fact_homology_def.label: Homology Definition
fact_homology_def.summary: Ancestral similarity shared by species due to common descent. (Index p.736)

homoplasy_concept.label: Homoplasy
homoplasy_concept.summary: Similarity not due to common ancestry, but rather convergent evolution.

fact_homoplasy_def.label: Homoplasy Definition
fact_homoplasy_def.summary: Independent evolution of similar features in different lineages. (Index p.741)

cladistics.label: Cladistics
cladistics.summary: A method of classifying animals and plants according to the proportion of measurable characteristics that they have in common.

rooted_trees.label: Rooted Trees
rooted_trees.summary: Trees that show the direction of time from a common ancestor. (Index p.736)

unrooted_trees.label: Unrooted Trees
unrooted_trees.summary: Trees that show relationships but not the ancestral root. (Index p.736)

fact_radiation_def.label: Adaptive Radiation Process
fact_radiation_def.summary: Occurs when a lineage rapidly diversifies to fill many ecological niches, e.g., Darwin's finches. (Index p.736)

fact_kt_boundary.label: K-T Boundary
fact_kt_boundary.summary: The Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary event involving an asteroid collision and mass extinction. (Index p.736, 743)

tempo_and_mode.label: Tempo and Mode
tempo_and_mode.summary: The rate and pattern of evolutionary change.

fact_hox_function.label: Hox Function
fact_hox_function.summary: Hox genes determine the identity of segments along the head-tail axis. (Index p.739, 741)

heterochrony.label: Heterochrony
heterochrony.summary: A change in the timing or rate of developmental events.

paedomorphosis.label: Paedomorphosis
paedomorphosis.summary: Retention of juvenile characteristics in the adult. (Index p.747)

progenesis.label: Progenesis
progenesis.summary: Early sexual maturation resulting in a juvenile adult form. (Index p.747)

female_choice.label: Female Choice
female_choice.summary: Intersexual selection where females choose mates based on specific traits. (Index p.749)

runaway_process.label: Fisherian Runaway
runaway_process.summary: A positive feedback loop where a trait and the preference for that trait evolve together. (Index p.749)

fundamental_definitions.label: Fundamental Definitions and Misconceptions
fundamental_definitions.summary: Clarification of terminology and the distinction between evolution and related biological processes.

evolution_def.label: Evolution
evolution_def.summary: Descent with modification; the historical occurrence of change in species over time.

abiogenesis_def.label: Abiogenesis
abiogenesis_def.summary: The theory of how the first living organisms appeared from non-living matter, often incorrectly conflated with evolution. [p2]

phenotype_concept.label: Phenotype
phenotype_concept.summary: The morphological, physiological, biochemical, behavioral, and other properties exhibited by a living organism, determined by genes and environment. [p2]

phenotype_heritability.label: Phenotypic Heritability
phenotype_heritability.summary: Phenotypic changes induced solely by environment (e.g., humans getting larger due to better diet) are not heritable and thus do not count as evolution. [p2]

evolution_misconceptions.label: Common Misconceptions
evolution_misconceptions.summary: Correcting non-scientific views of evolutionary processes.

evolution_not_progress.label: Evolution is Not Progress
evolution_not_progress.summary: Populations adapt to current surroundings; they do not necessarily become 'better' in an absolute sense. Success is contingent on contemporaries. [p2]

organism_environmental_interaction.label: Niche Construction
organism_environmental_interaction.summary: Organisms are not passive; they modify their environment (e.g., beavers building dams, plants producing oxygen) to suit them. [p2]

allele_def.label: Allele
allele_def.summary: An alternate version of a gene created by mutation. [p2]

locus_def.label: Locus
locus_def.summary: The specific location of a gene on a chromosome. [p2]

diploid_def.label: Diploid
diploid_def.summary: Organisms containing two alleles for every gene at every locus, one from each parent. [p2]

homozygous_def.label: Homozygous
homozygous_def.summary: An individual with two identical alleles at a specific locus. [p2]

heterozygous_def.label: Heterozygous
heterozygous_def.summary: An individual with two different alleles at a specific locus. [p2]

polymorphism_stats.label: Polymorphism Levels
polymorphism_stats.summary: The percentage of loci with more than one allele in a population.

poly_plants.label: Plant Polymorphism
poly_plants.summary: 45% of loci have >1 allele; given plants are heterozygous at ~15% of loci. [p2]

ld_formula.label: LD Calculation
ld_formula.summary: D = f(A1B1) * f(A2B2) - f(A1B2) * f(A2B1), where f(X) is frequency in population. D ranges from -1/4 to 1/4. [p2]

hw_formula.label: HW Formula
hw_formula.summary: For alleles A (p) and a (q), genotypes AA, Aa, and aa occur at frequencies p^2, 2pq, and q^2 respectively. [p2]

hw_deviation.label: HW Deviation
hw_deviation.summary: Non-random mating (e.g., assortative mating by race in humans) results in fewer heterozygotes than predicted. [p2]

evolutionary_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Evolution
evolutionary_mechanisms.summary: Processes that either decrease or increase genetic variation within a lineage.

mechanisms_decrease.label: Mechanisms that Decrease Genetic Variation
mechanisms_decrease.summary: Processes that remove alleles from the gene pool.

balancing_selection.label: Balancing Selection
balancing_selection.summary: Selection that maintains genetic variation by favoring heterozygotes (e.g., sickle-cell allele providing malaria resistance). [p3]

inclusive_fitness.label: Inclusive Fitness
inclusive_fitness.summary: The sum of direct fitness (own offspring) and indirect fitness (helping relatives reproduce). Explains altruistic-appearing behaviors. [p4]

reciprocal_altruism.label: Reciprocal Altruism
reciprocal_altruism.summary: Mutually beneficial pacts where organisms help each other, such as blood sharing in vampire bats. [p3]

adaptive_landscape.label: Adaptive Landscape (Sewall Wright)
adaptive_landscape.summary: A model where populations move toward local optima; transitions to global optima may be hindered by less adaptive intermediate states. [p5]

exaptation_concept.label: Adaptation vs. Exaptation
exaptation_concept.summary: Adaptation is a trait evolved for its current utility; exaptation is a trait evolved for one purpose but co-opted for another (e.g., penguin wings). [p5]

good_genes_model.label: Good Genes Model
good_genes_model.summary: Displays (e.g., red color in sticklebacks) signal viability or lack of parasites to mates. [p6]

runaway_selection.label: Runaway Sexual Selection (Fisher)
runaway_selection.summary: A positive feedback loop where a female preference for a trait and the trait itself are genetically linked, driving the trait to extreme lengths. [p6]

mechanisms_increase.label: Mechanisms that Increase Genetic Variation
mechanisms_increase.summary: Processes that introduce new alleles or combinations into the gene pool.

mutation_concept.label: Mutation
mutation_concept.summary: A change in a gene's DNA sequence (point mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, duplications). [p7]

mutation_fitness_impact.label: Fitness Impact of Mutations
mutation_fitness_impact.summary: Most mutations are neutral; of those with phenotypic effects, most are deleterious; a very small percentage are beneficial. [p7]

recombination_concept.label: Recombination
recombination_concept.summary: Gene shuffling during meiosis where homologous chromosomes break and rejoin, creating new allele combinations. [p9]

gene_flow_concept.label: Gene Flow
gene_flow_concept.summary: The transfer of alleles from one population to another via migration or horizontal transfer (e.g., P elements in Drosophila via mites). [p9]

common_descent.label: Common Descent
common_descent.summary: The principle that all species descend from a common ancestor, forming a branching tree of life. [p12]

biochemical_evidence.label: Biochemical Evidence
biochemical_evidence.summary: Universal genetic code; similarity in DNA sequences; existence of pseudogenes and introns. [p13]

codon_def.label: Codon
codon_def.summary: A block of three nucleotides designating a specific amino acid. [p13]

silent_replacement_sites.label: Silent vs Replacement Sites
silent_replacement_sites.summary: Silent sites change DNA without changing amino acids (evolve faster); replacement sites change amino acids (constrained by selection). [p13]

developmental_evidence.label: Developmental Evidence
developmental_evidence.summary: Similar developmental pathways in related organisms; vestigial structures (e.g., pelvic bones in snakes). [p14]

biogeography_evidence.label: Biogeographical Evidence
biogeography_evidence.summary: Distribution of species relative to their origin and dispersal (e.g., marsupials in Australia). [p14]

morphology_evidence.label: Morphological Evidence
morphology_evidence.summary: Homologous structures (e.g., vertebrate limb bones) modified for different uses. [p14]

speciation_concept.label: Speciation
speciation_concept.summary: The process of a single species becoming two or more species.

extinction_concept.label: Extinction
extinction_concept.summary: The removal of a species from the gene pool.

ordinary_extinction.label: Ordinary Extinction
ordinary_extinction.summary: Loss of species due to competitive exclusion or habitat disappearance. [p16]

history_of_life.label: History of Life
history_of_life.summary: The chronological sequence of biological evolution on Earth.

rna_world.label: RNA World Hypothesis
rna_world.summary: Hypothesis that the first replicating molecules were RNA due to its catalytic capabilities (polymerases). [p18]

early_life_lineages.label: Three Major Lineages
early_life_lineages.summary: Prokaryotes (bacteria), Archaebacteria, and Eukaryotes. Eukaryotes and Archaebacteria are most closely related. [p18]

photosynthesis_evolution.label: Evolution of Photosynthesis
photosynthesis_evolution.summary: PSI evolved first (H2S based); PSII evolved later, enabling oxygenic photosynthesis (H2O based), leading to the 'oxygen holocaust'. [p18]

endosymbiosis_theory.label: Endosymbiosis Theory (Margulis)
endosymbiosis_theory.summary: Mitochondria and Chloroplasts originated as free-living bacteria engulfed by ur-eukaryotes. [p18]

vertebrate_land_invasion.label: Vertebrate Land Invasion
vertebrate_land_invasion.summary: Movement of vertebrates to land by the Devonian period (~380mya), starting with amphibians like Ichthyostega. [p19]

theory_development.label: Development of Evolutionary Theory
theory_development.summary: The historical progression of scientific models of evolution.

darwinism.label: Darwinian Theory
darwinism.summary: Proposed common descent and natural selection as the mechanism. [p11]

fishers_theorem.label: Fisher's Fundamental Theorem
fishers_theorem.summary: The rate of adaptive change is proportional to the amount of genetic variation present. [p11]

wright_adaptive_landscape.label: Wright's Contribution
wright_adaptive_landscape.summary: Emphasized genetic drift in subpopulations and the adaptive landscape model. [p11]

scientific_standing.label: Scientific Standing and Critics
scientific_standing.summary: The consensus of the scientific community versus non-scientific objections.

scientific_consensus.label: Scientific Consensus
scientific_consensus.summary: Evolution and common descent are considered fact; debates exist only on the specific mechanisms. [p21]

creationism_critique.label: Critique of Scientific Creationism
creationism_critique.summary: Creationism is not a scientific theory as it lacks testable hypotheses, peer-reviewed data, and relies on religious dogma. [p21]

life_hierarchy.label: Hierarchical Organization of Life
life_hierarchy.summary: The nested structure of biological entities where evolutionary change can occur at multiple levels.

hierarchy_levels.label: Biological Levels
hierarchy_levels.summary: The sequential organization from genes to clades.
hierarchy_levels.details: Genes are located within individuals, individuals within populations, populations within species, and species within clades (ancestral species and all descendants). (p. 5)

multi_level_selection.label: Multi-level Selection
multi_level_selection.summary: The principle that selection can operate on entities other than the individual organism.
multi_level_selection.details: Selection can occur at the level of genes (e.g., noncoding DNA multiplication) or entire species (e.g., attributes making rodents more prone to speciate). (p. 5)

phenotypic_evolution.label: Phenotypic Evolution
phenotypic_evolution.summary: Evolutionary change resulting from modifications in the developmental process.

developmental_process.label: Developmental Process
developmental_process.summary: The transformation of a single-celled fertilized egg into an adult organism.
developmental_process.details: Phenotypes cannot be understood by DNA sequences alone; they require molecular and embryological knowledge of developmental constraints. (p. 5)

tree_thinking.label: Tree-Thinking Approach
tree_thinking.summary: Using the pattern of descent and relationship among species to guide macroevolutionary and population-level studies.
tree_thinking.details: Phylogenetic information is critical for interpreting all aspects of evolution above the population level. (p. 5)

phenotypic_plasticity.label: Phenotypic Plasticity
phenotypic_plasticity.summary: The ability of a single genotype to produce different phenotypes when exposed to different environments.

plasticity_adaptation.label: Adaptive Plasticity
plasticity_adaptation.summary: The evolution of genotypes that produce appropriate phenotypes depending on environmental circumstances.
plasticity_adaptation.details: The degree of plasticity itself can evolve if it affects the number of surviving offspring. (p. 6)

plasticity_costs.label: Costs of Plasticity
plasticity_costs.summary: The theoretical trade-offs that prevent populations from becoming infinitely malleable.
plasticity_costs.details: Adaptation often occurs via genetic differentiation rather than plasticity due to associated costs, though these are difficult to demonstrate. (p. 6)

behavioral_plasticity.label: Behavioral Plasticity and Culture
behavioral_plasticity.summary: Extreme manifestations of plasticity where learned behaviors are transmitted across generations.
behavioral_plasticity.details: Traditions or culture (e.g., tool use in chimps, cattle tending in humans) can set the stage for later genetic divergence. (p. 6)

mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Evolutionary Change
mechanisms.summary: The biological and mathematical processes that drive genetic and phenotypic divergence.

malthusian_struggle.label: Malthusian Struggle for Existence
malthusian_struggle.summary: The competition for resources arising because populations grow exponentially while food supplies grow arithmetically.
malthusian_struggle.details: This creates a struggle where individuals with slight advantages reproduce more successfully. (p. 16)

selective_efficacy.label: Efficacy of Selection
selective_efficacy.summary: The power of selection to drive substantial divergence over short or long periods.
selective_efficacy.details: Selection can be rapid (e.g., Galapagos finches, Trinidad guppies) or slow, contrary to Darwin's original expectation of weak selection. (p. 8)

drift_process.label: Process of Genetic Drift
drift_process.summary: Random mutations becoming established in nonfunctioning DNA or gene frequencies becoming fixed by chance matings.
drift_process.details: Nonfunctioning DNA tends to evolve differences through drift because natural selection does not remove mutations. (p. 5)

mutation.label: Mutation
mutation.summary: Changes in the DNA sequence that provide the raw material for evolution.
mutation.details: Includes base-pair substitutions and chromosomal rearrangements. (p. 21)

kimura_hypothesis.label: Kimura's Hypothesis
kimura_hypothesis.summary: The proposal that most DNA mutations remain in the genome because they are not eliminated by natural selection.
kimura_hypothesis.details: This is an extension of genetic drift and serves as a null hypothesis for testing selective value. (p. 26)

history.label: History of Evolutionary Thought
history.summary: The intellectual progression from ancient philosophies to modern molecular synthesis.

ancient_world.label: Ancient World Philosophies
ancient_world.summary: Early Greek and Roman views on the nature of biological diversity.

epicureanism.label: Epicureanism
epicureanism.summary: Materialist philosophy emphasizing random atomic motion and inevitable change.
epicureanism.details: Lucretius argued against supernatural explanations, viewing nature as purposeless and in flux. (p. 10)

platonic_idealism.label: Platonic Idealism
platonic_idealism.summary: The view that the universe consists of immutable, perfect ideal forms.
platonic_idealism.details: Focused on abstract categories (e.g., 'catness') rather than empirical observation. (p. 10)

aristotelian_thought.label: Aristotelian Thought
aristotelian_thought.summary: A blend of empirical observation with teleological (goal-oriented) thinking.
aristotelian_thought.details: Distinguished between efficient causes (immediate factors) and final causes (long-range purpose). (p. 11)

pre_darwinian.label: Pre-Darwinian Transmutation
pre_darwinian.summary: 18th and early 19th century ideas regarding the change of species.

linnaean_system.label: Linnaean Taxonomy
linnaean_system.summary: A hierarchical system of classification and binomial naming.
linnaean_system.details: Organized life from kingdom down to species based on structural characteristics. (p. 12)

cuvier_anatomy.label: Comparative Anatomy (Cuvier)
cuvier_anatomy.summary: The study of structural similarities (homologies) across species.
cuvier_anatomy.details: Cuvier emphasized the correlation of parts, arguing no part could change without affecting others. (p. 13)

uniformitarianism.label: Uniformitarianism
uniformitarianism.summary: The geological theory that earth's features are formed by slow, everyday forces.
uniformitarianism.details: Championed by Hutton and Lyell, opposing Catastrophism. (p. 13)

buffon_degeneration.label: Buffon's Degeneration
buffon_degeneration.summary: The theory that species transform by losing characters from an original ancestor.
buffon_degeneration.details: Proposed as a naturalistic explanation for the variety within groups like Felidae. (p. 14)

darwinian_era.label: The Darwinian Paradigm
darwinian_era.summary: The synthesis of natural selection and common descent established in 1859.

darwin_five_theories.label: Mayr's Five Components of Darwinism
darwin_five_theories.summary: The five theories that constitute the Darwinian paradigm.
darwin_five_theories.details: 1. Evolution as such (descent with modification), 2. Common Descent, 3. Gradualism, 4. Multiplication of Species, 5. Natural Selection. (p. 17)

darwin_influences.label: Darwin's Key Influences
darwin_influences.summary: The sources of Darwin's theoretical breakthroughs.
darwin_influences.details: Lyell (uniformitarianism), Malthus (population competition), and the Beagle voyage observations of island biogeography. (p. 15-16)

evolutionary_synthesis.label: The Evolutionary Synthesis (1930-1960)
evolutionary_synthesis.summary: The union of Darwinian selection with Mendelian genetics, taxonomy, and paleontology.

phase_1_math_pop_gen.label: Mathematical Population Genetics
phase_1_math_pop_gen.summary: The theoretical foundation of the synthesis.
phase_1_math_pop_gen.details: Fisher (selective forces on discrete genes), Wright (shifting balance theory and demes), and Haldane (gene interactions/physiology). (p. 22)

phase_2_natural_pop_gen.label: Genetics of Natural Populations
phase_2_natural_pop_gen.summary: Empirical testing of genetic variation in the wild.
phase_2_natural_pop_gen.details: Chetverikov and Dobzhansky demonstrated high levels of natural variation and balanced polymorphism. (p. 24)

phase_3_macro_evolution.label: Integration of Taxonomy and Paleontology
phase_3_macro_evolution.summary: Expanding the synthesis to macroevolutionary scales.
phase_3_macro_evolution.details: Mayr (biological species concept), Simpson (tempo and mode), and Gould/Eldredge (punctuated equilibrium). (p. 25)

molecular_era.label: The Molecular Biology Era
molecular_era.summary: The use of DNA and protein sequencing to refine evolutionary theory.

comparative_genomics.label: Comparative Genomics
comparative_genomics.summary: Comparing genomes across species to identify functional genes.
comparative_genomics.details: Functional genes diverge more slowly than nonfunctional DNA due to purifying selection. (p. 5)

evidence.label: Evidence for Evolution
evidence.summary: The consilience of inductions from multiple disciplines proving descent with modification.

fossil_progression.label: Geological Progression
fossil_progression.summary: The sequential appearance of life forms from simple to complex.
fossil_progression.details: Starts with stromatolites (3.5 bya), followed by eukaryotes, invertebrates, and eventually vertebrates. (p. 29)

fossil_transitions.label: Transitional Forms
fossil_transitions.summary: Fossils that bridge the gap between major taxa.
fossil_transitions.details: Examples include Archaeopteryx (reptile to bird), Synapsids (reptile to mammal), and Tiktaalik (fish to tetrapod). (p. 30-32)

comparative_biology_evidence.label: Comparative Biology
comparative_biology_evidence.summary: Evidence derived from structural and genetic similarities.

unity_of_type.label: Unity of Type (Homology)
unity_of_type.summary: Structural similarities resulting from shared ancestry rather than functional need.
unity_of_type.details: The 'one bone, two bones, many bones' pattern in tetrapod limbs. (p. 28)

nested_homologies.label: Nested Homologies
nested_homologies.summary: The hierarchical arrangement of shared traits reflecting the branching tree of life.
nested_homologies.details: Anoles possess toepads, hemipenes, amniotic membranes, and four legs, each marking a more inclusive clade. (p. 33-34)

markers_of_history.label: Markers of History (Constraints)
markers_of_history.summary: Biological features that result from 'tinkering' with inherited systems.
markers_of_history.details: Includes embryonic tails in humans, vestigial legs in snakes, and pseudogenes in primate genomes. (p. 34)

oceanic_islands.label: Oceanic Island Biota
oceanic_islands.summary: The specific composition of life on islands never connected to a mainland.
oceanic_islands.details: Inhabited by descendants of successful colonists (e.g., Bermuda) whose nearest relatives are on the closest mainland. (p. 35)

continental_isolation.label: Continental Isolation
continental_isolation.summary: The diversification of species due to long-term geographic separation.
continental_isolation.details: Marsupials in Australia diverged to fill ecological roles due to isolation from placental mammals. (p. 36)

observed_evolution_evidence.label: Evolution in Action
observed_evolution_evidence.summary: Direct observation of evolutionary change on human timescales.
observed_evolution_evidence.details: Examples include industrial melanism in Biston betularia and antibiotic resistance in S. aureus. (p. 37)

human_societal_impact.label: Evolution, Humans, and Society
human_societal_impact.summary: The application of evolutionary principles to human health, forensics, and psychology.

medical_evolution.label: Evolutionary Medicine
medical_evolution.summary: Combatting the adaptation of disease-causing organisms.
medical_evolution.details: Pesticide resistance costs billions in agriculture; viruses like HIV and Influenza adapt to human hosts. (p. 7)

human_evolution_future.label: The Future of Human Evolution
human_evolution_future.summary: The debate on whether human evolution has ceased or continues.
human_evolution_future.details: While medical care reduces some selective pressures, others (e.g., malaria, new diseases) and gene flow continue to drive change. (p. 9)

evolutionary_psychology.label: Evolutionary Psychology
evolutionary_psychology.summary: The study of human behavior as a product of adaptation.
evolutionary_psychology.details: A controversial field examining whether traits like altruism evolved as adaptations to ancestral conditions. (p. 9)

evolutionary_adaptation.label: Evolutionary Adaptation
evolutionary_adaptation.summary: The process by which populations change in response to selective pressures, including drugs and environmental shifts.

rapid_adaptation_hiv.label: Rapid Adaptation in HIV
rapid_adaptation_hiv.summary: Factors contributing to the extreme speed of drug resistance evolution in the human immunodeficiency virus.

hiv_fact_1.label: Drivers of HIV Resistance
hiv_fact_1.summary: High mutation rates, short generation time, large population sizes, and strong selection combined to make HIV adapt rapidly to drugs (p. 38).

hiv_fact_2.label: Drug Mixture Effectiveness
hiv_fact_2.summary: Drug mixtures attacking metabolism in different ways are more effective because the multiple mutations required for resistance to all drugs simultaneously are less likely to occur (p. 38).

geographic_environmental_influence.label: Geographic and Environmental Influence
geographic_environmental_influence.summary: The effect of new environments and natural changes on the evolution of species.

geo_fact_1.label: Introduction to New Areas
geo_fact_1.summary: Species introduced to new geographic areas (e.g., house sparrow Passer domesticus in North America, 1851) undergo divergence in size, shape, coloration, and physiology (p. 38).

geo_fact_2.label: Natural Environmental Tracking
geo_fact_2.summary: Darwin's finches (Geospiza) in the Galapagos demonstrate morphological evolution in response to climatically induced variations in food supply (p. 38).

speciation_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Speciation
speciation_mechanisms.summary: Processes that drive the divergence of lineages.

spec_fact_1.label: Geographic Separation
spec_fact_1.summary: Geographic separation enhances divergence by reducing or eliminating the homogenizing force of gene flow, leading to reproductive incompatibility (p. 38).

spec_fact_2.label: Reproductive Isolation
spec_fact_2.summary: Incipient reproductive isolation can arise under differential adaptation and is enhanced by selection against hybrids (p. 38).

poly_fact_1.label: Spartina anglica Case
poly_fact_1.summary: British salt marsh grass S. anglica (2n=122) evolved from a crossing of S. alterniflora (2n=60) and S. maritima (2n=62), where initial sterile hybrids overcame sterility via chromosome doubling (p. 38).

evolution_theory_fact.label: Evolution as Fact and Theory
evolution_theory_fact.summary: The distinction between the vernacular and scientific meanings of 'theory' and the evidence supporting descent with modification.

theory_fact_1.label: Scientific Theory Definition
theory_fact_1.summary: In science, a theory is not a conjecture but a connected series of propositions supported by and explanatory of many varied lines of evidence (p. 38).

theory_fact_2.label: Evidence for Evolution
theory_fact_2.summary: Evidence includes transitional fossils, the growth of genetics/genomics, and observations of rapid speciation within human lifetimes (p. 39).

genetics_phenotypes.label: From DNA to Phenotypes
genetics_phenotypes.summary: The molecular process by which genetic information is translated into observable characteristics.

molecular_basis.label: Molecular Basis of Phenotype
molecular_basis.summary: The structural and functional components of genetic information.

mol_def_dna.label: DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid)
mol_def_dna.summary: The molecule used to encode genetic information, composed of four nucleotides: Thymine (T), Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), and Guanine (G) (p. 40).

mol_def_gene.label: Gene
mol_def_gene.summary: A region of DNA encoding a functional unit (protein or RNA), consisting of a coding region and regulatory regions (p. 40-41).

mol_def_protein.label: Protein
mol_def_protein.summary: Covalently linked series of amino acids (polypeptides) whose biochemical properties determine biological function. Coded by three-nucleotide sequences called codons (p. 40).

mol_central_dogma.label: The Central Dogma
mol_central_dogma.summary: The general flow of information: DNA -> mRNA (via transcription) -> Protein (via translation) (p. 42).

var_fact_snp.label: Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP)
var_fact_snp.summary: A difference at a single nucleotide site. Nonsynonymous SNPs change the amino acid sequence; synonymous SNPs do not (p. 43).

var_fact_indels.label: Insertions and Deletions
var_fact_indels.summary: Variations caused by the addition or removal of nucleotides, which can remove regulatory elements or parts of coding regions (p. 44).

var_fact_duplication.label: Gene Duplication
var_fact_duplication.summary: The duplication of entire genes, allowing for increased protein production or divergence into new functions (p. 44).

pop_genetics.label: Population Genetics
pop_genetics.summary: The study of genetic distribution and change within populations.

pop_def_allele_freq.label: Allele Frequency
pop_def_allele_freq.summary: The fraction of all alleles at a locus in a population that have a particular sequence (p. 44).

pop_def_hwe.label: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE)
pop_def_hwe.summary: Genotype frequencies predicted from allele frequencies assuming no selection, mutation, migration, a large population, and random mating (p. 44).

pop_def_heterozygosity.label: Heterozygosity
pop_def_heterozygosity.summary: The frequency of individuals at a locus that are heterozygotes (carry two different alleles) (p. 40).

pop_def_ld.label: Linkage Disequilibrium (LD)
pop_def_ld.summary: The association between alleles at different loci where they appear together more or less often than by chance; measured by D (p. 45).

quant_def_variance.label: Phenotypic vs Genetic Variance
quant_def_variance.summary: Phenotypic variance is the total variation in a trait; additive genetic variance is the heritable portion (p. 45).

quant_def_heritability.label: Heritability
quant_def_heritability.summary: The fraction of total phenotypic variance that is attributed to additive genetic variance (p. 45).

quant_def_plasticity.label: Phenotypic Plasticity
quant_def_plasticity.summary: Changes in phenotype resulting from differences in the developmental environment (p. 46).

inheritance_forms.label: Forms of Inheritance
inheritance_forms.summary: The various ways alleles interact to produce phenotypes.

inh_def_epistasis.label: Epistasis
inh_def_epistasis.summary: The interaction between genes where the effect of one allele depends on the presence of alleles at other loci (p. 46).

inh_def_dominance.label: Dominance and Recessiveness
inh_def_dominance.summary: Dominant alleles produce effects regardless of the pair; recessive alleles require a homozygous state; codominant alleles show intermediate effects (p. 46).

inh_def_pleiotropy.label: Pleiotropy
inh_def_pleiotropy.summary: A condition where a single genetic locus has effects on more than one phenotypic trait (p. 40, 46).

phylo_tree_types.label: Phylogenetic Tree Types
phylo_tree_types.summary: Different ways of representing evolutionary relationships.

type_cladogram.label: Cladogram
type_cladogram.summary: An unscaled tree showing relationships (topology) but where branch lengths are meaningless (p. 51).

type_chronogram.label: Chronogram
type_chronogram.summary: A phylogenetic tree with branch lengths scaled to represent absolute time (p. 51).

type_phylogram.label: Phylogram
type_phylogram.summary: A tree in which branch lengths are scaled to the amount of character evolution (p. 51).

phylo_terminology.label: Phylogenetic Terminology
phylo_terminology.summary: Standard terms for describing the components of an evolutionary tree.

term_root.label: Root Node
term_root.summary: The ancestral node at the base of a tree, representing the most recent common ancestor of all included species (p. 51).

term_node.label: Node
term_node.summary: Points where branches split, representing speciation events (p. 53).

term_clade.label: Monophyletic Group (Clade)
term_clade.summary: A group consisting of a common ancestor and all its descendants (p. 51).

phylo_interpretation.label: Tree Interpretation
phylo_interpretation.summary: Guidelines for correctly reading phylogenetic trees and avoiding common fallacies.

int_fact_rotation.label: Branch Rotation
int_fact_rotation.summary: Branches can be rotated around any node without changing the evolutionary relationships; proximity on a page is meaningless (p. 54).

int_fact_basal_fallacy.label: The Basal Fallacy
int_fact_basal_fallacy.summary: The mistaken belief that species in species-poor lineages are 'primitive' or 'ancestral'; all extant species are equally distant from the root (p. 55).

int_fact_cousins.label: Cousin Relationships
int_fact_cousins.summary: Relationships among extant species are cousin relationships, not ancestor-descendant relationships (p. 58).

phylogenetic_inference.label: Phylogenetic Inference
phylogenetic_inference.summary: The methods used to reconstruct phylogenetic trees from data.

inf_parsimony.label: Parsimony Approach
inf_parsimony.summary: Preferring the tree that requires the fewest character state changes (minimum homoplasy) (p. 62).

parsim_fact_long_branch.label: Long-Branch Attraction
parsim_fact_long_branch.summary: Parsimony can be misled by unequal branch lengths, erroneously grouping taxa with high rates of change together (p. 62).

inf_likelihood.label: Maximum Likelihood (ML)
inf_likelihood.summary: Finding the combination of tree topology and branch lengths that maximizes the probability of generating the observed data (p. 63).

ml_fact_robustness.label: ML Robustness
ml_fact_robustness.summary: ML is more resistant to branch length inequality than parsimony, though it is sensitive to model misspecification (p. 64).

inf_distance.label: Distance-Based Approaches
inf_distance.summary: Trees reconstructed based on a matrix of pairwise divergences between tips; computationally fast but loses character-level information (p. 64).

inf_bayesian.label: Bayesian Inference
inf_bayesian.summary: Updating prior probabilities of tree parameters into posterior probabilities using the likelihood function and MCMC algorithms (p. 66).

bay_fact_mcmc.label: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
bay_fact_mcmc.summary: The simulation method used in Bayesian inference to sample from the joint posterior distribution of times, rates, and parameters (p. 66).

clock_def_basic.label: Molecular Clock Hypothesis
clock_def_basic.summary: The observation that DNA or amino acid sequences accumulate changes at a constant rate through time (p. 67).

clock_neutral_theory.label: Neutral Theory Connection
clock_neutral_theory.summary: Proposed by Kimura; suggests that most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of neutral mutations, explaining clocklike behavior (p. 67).

clock_dating_methods.label: Dating Methods
clock_dating_methods.summary: Statistical tests to validate and apply the molecular clock.

date_fact_relative_rate.label: Relative Rate Test
date_fact_relative_rate.summary: Compares rates of evolution in two species using an out-group to see if distances from the common ancestor are equal (p. 69).

date_fact_relaxed_clock.label: Relaxed Clock Models
date_fact_relaxed_clock.summary: Models that allow substitution rates to vary across lineages, such as the Lognormal drift/Brownian motion model in Bayesian analysis (p. 73).

clock_calibration.label: Fossil Calibrations
clock_calibration.summary: Using the fossil record to assign ages to nodes in a phylogenetic tree.

cal_fact_hard_bounds.label: Hard Bounds
cal_fact_hard_bounds.summary: Priors that assign zero probability to ages outside a specified interval (p. 73).

cal_fact_soft_bounds.label: Soft Bounds
cal_fact_soft_bounds.summary: Flexible distributions (e.g., Gamma) that assign low but non-zero probabilities outside the primary interval to account for uncertainty (p. 73).

molecular_dating.label: Molecular Dating and Bayesian Statistics
molecular_dating.summary: The use of statistical frameworks to estimate divergence times and evolutionary rates of lineages.

bayesian_framework.label: Bayesian Framework in Dating
bayesian_framework.summary: The only current framework capable of integrating information and uncertainties from diverse sources to estimate nodal ages.

bayesian_clock_violation.label: Molecular Clock Violation
bayesian_clock_violation.summary: Bayesian statistics deal with clock violations through the use of prior models of evolutionary rate change (p. 74).

bayesian_fossil_calibration.label: Fossil Calibration
bayesian_fossil_calibration.summary: Incorporates uncertainties in fossil calibrations by specifying prior distributions on divergence times (p. 74).

rate_drift_models.label: Rate Drift Models
rate_drift_models.summary: Models describing how evolutionary rates change over time across different lineages.

geometric_brownian_motion.label: Geometric Brownian Motion Model
geometric_brownian_motion.summary: A model where the logarithm of the rate (y = log(r)) drifts according to a Brownian motion process. Given ancestral log rate yA, current log rate y has a normal distribution with variance ts^2 (p. 74).

historical_biogeography.label: Historical Biogeography
historical_biogeography.summary: The study of how life and the earth evolved together, accounting for current geographic distributions in historical terms.

biogeography_glossary.label: Biogeography Fundamental Terms
biogeography_glossary.summary: Core definitions used in historical biogeographic analysis (p. 76).

ancestral_area.label: Ancestral Area / Center of Origin
ancestral_area.summary: Geographic area where a clade originated and began to diversify before spreading (p. 76).

area_of_endemism.label: Area of Endemism
area_of_endemism.summary: A geographic area that harbors multiple endemics (p. 76).

dispersal_def.label: Dispersal
dispersal_def.summary: Movement of organisms resulting in geographic range expansion; long-distance dispersal occurs across natural barriers (p. 76).

endemic_def.label: Endemic
endemic_def.summary: A species or clade naturally restricted to a particular geographic area (p. 76).

integrative_biogeography.label: Integrative Biogeography
integrative_biogeography.summary: Incorporation of multiple evidence sources, including lineage-splitting timing and movement likelihoods (p. 76).

niche_conservatism.label: Niche Conservatism
niche_conservatism.summary: Tendency for related species to retain ancestral ecological characteristics, manifesting as habitat tracking (p. 76).

pseudocongruence_biog.label: Pseudocongruence (Biogeography)
pseudocongruence_biog.summary: When area cladograms for different groups are the same despite diversifying at different times/causes (p. 76).

vicariance_def.label: Vicariance / Vicariance Event
vicariance_def.summary: The splitting of an ancestral geographic range by the formation of a barrier (e.g., drifting continents, climate change) (p. 76).

biogeography_history.label: Early Developments in Biogeography
biogeography_history.summary: Foundational observations and theories prior to modern cladistics.

buffons_law.label: Buffon's Law
buffons_law.summary: Widely separated but environmentally similar regions are typically inhabited by different species assemblages (p. 77).

darwin_wallace_biogeography.label: Darwin and Wallace's Contributions
darwin_wallace_biogeography.summary: Used biogeographic patterns as evidence for shared ancestry and explained disjunctions via migration/transport (p. 77).

wallace_line.label: Wallace's Line
wallace_line.summary: The biogeographic discontinuity between Australian and Oriental faunas (p. 77).

cladistic_biogeography.label: Cladistic Biogeography
cladistic_biogeography.summary: Approach using phylogenetic trees and area cladograms to identify common causes of distribution (p. 77).

area_cladogram.label: Area Cladogram
area_cladogram.summary: A branching diagram where names of terminal taxa are replaced by the areas of endemism they occupy (p. 76).

brooks_parsimony.label: Brooks Parsimony Analysis (BPA)
brooks_parsimony.summary: Decomposes area cladograms into binary characters representing area connections, analyzed by parsimony to derive a single area relationship tree (p. 78).

vicariance_biogeography_focus.label: Focus of Vicariance Biogeography
vicariance_biogeography_focus.summary: Emphasized vicariance-causing events (like continental movement) over one-off dispersal scenarios (p. 77).

ancestral_area_inference.label: Inference of Ancestral Areas
ancestral_area_inference.summary: Methods to reconstruct the geographic origins of individual lineages.

diva_method.label: DIVA (Dispersal-vicariance analysis)
diva_method.summary: An event-based parsimony procedure that minimizes implied dispersal and extinction events to reconstruct ancestral areas (p. 78).

dec_model.label: DEC Model
dec_model.summary: Dispersal-Extinction-Cladogenesis model; a maximum likelihood framework for inferring geographic range evolution (p. 79).

lagrange_software.label: Lagrange Software
lagrange_software.summary: Implements analytical solutions for probabilities of dispersal and extinction as functions of time using a rate matrix (p. 79).

intercontinental_patterns.label: Intercontinental Disjunction Patterns
intercontinental_patterns.summary: Empirical case studies of global lineage distribution.

laurasian_connections.label: Laurasian Connections
laurasian_connections.summary: Disjunctions between East Asia and East North America; often mediated by Beringia; shows evidence of niche conservatism (p. 79).

gondwanan_connections.label: Gondwanan Connections
gondwanan_connections.summary: Patterns involving southern continents; some previously attributed to breakup but now reinterpreted as younger Eocene movements or 'west-wind drift' (p. 80).

new_world_connections.label: New World Connections
new_world_connections.summary: The 'Great American Interchange' following the formation of the Isthmus of Panama; asymmetrical movement of mammals (North to South) vs plants (mixed) (p. 80).

phylogeography.label: Phylogeography
phylogeography.summary: The study of the history of populations within species using genealogical analysis of genetic data.

phylogeography_glossary.label: Phylogeography Fundamental Terms
phylogeography_glossary.summary: Core definitions for intra-species genetic analysis (p. 82).

coalescent_def.label: Coalescent
coalescent_def.summary: Genealogy of alleles tracing back in time to a common ancestral sequence (p. 82).

haplotype_def.label: Haplotype
haplotype_def.summary: Stretch of DNA passed across generations without recombination (p. 82).

lineage_sorting_def.label: Lineage Sorting
lineage_sorting_def.summary: Process where genealogies of genes within isolated populations move toward reciprocal monophyly via differential loss/replication (p. 82).

mismatch_dist_def.label: Mismatch Distribution
mismatch_dist_def.summary: Frequency plot of all pairwise sequence differences between sampled haplotypes (p. 82).

reciprocal_monophyly_def.label: Reciprocal Monophyly
reciprocal_monophyly_def.summary: When members of two defined groups are more closely related to their own group than to the other (p. 82).

single_locus_analysis.label: Direct Interpretation of Single-Locus Genealogies
single_locus_analysis.summary: Using one genetic region (often mtDNA) to infer population isolation and movement.

haplotype_networks.label: Haplotype Networks
haplotype_networks.summary: Visualizations of mutational steps among alleles and their frequencies, replacing bifurcating trees where ancestral/descendant haplotypes coexist (p. 84).

mismatch_distribution_analysis.label: Mismatch Distribution Analysis
mismatch_distribution_analysis.summary: Constant-size populations produce erratic peaks; expanding populations produce a single peak (wave) used to date expansions (p. 84).

comparative_phylogeography.label: Comparative Phylogeography
comparative_phylogeography.summary: Examination of population histories of multiple species in the same community to identify shared barriers or events.

concordant_breaks.label: Concordant Breaks
concordant_breaks.summary: Geographically coincident genetic breaks reflecting shared history, such as a new barrier splitting multiple taxa (p. 85).

pseudocongruence_phylogeo.label: Pseudocongruence (Phylogeography)
pseudocongruence_phylogeo.summary: Lineages dividing at the same place but at different times or from different origins (p. 85).

coalescent_theory_pop.label: Lineage Sorting and the Coalescent
coalescent_theory_pop.summary: Theoretical framework for the time it takes for alleles to become reciprocally monophyletic.

ne_lineage_sorting.label: Effective Population Size (Ne) and Sorting
ne_lineage_sorting.summary: Time to reciprocal monophyly is proportional to Ne. Mitochondrial genes take ~Ne generations; diploid nuclear genes take ~4Ne (p. 86).

coalescent_null_model.label: Coalescent Null Model
coalescent_null_model.summary: Provides a baseline for what recently isolated populations look like; allows addition of parameters for population size, isolation time, and migration (p. 86).

multilocus_analysis.label: Multilocus Gene Genealogies
multilocus_analysis.summary: Analyzing multiple loci to reduce variance and resolve gene tree vs. species tree conflict.

linkage_disequilibrium_clustering.label: Linkage Disequilibrium Clustering
linkage_disequilibrium_clustering.summary: Using associations between alleles at different loci to recognize isolated populations without a priori definitions (p. 86).

gene_tree_species_tree_conflict.label: Gene Tree vs. Species Tree Conflict
gene_tree_species_tree_conflict.summary: Single gene genealogies often do not reflect population history due to stochastic variation. Conflict is highest when population sizes are large and divergence was recent/rapid (p. 87).

population_history_testing.label: Testing Models of Population History
population_history_testing.summary: Using statistical frameworks to distinguish between alternative demographic hypotheses.

abc_testing.label: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)
abc_testing.summary: Used to estimate divergence times and test if multiple species pairs split simultaneously (p. 87).

information_theory_phylogeo.label: Information Theory in Phylogeography
information_theory_phylogeo.summary: Ranks alternative hypotheses by their power to explain data using evidence ratio scores to identify best-fit models (p. 87).

character_macroevolution.label: Concepts in Character Macroevolution
character_macroevolution.summary: Analysis of morphological characters as semiautonomous units of evolutionary change over millions of years.

darwinian_theories.label: Darwin's Five Principal Theories
darwinian_theories.summary: Fundamental conjectures testable via character variation (p. 90).

evolution_as_such.label: Evolution as Such
evolution_as_such.summary: Life has a long history of irreversible change with hereditary continuity (p. 90).

multiplication_of_species.label: Multiplication of Species
multiplication_of_species.summary: Geographic processes by which lineages branch into descendant lineages via isolation and divergence (p. 90).

gradualism_theory.label: Gradualism
gradualism_theory.summary: Small quantitative changes accumulate over generations to produce qualitative changes in structure (p. 90).

natural_selection_theory.label: Natural Selection
natural_selection_theory.summary: Random variation is filtered by fitness; favorable variants are transmitted at higher rates, gradually constructing new characters (p. 90).

character_homology.label: Evolutionary Homology
character_homology.summary: Characters that derive, with or without modification, from an equivalent character of a common ancestor.

orthology_def.label: Orthology
orthology_def.summary: Homology between sequences coalescing to a common ancestral molecule with no intragenomic duplication or horizontal transfer (p. 90).

paralogy_def.label: Paralogy
paralogy_def.summary: Homology where coalescence includes at least one intragenomic gene duplication (p. 90).

xenology_def.label: Xenology
xenology_def.summary: Homology resulting from at least one horizontal transfer between different organisms (p. 90).

serial_homology_def.label: Serial Homology / Homonomy
serial_homology_def.summary: Structurally similar features within one organism that fail the conjunction test due to duplication (p. 92).

homology_tests.label: Diagnostic Tests of Homology
homology_tests.summary: Principles used to separate homology from other forms of resemblance (p. 92).

similarity_test.label: Similarity Test
similarity_test.summary: Checks for nontrivial structural correspondence. High sequence similarity (>70%) is definitive at the molecular level (p. 92).

conjunction_test.label: Conjunction Test
conjunction_test.summary: A single organism should not express both hypothesized homologous structures at the same developmental stage (p. 92).

congruence_test.label: Congruence Test
congruence_test.summary: Homologies must form a nested hierarchy of groups (clades). If two characters partially overlap non-nestedly, at least one fails (p. 92).

parallelism_def.label: Parallelism
parallelism_def.summary: Independent origin of similar characters due to shared homologous developmental constraints. Passes similarity/conjunction but fails congruence (p. 93).

convergence_def.label: Convergence
convergence_def.summary: Superficially similar characters evolved by different developmental means. Fails similarity and congruence but passes conjunction (p. 90).

deep_homology.label: Deep Homology
deep_homology.summary: Similar morphological characters evolving in parallel via separate activation of homologous developmental pathways (p. 90).

genetic_assimilation.label: Genetic Assimilation
genetic_assimilation.summary: A trait originally induced by environment becomes stabilized by selective accumulation of genetic variants (p. 93).

adaptation_analysis.label: Testing Character Adaptation
adaptation_analysis.summary: Evaluating if a character evolved for its current biological utility.

adaptation_def_macro.label: Character Adaptation
adaptation_def_macro.summary: A character that evolved gradually by natural selection for a particular biological role (p. 90).

exaptation_def.label: Exaptation
exaptation_def.summary: Co-option of a character for a role other than the one for which it evolved (e.g., feathers for flight) (p. 96).

nonaptation_def.label: Nonaptation
nonaptation_def.summary: A character selectively indistinguishable from contrasting conditions in evolutionary history (p. 90).

disaptation_def.label: Disaptation
disaptation_def.summary: A character that reduces fitness. Primary: disadvantageous at origin. Secondary: becomes unfavorable due to environmental change (p. 90).

evolvability_concept.label: Character Evolvability
evolvability_concept.summary: The potential of a species to produce new morphological characters.

variability_vs_variation.label: Variability vs Variation
variability_vs_variation.summary: Variation is realized difference; variability is the propensity to vary, depending on mutation/recombination (p. 96).

alberch_evolvability_model.label: Alberch's Evolvability Model
alberch_evolvability_model.summary: Evolvability defined by the number of alternative developmental pathways accessible via continuous changes in parameters X1 and X2 (p. 97).

ancestral_state_reconstruction.label: Ancestral State Reconstruction
ancestral_state_reconstruction.summary: Inferring the phenotype of an ancestral species at internal nodes of a phylogeny.

parsimony_reconstruction.label: Parsimony (Occam's Razor)
parsimony_reconstruction.summary: Chooses states that minimize total change. Uses a step matrix for discrete states and squared-change for continuous traits (p. 101).

likelihood_reconstruction.label: Likelihood-based Reconstruction
likelihood_reconstruction.summary: Models evolution as a stochastic process. Uses rate matrices (Q) for discrete traits and probability distributions for continuous traits (p. 102).

trait_evolution_models.label: Models of Trait Evolution
trait_evolution_models.summary: Statistical descriptions of trait changes over time.

brownian_motion_model.label: Brownian Motion (Random Walk)
brownian_motion_model.summary: Trait values change stochastically in small increments; descendants fit a normal distribution centered on the ancestor (p. 102).

ornstein_uhlenbeck_model.label: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model
ornstein_uhlenbeck_model.summary: A constrained random walk where a 'rubber band' parameter pulls trait values toward an adaptive optimum (p. 102).

markov_discrete_model.label: Discrete Markov Models
markov_discrete_model.summary: Assumes exponentially distributed waiting times between transitions; rates are defined in a Q matrix (p. 102).

phylogenetic_signal.label: Phylogenetic Signal
phylogenetic_signal.summary: The degree to which a trait covaries with phylogeny.

blomberg_k_statistic.label: Blomberg's K
blomberg_k_statistic.summary: K > 1: relatives more similar than BM; K < 1: relatives less similar than BM (p. 103).

multiple_trait_analysis.label: Analysis of Multiple Traits
multiple_trait_analysis.summary: Studying correlated evolution while accounting for phylogenetic non-independence.

independent_contrasts.label: Phylogenetically Independent Contrasts (PIC)
independent_contrasts.summary: Felsenstein's method calculating differences in trait values at sister nodes to create independent data points (p. 103).

generalized_least_squares.label: Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
generalized_least_squares.summary: Uses a phylogenetic variance-covariance matrix to perform regressions, relaxing the requirement for Brownian motion (p. 104).

trait_diversification_link.label: Trait Evolution and Lineage Diversification
trait_diversification_link.summary: Exploring how phenotypic traits influence speciation and extinction rates.

key_innovations.label: Key Innovations
key_innovations.summary: Traits that increase diversification rates; tested via sister-clade comparisons (p. 104).

joint_trait_diversification_models.label: Joint Models
