tolerance_definition.summary: The ability to survive and reproduce in a given environment by evolving mutations that allow internal systems to function under extreme conditions. (p. 282)

regulation_definition.label: Physiological Regulation
regulation_definition.summary: Maintaining an internal state that differs from the environment to keep conditions within tolerable limits (e.g., thermoregulation). (p. 282)

biochemical_mechanisms.label: Biochemical Mechanisms of Adaptation
biochemical_mechanisms.summary: The molecular basis of how environmental factors affect performance.

protein_stability_fact.label: Protein Stability and Temperature
protein_stability_fact.summary: Amino acids that increase protein stability improve function at high temperatures but maladapt to low temperatures. (p. 284)

osmotic_tradeoff_fact.label: Osmotic Pressure Trade-off
osmotic_tradeoff_fact.summary: High solute concentrations prevent water loss in hyperosmotic environments but cause cells to swell and potentially die in hypo-osmotic environments. (p. 284)

generalist_cost_fact.label: Energetic Cost of Generalism
generalist_cost_fact.summary: Generalists must invest energy to synthesize multiple protein forms or turn over proteins frequently, compromising peak performance in any single condition. (p. 284)

regulation_energy_cost_fact.label: Energetic Cost of Regulation
regulation_energy_cost_fact.summary: Regulation requires metabolic energy (e.g., catabolizing carbohydrates for heat in mammals), creating a disadvantage in benign environments. (p. 284)

adaptive_variation_tolerance.label: Adaptive Variation in Tolerance
adaptive_variation_tolerance.summary: How tolerance evolves along environmental gradients.

latitudinal_gradient_fact.label: Latitudinal Thermal Tolerance
latitudinal_gradient_fact.summary: Tropical species tolerate high temperatures better but low temperatures worse than polar species; higher latitude species often tolerate a wider range. (p. 285)

mimulus_transplant_fact.label: Mimulus Altitude Adaptation
mimulus_transplant_fact.summary: Reciprocal transplants of Mimulus plants show that adaptation to high altitude results in maladaptation to low altitude due to trade-offs between photosynthesis and cold tolerance. (p. 285)

ecoli_experimental_evolution_fact.label: E. coli Nutritional Adaptation
ecoli_experimental_evolution_fact.summary: Adaptation to lactulose involved gene duplication, while adaptation to methyl-galactoside involved deletion of a suppressor region. (p. 285)

adaptive_variation_regulation.label: Adaptive Variation in Regulation
adaptive_variation_regulation.summary: Evolution of internal control mechanisms in response to environment.

endothermy_hydric_tradeoff.label: Thermal-Hydric Trade-off
endothermy_hydric_tradeoff.summary: Birds and mammals may allow bodies to cool to save energy or warm up to save water when dehydrated. (p. 286)

drosophila_water_regulation_fact.label: Drosophila Desiccation Resistance
drosophila_water_regulation_fact.summary: Temperate Drosophila evolve longer hydrocarbon chains in their cuticles to reduce water loss compared to tropical Drosophila. (p. 286)

adaptive_acclimation.label: Adaptive Acclimation
adaptive_acclimation.summary: The ability to adjust physiology in response to fluctuating environment.

acclimation_risk_fact.label: Risks of Acclimation
acclimation_risk_fact.summary: Acclimation requires energy and carries the risk of committing to the wrong strategy if past conditions do not predict future ones. (p. 286)

rodent_intestine_fact.label: Rodent Intestinal Plasticity
rodent_intestine_fact.summary: Rodents from high latitudes adjust intestine length more readily than those from low latitudes. (p. 286)

phospholipid_adjustment_fact.label: Drosophila Membrane Adjustment
phospholipid_adjustment_fact.summary: Populations in fluctuating temperatures evolve a better ability to adjust the ratio of two phospholipids in cellular membranes. (p. 286)

physiological_constraints.label: Constraints on Physiological Adaptation
physiological_constraints.summary: Factors slowing the evolution of optimal physiological phenotypes.

heritability_constraint.label: Heritability and Genetic Variation
heritability_constraint.summary: Adaptation is limited if the required genetic variation is absent or if mutations are too numerous to accumulate quickly. (p. 287)

gene_flow_constraint.label: Gene Flow and Maladaptive Alleles
gene_flow_constraint.summary: Immigration from different environments can introduce maladaptive alleles, creating clines in traits like metal tolerance in plants. (p. 287)

silversides_growth_fact.label: Atlantic Silversides Trade-off
silversides_growth_fact.summary: Northern genotypes outgrow southern ones but at the cost of increased predation risk due to high food consumption, limiting their spread. (p. 287)

evolution_of_ecological_niche.label: Evolution of the Ecological Niche
evolution_of_ecological_niche.summary: The evolution of the range of environments within which a species persists.

hutchinsonian_niche_concept.label: Hutchinsonian Niche
hutchinsonian_niche_concept.summary: The range of environmental conditions (abiotic and biotic) for which the intrinsic growth rate (r) of a population is positive. (p. 289)

niche_response_surface.label: Niche Response Surface
niche_response_surface.summary: A graphical representation of intrinsic growth rate (r) as a function of environmental variables. (p. 289)

daphnia_magna_niche_fact.label: Daphnia magna Niche Study
daphnia_magna_niche_fact.summary: Distribution in Yorkshire ponds is largely explained by pH and calcium requirements; populations outside the niche may be sustained by immigration (sinks). (p. 290)

niche_conservatism_concept.label: Niche Conservatism
niche_conservatism_concept.summary: The phenomenon where species or clades remain surprisingly constant in their niche requirements over time. (p. 288)

niche_complexities.label: Complexities in the Niche Concept
niche_complexities.summary: Nuances that complicate the basic Hutchinsonian definition.

niche_construction_fact.label: Niche Construction
niche_construction_fact.summary: Organisms impact their environments via resource depletion or chemical alterations, affecting their own persistence. (p. 292)

allee_effect_niche_fact.label: Allee Effects and Niches
allee_effect_niche_fact.summary: Positive effects of population size on growth rate can make the 'persistence niche' larger than the 'establishment niche.' (p. 292)

genetic_variation_in_niches.label: Genetic Variation in Niches
genetic_variation_in_niches.summary: The requirement for heritable variation to fuel niche evolution.

evolutionary_rescue_concept.label: Evolutionary Rescue
evolutionary_rescue_concept.summary: When a declining population persists because natural selection increases mean fitness rapidly enough to rebound. (p. 293)

adaptive_landscape_concept.label: Adaptive Landscape
adaptive_landscape_concept.summary: A metaphor portraying fitness as a function of genotype or phenotype in a given environment, often visualized as 'hill-climbing' toward an optimum. (p. 293)

tiger_swallowtail_fact.label: Tiger Swallowtail Niche Variation
tiger_swallowtail_fact.summary: Michigan caterpillars are intolerant of Alaskan temperatures, demonstrating intraspecific variation in ecological niches. (p. 293)

demographic_constraints_niche.label: Demographic Constraints on Niche Evolution
demographic_constraints_niche.summary: How population dynamics and landscape structure limit the ability to evolve a new niche.

sink_habitat_severity.label: Sink Habitat Severity
sink_habitat_severity.summary: In 'severe sinks' (r << 0), extinction is rapid, leaving little time for favorable mutations; in 'mild sinks', adaptation is more likely. (p. 294)

source_sink_dynamics_concept.label: Source-Sink Dynamics
source_sink_dynamics_concept.summary: Source habitats (inside niche) export individuals to sink habitats (outside niche), potentially sustaining populations that would otherwise go extinct. (p. 288)

migrational_load_fact.label: Migrational Load
migrational_load_fact.summary: In sexual species, immigration of maladaptive alleles from a source to a sink can dilute the effectiveness of local selection. (p. 295)

community_niche_evolution.label: Niches Evolving in Communities
community_niche_evolution.summary: The role of interspecific interactions in shaping niche movement.

competitive_release_fact.label: Competitive Release
competitive_release_fact.summary: The removal of a superior competitor or predator can allow a species to persist and subsequently adapt to local abiotic conditions. (p. 296)

knapweed_adaptation_fact.label: Spotted Knapweed Evolution
knapweed_adaptation_fact.summary: Introduced to North America, it rapidly evolved to live in diverse climatic regimes where native competitors were removed by disturbance. (p. 296)

adaptation_to_biotic_environment.label: Adaptation to the Biotic Environment
adaptation_to_biotic_environment.summary: Evolutionary responses to the web of interactions with other organisms.

biotic_vs_abiotic_selection.label: Biotic vs. Abiotic Selection
biotic_vs_abiotic_selection.summary: Biotic agents are 'moving targets' because they evolve/coevolve, unlike static abiotic factors (e.g., temperature). (p. 298)

generation_time_asymmetry.label: Generation Time Asymmetry
generation_time_asymmetry.summary: Large differences in generation times (e.g., scale insects vs. trees) allow the short-lived partner to adapt much more rapidly. (p. 299)

conflicting_biotic_selection.label: Conflicting Biotic Selection
conflicting_biotic_selection.summary: Diverse interactors may select for opposing trait values, preventing a single optimal phenotype (e.g., tadpoles facing diverse predators). (p. 300)

biotic_adaptation_evidence.label: Evidence for Biotic Adaptation
biotic_adaptation_evidence.summary: Empirical cases showing local adaptation to biotic interactors.

clover_grass_fact.label: Clover-Grass Local Adaptation
clover_grass_fact.summary: Trifolium repens grows best when paired with Lolium perenne genotypes from its own field. (p. 300)

guppy_predator_fact.label: Guppy Prey Adaptation
guppy_predator_fact.summary: Guppies from high-predation environments have higher fitness in the presence of predators than those from low-predation sites. (p. 300)

conifer_cone_fact.label: Conifer Cone Selection
conifer_cone_fact.summary: Lodgepole pine cones are shaped by the dominant predator: wide/few seeds for squirrels, thick scales/more seeds for crossbill birds. (p. 300)

biotic_extinction_fact.label: Adaptation-Driven Extinction
biotic_extinction_fact.summary: A parasite may adapt to be so virulent that it drives its host to extinction; observed in temporal sequences of Daphnia and microsporidian parasites. (p. 301)

introduced_species_evolution.label: Evolution of Introduced Species
introduced_species_evolution.summary: Impact of novel biotic interactors on naive populations.

enemy_escape_hypothesis.label: Enemy Escape Hypothesis
enemy_escape_hypothesis.summary: Introduced species may experience explosive growth by escaping natural enemies or possessing 'novel weapons' against naive natives. (p. 301)

cane_toad_snake_fact.label: Cane Toad-Snake Coevolution
cane_toad_snake_fact.summary: Toxicity of cane toads in Australia selected for snakes with smaller mouths, which prevents them from eating large, highly toxic toads. (p. 301)

biotic_adaptation.label: Adaptation to the Biotic Environment
biotic_adaptation.summary: The process by which organisms evolve morphological, behavioral, and genetic traits in response to interactions with other species and their own population densities.

relative_abundance_selection.label: Selection via Relative Species Abundance
relative_abundance_selection.summary: Fluctuations in the relative abundance of species alter the strength and direction of selection from the biotic environment.

density_vs_frequency_dependence.label: Density and Frequency Dependence
density_vs_frequency_dependence.summary: Ecological properties that act differently based on the number of individuals (density) or the proportion of interactors (frequency).

fact_density_frequency_cascade.label: Cascading Changes
fact_density_frequency_cascade.summary: Changes in density and relative frequency of interactions within and among species can lead to cascading changes in other species (p. 302).

black_mustard_case_study.label: Black Mustard (Brassica nigra) Adaptation
black_mustard_case_study.summary: A study demonstrating opposing selection pressures from generalist and specialist herbivores.

fact_generalist_selection.label: Generalist Herbivore Selection
fact_generalist_selection.summary: Generalist herbivores (e.g., slugs and snails) impose strong selection for high levels of phytochemical defense (p. 302).

fact_specialist_selection.label: Specialist Herbivore Selection
fact_specialist_selection.summary: Specialist herbivores are unharmed by phytochemical defenses and prefer larger, more defended plants (p. 302).

fact_sinigrin_tradeoff.label: Sinigrin Production Trade-off
fact_sinigrin_tradeoff.summary: Sinigrin reduces soil fungal densities, aiding competition against other species, but is costly and selected against in high-density patches of black mustard plants (p. 302).

population_density_adaptation.label: Adaptation to Population Density
population_density_adaptation.summary: Traits that are favored at high population densities often differ from those favored at low densities.

fact_human_urban_resistance.label: Human Urban Adaptation
fact_human_urban_resistance.summary: Alleles associated with resistance to tuberculosis and leprosy are more frequent in older urban settlements, suggesting adaptation to high-density living (p. 302).

fact_lolium_perenne_rust.label: Lolium perenne Disease Resistance
fact_lolium_perenne_rust.summary: Selection on disease resistance to rust fungus in L. perenne varies significantly between high-density and low-density plots (p. 302).

animal_personality_traits.label: Animal Personality and Density
animal_personality_traits.summary: Behavioral traits (aggression, dispersal, sociality) exhibit costs and benefits that are density or frequency dependent.

fact_bryozoan_dispersal.label: Bryozoan Dispersal Trade-off
fact_bryozoan_dispersal.summary: Long-distance dispersing bryozoans colonize more areas but have lower reproductive rates than short-dispersal colonizers (p. 302).

fact_social_spider_aggression.label: Social Spider Aggression
fact_social_spider_aggression.summary: Aggressive, bold genotypes are better defenders of resources but suffer costs as the frequency of aggressive individuals increases (p. 302).

nonselective_processes.label: Nonselective Evolutionary Processes
nonselective_processes.summary: Mechanisms of evolution other than natural selection that change genotype and allele frequencies over time.

effective_population_size.label: Effective Population Size (Ne)
effective_population_size.summary: A theoretical population size that accounts for variations in sex ratio, progeny number, and population size across generations.

fact_ne_formula_sex_ratio.label: Ne and Sex Ratio
fact_ne_formula_sex_ratio.summary: Ne = (4 * Nf * Nm) / (Nm + Nf), where Nf and Nm are numbers of breeding females and males (p. 311).

fact_ne_variance_progeny.label: Ne and Progeny Variance
fact_ne_variance_progeny.summary: Ne = (4N) / (V/2 + 2), where V is the variance in the number of progeny (p. 311).

fact_ne_bottleneck_harmonic.label: Ne Over Generations
fact_ne_bottleneck_harmonic.summary: The overall Ne over t generations is the harmonic mean: 1/Ne = (1/t) * Sum(1/Ne.i) (p. 311).

drift_phenomena.label: Drift Phenomena
drift_phenomena.summary: Specific events that trigger strong genetic drift due to restricted population size.

fact_genetic_bottleneck.label: Genetic Bottleneck
fact_genetic_bottleneck.summary: A period during which only a few individuals survive and become the ancestors of future generations (p. 308).

fact_founder_effect.label: Founder Effect
fact_founder_effect.summary: The impact on genetic variation when a population grows from a few founder individuals (p. 308).

fact_fixation_probability.label: Probability of Fixation
fact_fixation_probability.summary: For a neutral allele, the probability of fixation u(q) is equal to its initial frequency q0 (p. 310).

neutral_theory_drift.label: Neutral Theory of Molecular Evolution
neutral_theory_drift.summary: Theory proposed by Motoo Kimura stating that most molecular genetic variation is selectively neutral and driven by mutation and drift.

fact_molecular_clock.label: Molecular Clock
fact_molecular_clock.summary: The rate of allele substitution k is equal to the mutation rate u, independent of effective population size (p. 312).

fact_equilibrium_heterozygosity.label: Equilibrium Heterozygosity (He)
fact_equilibrium_heterozygosity.summary: He = (4Neu) / (4Neu + 1), where Ne is effective population size and u is mutation rate (p. 313).

coalescence_theory.label: Coalescence
coalescence_theory.summary: A retrospective approach to population genetics examining the point in the past where common ancestry occurs for alleles.

fact_coalescence_definition.label: Coalescence Definition
fact_coalescence_definition.summary: The event in the past at which common ancestry occurs for two alleles at a gene because of genetic drift (p. 308).

mutation_process.label: Mutation
mutation_process.summary: A heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of the genome from parent to offspring; the ultimate source of genetic variation.

mutation_types.label: Types of Mutations
mutation_types.summary: Different categories of genomic changes based on the nature of the sequence alteration.

fact_base_substitutions.label: Base Substitutions
fact_base_substitutions.summary: Replacement of one nucleotide with another. Includes transitions (purine-purine or pyrimidine-pyrimidine) and transversions (purine-pyrimidine) (p. 316).

fact_indels.label: Insertions and Deletions (Indels)
fact_indels.summary: Addition or removal of sequences. Includes Short Tandem Repeats (STRs) and Copy-Number Variants (CNVs) (p. 316).

fact_genome_rearrangements.label: Genome Rearrangements
fact_genome_rearrangements.summary: Includes inversions (segment reverses orientation) and translocations (segment moves to a different location) (p. 316).

fact_transposable_elements.label: Transposable Elements (TEs)
fact_transposable_elements.summary: Selfish genetic elements that encode their own replication independently of the host genome (p. 316).

mutation_causes.label: Causes of Mutation
mutation_causes.summary: Factors that induce DNA damage or replication errors.

fact_endogenous_mutagens.label: Endogenous Mutagens
fact_endogenous_mutagens.summary: Internal causes including replication errors, TEs, and free-radical by-products of metabolism (p. 316).

fact_exogenous_mutagens.label: Exogenous Mutagens
fact_exogenous_mutagens.summary: External causes such as environmental mutagens (e.g., UV radiation) (p. 316).

mutation_evolutionary_dynamics.label: Mutation Evolutionary Dynamics
mutation_evolutionary_dynamics.summary: The interaction between mutation, selection, and population size.

fact_mutation_selection_balance.label: Mutation-Selection Balance (MSB)
fact_mutation_selection_balance.summary: Equilibrium frequency of a deleterious mutant allele q = m/s, where m is mutation rate and s is selection coefficient (p. 317).

fact_nearly_neutral_theory.label: Nearly Neutral Theory
fact_nearly_neutral_theory.summary: Dynamics are governed by genetic drift rather than selection if the strength of selection s < 1/(2Ne) (p. 317).

fact_error_threshold.label: Error Threshold (Eigen)
fact_error_threshold.summary: The mutation rate puts an upper bound on the length of a biological sequence; exceeding this leads to 'error catastrophe' (p. 320).

fact_mullers_ratchet.label: Muller's Ratchet
fact_mullers_ratchet.summary: The process by which finite asexual populations accumulate deleterious mutations over time, potentially leading to a 'mutational meltdown' and extinction (p. 320).

migration_geographic_variation.label: Geographic Variation and Migration
migration_geographic_variation.summary: The spatial distribution of genetic diversity and the role of gene flow in shaping population structure.

spatial_structure_causes.label: Causes of Spatial Genetic Structure
spatial_structure_causes.summary: Factors that create nonrandom distributions of alleles across a landscape.

fact_isolation_by_distance.label: Isolation by Distance
fact_isolation_by_distance.summary: Decreasing genetic similarity with increasing distance due to shared ancestry and limited dispersal (p. 322).

fact_clines.label: Clines
fact_clines.summary: A gradient of continuous variation through space for a genetic or phenotypic character within a species (p. 322).

fact_habitat_selection.label: Habitat Selection
fact_habitat_selection.summary: The nonrandom distribution of individuals after dispersal across habitats, often driven by genotype-dependent preferences (p. 322).

gene_flow_mechanisms.label: Gene Flow
gene_flow_mechanisms.summary: The partial mixing between different populations via the movement of individuals or gametes.

fact_gene_swamping.label: Gene Swamping
fact_gene_swamping.summary: Occurs when gene flow is so high that it overrides local selection, preventing local adaptation (p. 324).

fact_migration_load.label: Migration Load
fact_migration_load.summary: The decrease in mean fitness of a population caused by the immigration of maladapted individuals (p. 324).

fact_genetic_rescue.label: Genetic Rescue
fact_genetic_rescue.summary: An increase in a population's mean fitness due to the introduction of genetically divergent individuals (p. 322).

migration_consequences.label: Consequences of Population Structure
migration_consequences.summary: The evolutionary impacts of mating and competing with spatial neighbors.

fact_heterosis.label: Heterosis
fact_heterosis.summary: Higher fitness of progeny born to parents originating from different populations (hybrid vigor) (p. 322).

fact_outbreeding_depression.label: Outbreeding Depression
fact_outbreeding_depression.summary: Lower fitness of progeny from divergent populations due to loss of local adaptation or genetic incompatibilities (p. 322).

recombination_sex.label: Recombination and Sex
recombination_sex.summary: The generation of new genetic combinations through the sexual union of individuals and molecular DNA exchange.

molecular_recombination.label: Molecular Recombination
molecular_recombination.summary: The physical process of DNA exchange, primarily serving to repair double-stranded breaks (DSB).

fact_centimorgan.label: Centimorgan (cM)
fact_centimorgan.summary: A distance on a genetic map where 1 cM corresponds to a 1% probability of crossover (p. 328).

fact_gene_conversion.label: Gene Conversion
fact_gene_conversion.summary: The nonreciprocal transfer of genetic information, converting one allele in a heterozygote into the other during repair (p. 328).

fact_recombination_hotspots.label: Recombination Hot Spots
fact_recombination_hotspots.summary: Small regions where recombination is highly concentrated; in mammals, these are initiated by PRDM9 and targeted by Spo11 (p. 330).

fact_ld_formula.label: LD Calculation
fact_ld_formula.summary: DAB = pAB - pApB, where pAB is the actual frequency of the allele pair and pApB is the expected frequency if random (p. 331).

fact_ld_causes.label: Causes of LD
fact_ld_causes.summary: Generated by epistatic selection, migration (hybrid zones), and random genetic drift (p. 331-332).

recombination_and_selection.label: Recombination and Selection
recombination_and_selection.summary: The role of recombination in facilitating or hindering natural selection.

fact_hitchhiking.label: Genetic Hitchhiking
fact_hitchhiking.summary: The increase in frequency of a neutral allele because it is physically associated with a selectively favorable allele (p. 328).

fact_recombination_benefit.label: Benefits of Recombination
fact_recombination_benefit.summary: Recombination allows selection to disentangle the effects of specific alleles from the random genetic background and prevents interference between favorable mutations (p. 333).

fact_general_load_definition.label: Genetic Load Definition
fact_general_load_definition.summary: The difference between the average fitness of individuals in a population and the fitness of the best possible genotype (p. 334).

mutation_load.label: Mutation Load
mutation_load.summary: The specific reduction in mean fitness due to deleterious alleles maintained by mutation-selection balance.

fact_haldanes_mutation_load.label: Haldane's Result
fact_haldanes_mutation_load.summary: For a single locus, mutation load Lmut = 2m, which is independent of the strength of selection against the mutation (p. 334).

fact_genome_wide_load.label: Genome-wide Mutation Load
fact_genome_wide_load.summary: The mean fitness of the whole genome W = e^(-U), where U is the average number of new mutations per diploid genome per generation (p. 335).

root_evolutionary_processes.label: Evolutionary Processes
root_evolutionary_processes.summary: Comprehensive domain covering the genetic and molecular mechanisms that influence population fitness, mating strategies, and genomic evolution.

core_genetic_load.label: Genetic Load
core_genetic_load.summary: The reduction in mean fitness of a population relative to a hypothetical mutation-free optimal genotype.

sub_mutation_load.label: Mutation Load
sub_mutation_load.summary: Load specifically caused by the accumulation and presence of deleterious mutations.

fact_mut_load_def.label: Mutation Load Definition
fact_mut_load_def.summary: The degree to which the average individual is less fit relative to a mutation-free individual placed in the population; refers specifically to the reduction in 'mean fitness' (p. 336).

fact_mut_load_general_formula.label: General Mutation Load Formula
fact_mut_load_general_formula.summary: L = U / (y - z), where U is the mutation rate per individual per generation, z is the mean number of mutations carried by winners of selection, and y is the mean number carried by losers (p. 336).

fact_mut_load_asexual.label: Asexual Mutation Load
fact_mut_load_asexual.summary: In asexual populations, the load is given by Haldane's result: L = 1 - e^(-U). This load is not affected by epistasis or dominance (p. 337).

fact_mut_load_epistasis.label: Epistasis and Mutation Load
fact_mut_load_epistasis.summary: Synergistic (negative) epistasis reduces mutation load because more mutations are eliminated per selective death. Positive epistasis increases mutation load relative to Haldane's prediction (p. 336).

fact_mut_load_human_example.label: Human Mutation Load Example
fact_mut_load_human_example.summary: With a genome-wide deleterious mutation rate U = 4.2, the predicted mean fitness (W) is 0.015, representing a mutation load of 98.5% (p. 339).

sub_specialized_loads.label: Specialized Loads
sub_specialized_loads.summary: Other forms of genetic load resulting from drift, migration, segregation, and selection.

fact_drift_load.label: Drift Load
fact_drift_load.summary: Reduction in fitness due to deleterious alleles deviating from their deterministic expected value under mutation-selection balance. Occurs when selection is weak relative to population size (s << 1/4Ne) (p. 337).

fact_segregation_load.label: Segregation and Recombination Load
fact_segregation_load.summary: Loss of fitness due to the breakup of favorable allele combinations. For a single locus with heterozygote advantage (WAA=1-s, WAa=1, Waa=1-t), segregation load L = st/(s+t) (p. 338).

fact_gender_load.label: Gender Load
fact_gender_load.summary: Constraint from sex-specific optima. Intralocus conflict results in segregating gender load (negative intrasexual genetic correlation); Interlocus conflict (e.g., remating rates) leads to fixed gender load (p. 338).

fact_substitution_load.label: Substitution Load
fact_substitution_load.summary: The 'cost of natural selection' representing selective deaths required to fix an allele. Formally, for an allele at frequency p, Lsub = 2 ln(1/p) (p. 338).

core_inbreeding.label: Inbreeding
core_inbreeding.summary: Mating between individuals with recent common ancestors, increasing homozygosity beyond Hardy-Weinberg expectations.

sub_inbreeding_mechanics.label: Inbreeding Mechanics
sub_inbreeding_mechanics.summary: The mathematical and biological basis of increased homozygosity.

fact_inbreeding_def.label: Inbreeding Definition
fact_inbreeding_def.summary: Mating between individuals with common ancestors; can be caused by limited mate availability (bottlenecks) or mating patterns (selfing/sib-mating) (p. 341).

fact_f_coeff.label: Inbreeding Coefficient (f)
fact_f_coeff.summary: The probability that two alleles at a locus in a diploid individual are identical by descent (IBD). Selfing produces f=0.5, sib-mating produces f=0.25 (p. 341).

sub_inbreeding_consequences.label: Inbreeding Consequences
sub_inbreeding_consequences.summary: The phenotypic and evolutionary results of increased homozygosity.

fact_inbreeding_depression.label: Inbreeding Depression
fact_inbreeding_depression.summary: Reduced survival or fertility of inbred progeny. Primarily caused by the expression of rare, partially recessive detrimental mutations (mutation-selection balance hypothesis) rather than overdominance (p. 344-345).

fact_purging.label: Purging
fact_purging.summary: The process where inbreeding exposes recessive deleterious alleles to selection in the homozygous state, thereby reducing the genetic load (p. 345).

fact_haldanes_sieve.label: Haldane's Sieve
fact_haldanes_sieve.summary: In inbreeding populations, advantageous mutations are more likely to spread even if recessive, as inbreeding produces homozygotes more readily than outcrossing (p. 344).

core_sge.label: Selfish Genetic Elements (SGEs)
core_sge.summary: Heritable units that spread through a population despite having adverse effects on the individual's fitness.

sub_sge_taxonomy.label: SGE Taxonomy
sub_sge_taxonomy.summary: Classification of SGEs based on the arena of competition.

fact_genome_parasites.label: Genome Parasites
fact_genome_parasites.summary: Elements that multiply within the genome, such as Transposable Elements (TEs) using 'copy and paste' or 'cut and paste' mechanisms (p. 349).

fact_soma_parasites.label: Soma and Cell Parasites
fact_soma_parasites.summary: Elements multiplying within cells or bodies, such as cancerous cell lineages or petite mitochondria in yeast (p. 350).

fact_reproductive_parasites.label: Reproductive Parasites
fact_reproductive_parasites.summary: SGEs that alter host reproduction to increase their own transmission, including meiotic drivers, allelic killers, and cytoplasmic distorters (p. 350).

sub_sge_mechanisms.label: SGE Mechanisms
sub_sge_mechanisms.summary: Technical methods by which reproductive SGEs achieve non-Mendelian inheritance.

fact_meiotic_drive.label: Meiotic Drive
fact_meiotic_drive.summary: Preferential segregation of a chromosomal element to the egg pole in asymmetrical female meiosis (e.g., Ab10/knob system in maize) (p. 350).

fact_allelic_killers.label: Allelic Killers
fact_allelic_killers.summary: Post-meiotic mechanisms that disable gametes or offspring carrying alternative alleles. Requires a killer locus and a responder locus (e.g., SD in Drosophila, t haplotype in mice) (p. 351).

fact_cytoplasmic_distorters.label: Cytoplasmic Distorters
fact_cytoplasmic_distorters.summary: Uniparental organelles or symbionts that bias sex ratios. Examples: Cytoplasmic Male Sterility (CMS) in plants and Wolbachia in insects (p. 351-352).

core_mating_systems.label: Evolution of Mating Systems
core_mating_systems.summary: The study of the transition between outcrossing (cross-fertilization) and self-fertilization (selfing).

sub_mating_strategies.label: Outcrossing vs Selfing Strategies
sub_mating_strategies.summary: The ecological and biological trade-offs between mating modes.

fact_bakers_law.label: Baker's Law
fact_bakers_law.summary: The observation that selfing individuals can establish colonies at low density or after long-distance dispersal (p. 360).

fact_reproductive_assurance.label: Reproductive Assurance Hypothesis
fact_reproductive_assurance.summary: Selfing is favored when pollinator or mate availability is low, ensuring seed production when outcrossing fails (p. 361).

sub_mating_selection.label: Mechanisms of Selection on Mating
sub_mating_selection.summary: Factors determining whether selfing or outcrossing alleles spread.

fact_transmission_advantage.label: Transmission Advantage of Selfing
fact_transmission_advantage.summary: Selfers contribute more gene copies to the next generation because they are both the maternal and paternal parent (p. 361).

fact_mating_costs.label: Costs of Selfing
fact_mating_costs.summary: Spread of selfing is limited by: Inbreeding depression (d), Pollen discounting (loss of outcrossed siring success), and Seed discounting (reduction in outcrossed seed production) (p. 361).

sub_mating_evolutionary_fate.label: Evolutionary Fate of Selfers
sub_mating_evolutionary_fate.summary: Long-term macroevolutionary consequences of high selfing rates.

fact_mating_dead_end.label: Selfing as an Evolutionary Dead End
fact_mating_dead_end.summary: Selfing lineages are often short-lived due to reduced adaptive genetic variation, low recombination, and mutational decay (Muller's Ratchet) (p. 362).

core_molecular_evolution.label: Molecular Evolution
core_molecular_evolution.summary: The study of changes in DNA, RNA, and protein sequences over generations.

sub_mol_ev_theory.label: Theories of Molecular Evolution
sub_mol_ev_theory.summary: Frameworks used to interpret the rate and nature of molecular change.

fact_neutral_theory.label: Neutral Theory
fact_neutral_theory.summary: Proposes that most molecular variation is selectively neutral, making genetic drift the primary driver of molecular change over time (p. 367).

fact_mol_clock.label: Molecular Clock
fact_mol_clock.summary: The observation of roughly linear accumulation of genetic changes over time, used to infer the date of a last common ancestor (p. 367).

sub_mol_ev_processes.label: Processes of Molecular Evolution
sub_mol_ev_processes.summary: The fundamental mechanisms leading to sequence divergence.

fact_mol_ev_mechanisms.label: Mutation and Fixation
fact_mol_ev_mechanisms.summary: Molecular evolution results from the interplay between heritable mutations (introduced during gamete production) and fixation (the process where a mutation replaces all other variants) (p. 367).

fact_selection_types.label: Positive vs Purifying Selection
fact_selection_types.summary: Positive selection leads to the fixation of advantageous mutations. Purifying selection removes harmful mutations to maintain biological function (p. 367).

drift_pop_size.label: Drift and Population Size
drift_pop_size.summary: The influence of genetic drift varies by population scale.
drift_pop_size.details: Drift leads to rapid changes in small populations but is significantly less influential in large populations (p. 369).

drift_fixation.label: Outcome of Drift
drift_fixation.summary: The ultimate result of drift acting alone on a mutation.
drift_fixation.details: The outcome of drift alone is always the loss (0% frequency) or fixation (100% frequency) of every new mutation; fixation means the mutation replaces all previous variants at that site (p. 369).

positive_selection.label: Positive Selection (Adaptation)
positive_selection.summary: Selection that directly increases a variant's frequency due to increased relative reproductive success.

positive_selection_rate.label: Rate of Positive Selection
positive_selection_rate.summary: The speed at which adaptive traits fix compared to drift.
positive_selection_rate.details: Positive selection can cause rapid changes in allele frequencies over tens of generations, whereas drift in large populations may take millions of generations (p. 369).

purifying_selection.label: Purifying Selection
purifying_selection.summary: Selection that removes harmful or deleterious mutations from a population.

purifying_selection_effect.label: Effect of Purifying Selection
purifying_selection_effect.summary: The role of purifying selection in maintaining genomic stability.
purifying_selection_effect.details: Purifying selection prevents the slow, inexorable march of neutral mutation fixations in finite populations by eliminating mutations that reduce reproductive output (p. 369).

clock_as_mechanism.label: Molecular Clock as Mechanism
clock_as_mechanism.summary: Inference regarding the cause of molecular change.
clock_as_mechanism.details: The roughly constant accumulation of change suggests that chance (drift), rather than local adaptation, causes much of the observed molecular change (p. 369).

clock_as_tool.label: Molecular Clock as Tool
clock_as_tool.summary: Using the clock to date evolutionary divergence.
clock_as_tool.details: If calibrated with organisms of known age (e.g., from fossils), the clock can be used to date organisms without a fossil record (p. 369).

neutral_theory_premises.label: Premises of Neutral Theory
neutral_theory_premises.summary: The underlying assumptions of the theory.
neutral_theory_premises.details: The theory allows that many mutations are strongly deleterious (removed immediately) and a few are adaptive; however, the majority of variation seen within and between species is selectively equivalent (neutral) and determined by drift (p. 370).

neutral_fixation_prob.label: Probability of Neutral Fixation
neutral_fixation_prob.summary: The chance a neutral allele becomes fixed.
neutral_fixation_prob.details: The probability that a neutral allele will eventually become fixed is equal to its current frequency in the population (p. 371).

neutral_substitution_rate.label: Neutral Substitution Rate
neutral_substitution_rate.summary: The rate at which new alleles fix in a population.
neutral_substitution_rate.details: The substitution rate is essentially equal to the neutral mutation rate per generation (p. 371).

neutral_time_to_fixation.label: Average Time to Fixation
neutral_time_to_fixation.summary: The duration required for neutral mutations to reach fixation.
neutral_time_to_fixation.details: For neutral mutations destined for fixation, the average time is approximately four times the long-term population size (p. 371).

genome_evolution.label: Genome Evolution
genome_evolution.summary: The evolution of the entire DNA content of an organism, including architecture and size.

genome_architecture.label: Genome Architecture
genome_architecture.summary: The organization and size of genomes across life forms.

c_value_paradox.label: C-Value Paradox
c_value_paradox.summary: The observation that genome size does not correlate with organismal complexity.
c_value_paradox.details: The C-value (mass of DNA in a haploid cell) shows no clear correlation with the complexity of the organism (p. 374).

prokaryote_vs_eukaryote_architecture.label: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Architecture
prokaryote_vs_eukaryote_architecture.summary: Structural differences in the genomes of different cell types.

prokaryote_genome.label: Prokaryotic Genomes
prokaryote_genome.summary: Compact genomic structures in bacteria and archaea.
prokaryote_genome.details: Small and compact, comprising circular DNA with limited intergenic space and genes organized into operons (cotranscribed units) (p. 374).

eukaryote_genome.label: Eukaryotic Genomes
eukaryote_genome.details: Much larger, contained on linear chromosomes, featuring modular gene regulation and massive amounts of noncoding DNA including introns and UTRs (p. 374).

genome_restructuring.label: Genome Restructuring
genome_restructuring.summary: Mechanisms that alter the size and organization of the genome.

recombination_mechanisms.label: Recombination and Restructuring
recombination_mechanisms.summary: The role of double-strand break (DSB) repair in genomic change.

ectopic_recombination.label: Ectopic Recombination
ectopic_recombination.summary: Recombination between non-homologous but similar sequences.
ectopic_recombination.details: Occurs between repetitive elements, leading to large-scale chromosomal rearrangements like duplications, deletions, inversions, or translocations (p. 376).

recombination_hot_spots.label: Recombination Hot Spots
recombination_hot_spots.summary: Regions of the genome with high crossover rates.

prdm9_factor.label: Prdm9 Transcription Factor
prdm9_factor.summary: A driver of hot spot location in humans.
prdm9_factor.details: Prdm9 is required for activating hot spots in humans by interacting with a degenerate 13-base-pair motif; it is under strong positive selection (p. 376).

dna_transposons.label: DNA Transposons
dna_transposons.summary: Mobile elements using a specific excision mechanism.
dna_transposons.details: Replicate via a 'cut-and-paste' mechanism involving the enzyme transposase (p. 376).

retrotransposons.label: Retrotransposons
retrotransposons.summary: Mobile elements using an RNA intermediate.
retrotransposons.details: Replicate via a 'copy-and-paste' mechanism involving an RNA intermediate and reverse transcriptase (p. 376).

noncoding_element_evolution.label: Evolution of Noncoding Elements
noncoding_element_evolution.summary: The origin and role of UTRs and introns.

utr_functions.label: Untranslated Regions (UTRs)
utr_functions.summary: Non-translated sequences at the ends of mRNA.
utr_functions.details: 5' UTRs precede translation initiation; 3' UTRs follow termination and are critical for mRNA stability and nuclear export (p. 377).

intron_evolution.label: Intron Evolution
intron_evolution.summary: The proliferation and processing of intragenic sequences.

spliceosome_introns.label: Spliceosomal Introns
spliceosome_introns.summary: Introns processed by the spliceosome complex.
spliceosome_introns.details: Present in all eukaryotes; their density allows for alternative splicing, increasing transcript diversity per locus (p. 377).

nhej_introns.label: Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Introns
nhej_introns.summary: The role of NHEJ in intron gain and loss.
nhej_introns.details: Intron gain may result from the ectopic insertion of DNA fragments during NHEJ repair of double-strand breaks (p. 378).

genome_drivers.label: Drivers of Genome Evolution
genome_drivers.summary: The forces that determine genome size and complexity.

adaptive_drivers.label: Adaptive Drivers
adaptive_drivers.summary: Selection pressures that influence genome size.

mutation_bias_deletion.label: Mutation Bias (Deletion)
mutation_bias_deletion.summary: The tendency for deletions to outweigh insertions.
mutation_bias_deletion.details: Small deletions often occur more frequently than insertions (e.g., in C. elegans), which may favor a smaller genome (p. 378).

nucleoskeletal_hypothesis.label: Nucleoskeletal Hypothesis
nucleoskeletal_hypothesis.summary: A theory linking genome size to cell size.
nucleoskeletal_hypothesis.details: Proposes that genome size shapes the nucleus, and cell size and nucleus size coevolve; larger cells require larger nuclei/genomes (p. 378).

selfish_dna_hypothesis.label: Selfish DNA Hypothesis
selfish_dna_hypothesis.summary: Genome expansion driven by transposable elements.
selfish_dna_hypothesis.details: Posits that genome expansion is mediated by the proliferation of mobile elements until they reduce host fitness enough for selection to stop them (p. 378).

constructive_neutral_evolution.label: Constructive Neutral Evolution (CNE)
constructive_neutral_evolution.summary: The fixation of complex elements due to reduced selection efficacy.
constructive_neutral_evolution.details: Proposed by Stoltzfus and Lynch; in small eukaryotic populations, genetic drift is amplified, allowing neutral or slightly deleterious complex features (like introns) to become fixed (p. 379).

rates_of_molecular_change.label: Rates of Molecular Change
rates_of_molecular_change.summary: Classification of genomic regions based on their rate of evolution.

negative_selection_cg.label: Negative Selection (Purifying)
negative_selection_cg.summary: Regions evolving slower than the background rate.
negative_selection_cg.details: Indicates a functional region where most mutations decrease fitness and are purged; e.g., histone genes (p. 380).

neutral_evolution_cg.label: Neutral Evolution
neutral_evolution_cg.summary: Regions evolving at the background rate.
neutral_evolution_cg.details: Typically do not encode functional elements; examples include pseudogenes and inactivated TEs (p. 380).

positive_selection_cg.label: Positive Selection (Darwinian)
positive_selection_cg.summary: Regions evolving faster than the background rate.
positive_selection_cg.details: Mutations in these regions provide a fitness advantage and are fixed more rapidly than neutral mutations (p. 381).

gene_content_comparison.label: Gene Content Comparison
gene_content_comparison.summary: Analysis of shared and unique genes across species.

orthologues.label: Orthologues
orthologues.summary: Genes in different species derived from a common ancestor.
orthologues.details: Identified using tools like BLAST; clusters of orthologues reveal core processes essential for survival across taxa (p. 382).

synteny.label: Synteny
synteny.summary: The conservation of gene order along chromosomes.
synteny.details: Shared gene order indicates a common ancestor; in bacteria, it often signals related function (operons); in animals, e.g., Hox gene cluster (p. 382).

regulatory_region_identification.label: Identifying Regulatory Regions
regulatory_region_identification.summary: Methods to find transcription factor binding sites.

phylogenetic_shadowing.label: Phylogenetic Shadowing
phylogenetic_shadowing.summary: Identification of conserved blocks by aligning multiple species.
phylogenetic_shadowing.details: Scores rates of change on a per-nucleotide basis to identify boundaries of functional regulatory elements (p. 384).

motif_enrichment.label: Motif Enrichment
motif_enrichment.details: Assumes binding sites for a transcription factor are shared among genes with common expression patterns; counts observed motifs against a background distribution (p. 384).

copy_number_variation_cg.label: Copy Number Variation (CNV)
copy_number_variation_cg.summary: Variation in the number of copies of genomic regions between individuals.
copy_number_variation_cg.details: Can be adaptive (e.g., drug resistance in C. albicans) or linked to disease (e.g., autism/cancer in humans); detected via microarrays or NGS read depth (p. 384).

ultraconserved_elements.label: Ultraconserved Elements
ultraconserved_elements.summary: Long segments of DNA with extremely high similarity across distant species.
ultraconserved_elements.details: Stretches of 100+ bp with >90% identity; often do not encode proteins but may be functional regulatory elements (p. 386).

sex_determination_systems.label: Sex Determination Systems
sex_determination_systems.summary: The diverse mechanisms used to trigger sexual differentiation.

gsd.label: Genotypic Sex Determination (GSD)
gsd.summary: Sex determined primarily by genetic factors.

male_heterogamety.label: Male Heterogamety
male_heterogamety.summary: Males have different sex chromosomes (e.g., XY).
male_heterogamety.details: Found in mammals and Drosophila; males are XY, females are XX (p. 387).

female_heterogamety.label: Female Heterogamety
female_heterogamety.summary: Females have different sex chromosomes (e.g., ZW).
female_heterogamety.details: Found in birds, snakes, and butterflies; females are ZW, males are ZZ (p. 387).

haplodiploidy.label: Haplodiploidy
haplodiploidy.details: Males are haploid (unfertilized eggs), females are diploid (fertilized eggs); common in Hymenoptera (p. 395).

esd.label: Environmental Sex Determination (ESD)
esd.details: Cues include temperature (crocodiles, turtles), photoperiod (amphipods), or social hierarchy (anemone fish) (p. 395).

sexual_antagonism.label: Sexual Antagonism
sexual_antagonism.summary: Alleles that provide fitness benefits to one sex but costs to the other.

antagonism_and_recombination.label: Antagonism and Recombination Suppression
antagonism_and_recombination.summary: How sexual antagonism leads to distinct sex chromosomes.
antagonism_and_recombination.details: Selection favors the suppression of recombination between the sex-determining region and sexually antagonistic alleles to ensure beneficial genes are restricted to the favored sex (p. 389).

y_w_degeneration.label: Y (W)-Chromosome Degeneration
y_w_degeneration.summary: The loss of genes and accumulation of repetitive DNA on the heterogametic chromosome.

mullers_ratchet.label: Muller's Ratchet
mullers_ratchet.summary: Irreversible accumulation of deleterious mutations in non-recombining chromosomes.
mullers_ratchet.details: In finite populations, the mutation-free class of chromosomes can be lost stochastically; without recombination, this loss is irreversible (p. 391).

genetic_hitchhiking.label: Genetic Hitchhiking
genetic_hitchhiking.summary: The fixation of deleterious mutations alongside beneficial ones.
genetic_hitchhiking.details: A beneficial mutation occurring on a chromosome with deleterious mutations will drag the deleterious mutations to fixation if recombination is absent (p. 391).

ruby_in_rubbish.label: Ruby in the Rubbish
ruby_in_rubbish.summary: The loss of weakly beneficial mutations due to strong deleterious linkages.
ruby_in_rubbish.details: Weakly beneficial mutations linked to strongly deleterious mutations are eliminated by purifying selection on a non-recombining Y chromosome (p. 391).

dosage_compensation.label: Dosage Compensation
dosage_compensation.summary: Mechanisms to balance the expression of sex-linked genes in the heterogametic sex.

drosophila_compensation.label: Drosophila Dosage Compensation
drosophila_compensation.summary: Male-specific upregulation of the X chromosome.
drosophila_compensation.details: A male-specific ribonucleoprotein complex targets the X chromosome to increase transcription, balancing X and autosomal products (p. 392).

mammalian_compensation.label: Mammalian Dosage Compensation
mammalian_compensation.summary: A two-step process involving upregulation and female X-inactivation.
mammalian_compensation.details: Initial upregulation of X in both sexes is followed by the complete inactivation of one X chromosome in females using noncoding RNAs (p. 392).

gene_duplication.label: Gene Duplication
gene_duplication.summary: The process by which a segment of DNA containing genes is duplicated.

duplication_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Gene Duplication
duplication_mechanisms.summary: Ways in which duplicate genes are generated.

unequal_crossing_over.label: Unequal Crossing-Over
unequal_crossing_over.summary: Non-reciprocal exchange between mispaired homologous chromosomes.
unequal_crossing_over.details: Results in tandem duplicates arrayed next to each other on the chromosome (p. 398).

retroposition.label: Retroposition
retroposition.summary: Duplication via reverse transcription of mRNA.
retroposition.details: mRNA is reverse transcribed to cDNA and inserted randomly into the genome; retroduplicates lack introns and promoters (p. 398).

chromosomal_duplication.label: Chromosomal and Genome Duplication
chromosomal_duplication.summary: Large-scale duplication of chromosomes or the entire genome.
chromosomal_duplication.details: Chromosomal duplication occurs via nondisjunction (aneuploidy). Genome duplication (polyploidization) can be autopolyploidy (single species) or allopolyploidy (hybrid species) (p. 398).

duplication_fixation.label: Fixation of Duplicate Genes
duplication_fixation.summary: Factors determining if a duplication persists in a population.

deleterious_duplication.label: Deleterious Duplication
deleterious_duplication.details: May impose energy costs, break sensitive dosage balance (e.g., autosomal trisomies), or disrupt other functional elements (p. 399).

beneficial_duplication.label: Beneficial Duplication
beneficial_duplication.details: Provides extra gene product when needed (e.g., rRNA genes for ribosomes, salivary amylase for starch diets) (p. 399).

duplication_outcomes.label: Outcomes of Duplicate Genes
duplication_outcomes.summary: The evolutionary paths of fixed duplicate genes.

pseudogenization.label: Pseudogenization
pseudogenization.summary: The loss of function in one of the duplicate genes.
pseudogenization.details: Because duplicates are functionally redundant, mutations that knock out one copy often have no fitness cost, leading to its conversion into a pseudogene (p. 400).

divergent_resolution.label: Divergent Resolution
divergent_resolution.details: When different duplicate genes are lost in isolated populations, hybrids may lack essential functions, creating reproductive isolation (p. 400).

neofunctionalization.label: Neofunctionalization
neofunctionalization.summary: The acquisition of a completely new function by one duplicate.
neofunctionalization.details: One copy maintains the ancestral function while the other evolves a new, qualitatively different function (p. 401).

subfunctionalization.label: Subfunctionalization
subfunctionalization.summary: The division of ancestral functions between two duplicates.
subfunctionalization.details: The progenitor's functions are split between daughter genes such that both are now required to fulfill the original role (p. 397).

concerted_evolution.label: Concerted Evolution
concerted_evolution.summary: Homogenization of gene family members within a species.
concerted_evolution.details: Occurs via gene conversion, making members of a gene family within one species more similar to each other than to orthologues in other species (p. 397/401).

retention_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms for Stable Retention of Duplicate Genes
retention_mechanisms.summary: The evolutionary pathways that allow duplicate genes to be maintained in the genome rather than becoming pseudogenes.

neo_fact_1.label: ECP Example
neo_fact_1.summary: Eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN) duplicated; the resulting ECP acquired antibacterial activity not found in EDN, driven by positive Darwinian selection (p. 402).

sub_fact_1.label: Zebrafish engrailed-1 Example
sub_fact_1.summary: In zebrafish, eng1 is expressed in the pectoral appendage bud and eng1b in hindbrain/spinal cord neurons; in tetrapods (mice/chickens), a single En1 gene covers both domains (p. 402).

escape_adaptive_conflict.label: Escape from Adaptive Conflict (EAC)
escape_adaptive_conflict.summary: A hybrid model where an ancestral gene has dual functions that conflict (optimizing one compromises the other). Duplication allows each copy to optimize one function without conflict.

eac_fact_1.label: Yeast GAL Genes Example
eac_fact_1.summary: GAL1 and GAL3 in yeast evolved from a progenitor with dual functions; replacing either with the progenitor reduces fitness, indicating quantitative improvement of ancestral functions (p. 402).

dosage_advantage.label: Dosage Advantage / Concerted Evolution
dosage_advantage.summary: Retention occurs when a high concentration of the gene product is beneficial to the organism.

duplication_rates.label: Rates of Gene Duplication
duplication_rates.summary: The frequency at which gene duplication occurs and is fixed within a population.

rate_fact_1.label: Fixed Duplication Rate
rate_fact_1.summary: Fixed duplicate genes arise at approximately 0.01 per gene per million years in eukaryotic model organisms (p. 403).

rate_fact_2.label: Mutational Rate vs Fixation
rate_fact_2.summary: Mutational rates (10^-6 in yeast, 10^-7 in C. elegans) are orders of magnitude higher than fixation rates, suggesting most duplications are deleterious (p. 403).

duplicability_determinants.label: Determinants of Gene Duplicability
duplicability_determinants.summary: Factors influencing the probability that a gene is duplicated, fixed, and stably retained.

balance_hypothesis.label: Balance Hypothesis
balance_hypothesis.summary: Genes encoding members of protein complexes have reduced individual duplication rates to avoid deleterious dosage imbalances; however, they are preferentially retained after Whole Genome Duplication (WGD) (p. 403).

complexity_hypothesis.label: Gene Complexity Hypothesis
complexity_hypothesis.summary: More complex genes (longer proteins, more domains, more cis-regulatory motifs) have higher duplicability due to higher retention probabilities via faster subfunctionalization (p. 404).

functional_redundancy.label: Functional Redundancy
functional_redundancy.summary: The functional similarity between duplicate genes, where deleting one has a smaller fitness effect than deleting a singleton gene.

redundancy_hypotheses.label: Hypotheses for Long-term Redundancy
redundancy_hypotheses.summary: Theories explaining why some duplicates remain redundant for millions of years.

backup_hypothesis.label: Backup Hypothesis
backup_hypothesis.summary: Redundancy protects against deleterious mutations, acting like a 'spare tire' (p. 404).

piggyback_hypothesis.label: Piggy-back Hypothesis
piggyback_hypothesis.summary: Overlapping functions are by-products of strong protein structural constraints while the genes perform non-overlapping functions (p. 404).

expression_reduction_hypothesis.label: Expression Reduction Hypothesis
expression_reduction_hypothesis.summary: A form of subfunctionalization where total expression is split (e.g., 60/40), requiring both copies for full fitness, creating an appearance of redundancy (p. 404).

functional_diversification.label: Functional Diversification
functional_diversification.summary: The process by which duplicate genes evolve different activities, specificities, or expression patterns.

isozyme_fact.label: Isozymes
isozyme_fact.summary: Duplicate genes encoding enzymes that catalyze the same reaction but have different catalytic parameters or expression domains (p. 405).

or_gene_fact.label: Odorant Receptor (OR) Genes
or_gene_fact.summary: The largest gene family in vertebrates; expansion via duplication allows detection of 10,000+ odorants (p. 405).

new_gene_evolution.label: Evolution of New Genes
new_gene_evolution.summary: The origination of genes in genomic locations where they did not previously exist and the subsequent evolution of novel functions.

origination_mechanisms.label: Mutational Mechanisms of New Gene Origination
origination_mechanisms.summary: The specific genetic processes that create new protein-coding genes.

gilbert_model.label: Gilbert Model
gilbert_model.summary: Origination via exon/domain shuffling, creating chimeric genes (p. 407).

brosius_model.label: Brosius Model
brosius_model.summary: Origination via retroposition (RNA-based duplication); results in retrogenes lacking introns with a poly(A) tail (p. 407).

te_domestication.label: Transposable Element (TE) Domestication
te_domestication.summary: TEs are incorporated into nuclear genes to create new coding regions; e.g., Alu TE in human DAF gene (p. 407).

lgt_mechanism.label: Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT)
lgt_mechanism.summary: Transfer of gene copies between different organisms; documented in eukaryotes (e.g., Wolbachia in Drosophila) (p. 407).

frameshift_mechanism.label: Frameshift Mutation Model
frameshift_mechanism.summary: Reading frame shifts in duplicate copies create novel protein families (p. 407).

de_novo_origination.label: De Novo Origination
de_novo_origination.summary: Genes arising from previously noncoding or intergenic regions accumulating mutations to create open reading frames (p. 407).

new_gene_patterns.label: Patterns of New Gene Evolution
new_gene_patterns.summary: Observations regarding the genomic distribution and expression of new genes.

gene_trafficking.label: Gene Trafficking
gene_trafficking.summary: The movement of genes between sex chromosomes and autosomes; Drosophila shows X-to-autosome bias, while mammals show bidirectional trafficking (p. 409).

testis_expression_pattern.label: Testis-Specific Expression
testis_expression_pattern.summary: X-derived autosomal retrogenes frequently evolve testis-specific expression in both Drosophila and mammals (p. 410).

forces_on_new_genes.label: Evolutionary Forces Acting on New Genes
forces_on_new_genes.summary: The roles of selection and drift in the fixation and optimization of new genes.

fixation_forces.label: Forces During Fixation
fixation_forces.summary: Initial duplication is often slightly deleterious (purifying selection), but some (e.g., toxin response genes) are favored by positive selection (p. 410).

post_fixation_forces.label: Forces Post-Fixation
post_fixation_forces.summary: Rapid sequence evolution driven by positive selection initially, followed by slower evolution shaped by purifying selection (p. 411). Example: Jingwei gene (p. 411).

expression_evolution.label: Evolution of Gene Expression
expression_evolution.summary: Changes in the timing, location, and amount of gene product, often playing a larger role in phenotypic divergence than protein-coding changes.

regulatory_sources.label: Genomic Sources of Regulatory Evolution
regulatory_sources.summary: The DNA and protein components that control transcription.

cis_regulatory_elements.label: Cis-Regulatory Elements (CREs)
cis_regulatory_elements.summary: DNA sequences near the gene, including the basal promoter (highly conserved) and enhancers (more divergent, lower pleiotropy) (p. 415).

trans_regulatory_factors.label: Trans-Regulatory Factors
trans_regulatory_factors.summary: Transcription factor (TF) proteins that bind to CREs to regulate expression (p. 415).

enhancer_conservation.label: Enhancer Sequence Conservation
enhancer_conservation.summary: Enhancers can undergo extensive sequence rearrangement and TF binding site changes while maintaining the same spatiotemporal activity (p. 417).

enhancer_origination.label: Origination of New Enhancers
enhancer_origination.summary: Most new enhancers arise via duplication and divergence, transposition, or co-option (repurposing existing elements) (p. 417).

tf_evolution.label: Evolution of Transcription Factors
tf_evolution.summary: TFs are highly conserved, especially in DNA binding domains; divergence occurs primarily via changes in their target genes (p. 418).

pax6_example.label: Pax-6/eyeless Example
pax6_example.summary: Orthologous Pax-6 (mouse) and eyeless (Drosophila) can induce ectopic eyes in Drosophila, demonstrating deep conservation of master regulators (p. 418).

epigenetics.label: Epigenetics
epigenetics.summary: Stable, reversible phenotypic changes without changes in the underlying DNA genotype.

molecular_epigenetics.label: Molecular Epigenetics
molecular_epigenetics.summary: The chemical modifications of DNA and proteins that regulate gene activity.

histone_modification.label: Histone Modification
histone_modification.summary: Chemical changes to histone proteins (e.g., acetylation, methylation) that alter chromatin packaging; acetylation is generally associated with activity (p. 422).

dna_methylation.label: DNA Methylation
dna_methylation.summary: Attachment of methyl groups to cytosine (5-methylcytosine), generally associated with gene silencing and the suppression of transposable elements (p. 422).

maintenance_proteins.label: Maintenance Proteins (PcG and trxG)
maintenance_proteins.summary: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins keep genes silent, while trithorax group (trxG) proteins keep them active, creating epigenetic memory (p. 422).

epigenetic_processes.label: Epigenetic Processes
epigenetic_processes.summary: Specific biological phenomena driven by epigenetic mechanisms.

genomic_imprinting.label: Genomic Imprinting
genomic_imprinting.summary: Parent-of-origin specific expression of alleles; often explained by the 'conflict of interest' between maternal and paternal genes regarding embryo growth (p. 423).

x_inactivation.label: X-Inactivation
x_inactivation.summary: Random silencing of one X chromosome in female mammals to balance gene dosage, initiated by the Xist noncoding RNA (p. 423).

paramutation.label: Paramutation
paramutation.summary: An interaction where one allele permanently silences another allele with an identical DNA sequence (e.g., maize b1 gene) (p. 423).

reprogramming.label: Reprogramming
reprogramming.summary: The resetting of epigenetic marks, occurring in early embryos and primordial germ cells to restore pluripotency (p. 423).

plant_transgenerational.label: Plant Transgenerational Effects
plant_transgenerational.summary: Examples include heritable epialleles (toadflax, tomato, melon) and induced responses to stress/predators (Mimulus trichomes, Arabidopsis heat response) (p. 424).

animal_transgenerational.label: Animal Transgenerational Effects
animal_transgenerational.summary: Examples include the Agouti viable yellow (Avy) mouse coat color, C. elegans viral silencing/odor preferences, and rat maternal care behaviors (p. 424-425).

network_evolution.label: Evolution of Molecular Networks
network_evolution.summary: The study of biological interactions represented as graphs to understand cellular organization and robustness.

network_terminology.label: Network Terminology
network_terminology.summary: The basic building blocks of a biological network.

node_def.label: Node
node_def.summary: A component of a network (e.g., metabolite, protein, gene) that enters into pairwise interactions (p. 429).

edge_def.label: Edge
edge_def.summary: An interaction between two nodes; can be directed (arrows, representing flow or regulation) or undirected (lines, representing physical association) (p. 429).

global_organization.label: Global Network Organization
global_organization.summary: The overall connectivity pattern of a network.

random_networks.label: Random Networks
random_networks.summary: Networks where edges are drawn with equal probability; node degree follows a Poisson distribution (p. 431).

scale_free_networks.label: Scale-Free Networks
scale_free_networks.summary: Networks characterized by a power-law degree distribution, featuring a few highly connected 'hubs' and many poorly connected nodes; they exhibit the 'small world' property (p. 431).

hub_hypothesis.label: The Hub Hypothesis
hub_hypothesis.summary: Hypothesizes that hubs are more critical to fitness and that scale-free organization makes networks robust to random mutation/failure (p. 432).

local_organization.label: Local Network Organization
local_organization.summary: The patterns of connection among small subsets of nodes, referred to as network motifs.

feedforward_loop.label: Feedforward Loop
feedforward_loop.summary: A motif where transcription factor X regulates TF Y, and both X and Y jointly regulate target gene Z; can act as a filter for short pulses of X (p. 430).

network_organization.label: Biological Network Organization
network_organization.summary: The study of global and local patterns of connectivity in biological systems, such as protein-protein interaction (PPI) and gene regulatory networks (GRNs).

ppi_essentiality.label: Protein-Interaction Degree and Essentiality
ppi_essentiality.summary: The relationship between a protein's connectivity (degree) and its requirement for organismal viability.

fact_ppi_correlation.label: Positive Correlation of Hubs
fact_ppi_correlation.summary: A significant positive correlation exists between protein-interaction degree and essentiality; hubs are more likely to be required for viability (p. 433).

fact_ppi_heterogeneity.label: Functional Heterogeneity of Edges
fact_ppi_heterogeneity.summary: Unlike the Internet, edges in PPI networks capture a heterogeneous set of biological functions, some of which are information transmission (e.g., kinase phosphorylation), while others are not (p. 433).

genome_content_scaling.label: Genome Content Scaling
genome_content_scaling.summary: How the number of genes in specific functional categories scales relative to the total genome size.

fact_transcription_factor_scaling.label: Transcription Factor Power Law
fact_transcription_factor_scaling.summary: The number of genes encoding transcription factors scales as a power law (approximately squared) relative to the total number of genes in the genome (p. 433).

null_models_evolution.label: Null Models of Network Evolution
null_models_evolution.summary: The theoretical frameworks used to distinguish between adaptive and non-adaptive causes of network structure.

fact_adaptationist_bias.label: Adaptationist View of Robustness
fact_adaptationist_bias.summary: Early attempts to explain scale-free networks often viewed robustness to random failure as a selectively advantageous cause of connectivity distribution, rather than a by-product (p. 433).

fact_lynch_wagner_critique.label: Lack of Population Genetic Grounding
fact_lynch_wagner_critique.summary: Michael Lynch and Andreas Wagner argue that network evolution lacks rigorous population genetics null models, unlike molecular evolution (p. 433).

regulatory_dynamics.label: Regulatory Network Dynamics
regulatory_dynamics.summary: The relationship between the structure of a regulatory network and its temporal behavior.

gap_kinetic_constants.label: Lack of Kinetic Rate Constants
gap_kinetic_constants.summary: The difficulty in measuring in vivo transcription factor binding/release and mRNA production/degradation rates (p. 433).

gap_combinatorial_logic.label: Combinatorial Logic Gap
gap_combinatorial_logic.summary: Transcriptional regulation is combinatorial, using logic functions (e.g., AND logic where both activators are needed; OR logic where either is sufficient), but these are mostly unknown (p. 434).

network_robustness.label: Regulatory Robustness
network_robustness.summary: The property where many combinations of parameter values are consistent with the observed data, meaning exact kinetic values may not matter for stability (p. 433-434).

fact_repressor_stability.label: Repressor Feedback Stability
fact_repressor_stability.summary: A transcription factor that represses its own expression tends toward stability or stable oscillation (p. 434).

fact_activator_instability.label: Activator Feedback Instability
fact_activator_instability.summary: A transcription factor that activates its own expression is unstable and can produce switch-like transitions (p. 434).

network_motifs.label: Network Motifs
network_motifs.summary: Small, overrepresented regulatory subnetworks with predictable kinetic behaviors.

fact_feedforward_loop.label: Feedforward Loop (FFL)
fact_feedforward_loop.summary: A motif where two TFs jointly regulate a target and one TF regulates the other; with AND logic, it acts as a noise filter, requiring a sustained pulse for activation (p. 434).

subcircuit_types.label: Developmental Subcircuits
subcircuit_types.summary: Modular groups of genes that function as units in development.

plug_ins.label: Plug-ins
plug_ins.summary: Small subcircuits that perform specific molecular functions but are deployed for many different developmental purposes (p. 434).

kernels.label: Kernels
kernels.summary: Evolutionarily conserved, densely interconnected regulatory factors that execute a single developmental function; loss leads to failure (p. 434).

fact_kernel_divergence.label: Phylogenetic Divergence Hypothesis
fact_kernel_divergence.summary: Deep phylum-level divergences correspond to kernels; intermediate divergences to plug-ins; recent divergences to terminal-differentiation genes (p. 434).

developmental_drift.label: Developmental Systems Drift
developmental_drift.summary: The phenomenon where the essential output of a regulatory subcircuit remains unchanged despite changes in its membership and interconnections (p. 434).

candidate_gene_approach.label: Candidate Gene Approach
candidate_gene_approach.summary: Investigating genes suspected of playing a role in trait evolution based on expression patterns or homology (p. 446).

fact_bmp4_calmodulin.label: Finch Beak Regulation
fact_bmp4_calmodulin.summary: Bmp4 and Calmodulin are differentially expressed in Galápagos finches to produce deep/broad vs. long beaks (p. 446).

qtl_mapping_evo.label: QTL Mapping in Evo-Devo
qtl_mapping_evo.summary: Using laboratory crosses to pinpoint causative mutations responsible for species-level differences (p. 446).

fact_svb_trichomes.label: shavenbaby-ovo (svb) Locus
fact_svb_trichomes.summary: The svb locus and its cis-regulatory elements control larval trichome patterns in Drosophila (p. 446).

molecular_mechanisms.label: Molecular Mechanisms of Development
molecular_mechanisms.summary: The biochemistry of gene regulation that builds tissues and organs.

transcription_factors.label: Transcription Factors (TFs)
transcription_factors.summary: Proteins that bind to DNA to induce or repress the transcription of target genes (p. 445).

enhancers.label: Enhancers / Cis-Regulatory Elements
enhancers.summary: DNA sequences that regulate the temporal and spatial expression of genes when bound by specific TFs (p. 445).

reciprocal_transplantation.label: Reciprocal Locus Transplantation
reciprocal_transplantation.summary: An experimental method using transgenics to determine if expression differences between species are due to cis-regulatory changes or trans-regulatory environment changes (p. 447).

modular_grns.label: Modular Gene Regulatory Networks
modular_grns.summary: Interacting groups of genes activated together in a context-independent manner.

selector_genes.label: Selector Genes
selector_genes.summary: Regulatory genes that specify cell, tissue, or regional identity (e.g., Hox genes) (p. 448).

fact_hox_appendages.label: Hox Gene Specification
fact_hox_appendages.summary: Hox genes specify the identity of arthropod appendages (feeding vs. walking legs) and inhibit limb development in the abdomen of flies (p. 448).

fact_pitx1_pelvic.label: Pitx1 and Pelvic Fins
fact_pitx1_pelvic.summary: Deletion of a pelvic-specific enhancer of Pitx1 leads to pelvic fin loss in sticklebacks without affecting pectoral fins (p. 449).

cooption_mechanisms.label: Network Co-option
cooption_mechanisms.summary: The process of deploying an existing modular GRN in a novel location or time to create a new trait (p. 449).

fact_dll_appendages.label: Distal-less (Dll) Co-option
fact_dll_appendages.summary: The Dll gene initiates the limb network and can be co-opted to produce ectopic outgrowths or beetle horns (p. 448-449).

fact_pax6_eyes.label: Pax6 and Eye Development
fact_pax6_eyes.summary: Pax6 is a master regulator of eye development throughout Metazoa; ectopic expression can induce ectopic eyes (p. 448).

plasticity_robustness.label: Plasticity and Robustness
plasticity_robustness.summary: The capacity of a genotype to produce different phenotypes in response to the environment versus the capacity to resist perturbation.

developmental_robustness.label: Developmental Robustness
developmental_robustness.summary: Insensitivity to environmental or genetic perturbations, often achieved via regulatory wiring or gene duplication, creating cryptic genetic variation (p. 450).

genetic_architecture.label: Genetic Architecture of Evolution
genetic_architecture.summary: The number and effect sizes of genetic changes that drive phenotypic adaptation.

infinitesimal_model.label: Infinitesimal Model
infinitesimal_model.summary: The view that evolution occurs via an infinite number of genetic changes, each with an extremely small phenotypic effect (Fisher) (p. 452).

geometric_model.label: Geometric Model
geometric_model.summary: The view that phenotypic evolution involves a few genetic changes with large effects and many with smaller effects (Kimura/Orr) (p. 452).

supergenes_inversions.label: Supergenes and Chromosomal Inversions
supergenes_inversions.summary: Clusters of genes that are coinherited because chromosomal rearrangements (inversions) suppress recombination (p. 453-454).

fact_mimicry_heliconius.label: Heliconius Wing Patterns
fact_mimicry_heliconius.summary: Supergene complexes control mimicry in Heliconius butterflies, where multiple traits map to a single locus (p. 453).

fact_mimulus_inversion.label: Mimulus guttatus Local Adaptation
fact_mimulus_inversion.summary: A chromosomal inversion in yellow monkeyflowers controls flowering time and morphology, conferring fitness in cool/wet vs. hot/dry habitats (p. 454).

molecular_basis_phenotype.label: Molecular Basis of Phenotypic Change
molecular_basis_phenotype.summary: The distinction between changes in protein-coding sequences and cis-regulatory regions.

coding_mutations.label: Coding Sequence Mutations
coding_mutations.summary: Changes to the amino acid sequence of a protein; a single nucleotide mutation can cause large phenotypic effects (e.g., Mc1r gene) (p. 454).

regulatory_mutations.label: Regulatory Mutations
regulatory_mutations.summary: Changes to enhancers that control where and when a gene is expressed; can be single events (sticklebacks) or multiple base-pair changes (fruit flies) (p. 454).

repeated_evolution.label: Repeated Phenotypic Evolution
repeated_evolution.summary: The appearance of similar phenotypes in independent lineages (Parallel: related; Convergent: distant).

reused_genes_reasons.label: Reasons for Repeated Use of Genes
reused_genes_reasons.summary: Factors that make certain genes 'hot spots' for repeated evolution (p. 455-456).

fact_mutational_bias.label: Mutational Bias
fact_mutational_bias.summary: Some genes are larger targets for mutation or are in fragile genomic regions (e.g., Pitx1 enhancer in sticklebacks) (p. 455).

fact_pleiotropic_constraints.label: Pleiotropic Constraints
fact_pleiotropic_constraints.summary: Genes with low pleiotropy (few side effects) or mutations in tissue-specific enhancers are more likely to be reused (e.g., Mc1r) (p. 456).

fact_historical_contingency.label: Historical Contingency
fact_historical_contingency.summary: Standing genetic variation in an ancestral population can be repeatedly selected in new environments (e.g., Ectodysplasin in sticklebacks) (p. 456).

genomic_mapping.label: Genomic Mapping of Complex Traits
genomic_mapping.summary: Methods to identify the genetic basis of phenotypes controlled by multiple factors.

qtl_mapping_complex.label: QTL Mapping for Complex Traits
qtl_mapping_complex.summary: Mapping quantitative trait loci by looking for cosegregation in offspring from laboratory crosses (p. 459).

interval_mapping.label: Interval Mapping
interval_mapping.summary: Using markers flanking a genomic position to estimate the probability of a QTL existing at that location (p. 460).

lod_score.label: LOD Score
lod_score.summary: The log10-transformed likelihood ratio used to identify QTL peaks on a chromosome (p. 460).

association_testing.label: Association Testing / GWAS
association_testing.summary: Comparing phenotypes and genotypes in large samples of unrelated individuals to find markers linked to traits (p. 461).

missing_heritability.label: Missing Heritability
missing_heritability.summary: The observation that identified GWAS variants explain only a fraction of the genetic variance estimated from family studies (p. 464).

genomic_variation.label: Genomic Variation and Trait Mapping
genomic_variation.summary: Methods for identifying the genetic origins of phenotypic differences within populations.

gwas.label: Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)
gwas.summary: An approach to identify loci contributing to trait variation by sampling unrelated individuals from a population.
