gwas_methodology.label: GWAS Methodology
gwas_methodology.summary: The process of identifying SNPs and genotyping large samples.

fact_gwas_sample_size.label: Sample Size Requirements
fact_gwas_sample_size.summary: Sampling hundreds of individuals may suffice for finding loci that contribute disproportionately to trait variation (p. 465).

fact_gwas_snp_process.label: SNP Array Development
fact_gwas_snp_process.summary: Sequence genomes of few individuals using next-gen sequencing, identify common SNPs, and develop an array for larger population genotyping (p. 465).

gwas_resources.label: GWAS Resources
gwas_resources.summary: Tools and databases used for association testing.

fact_gwas_resource_cost.label: Cost Accessibility
fact_gwas_resource_cost.summary: Rapid advances in sequencing/genotyping are making GWAS accessible to biologists studying non-traditional genetic models (p. 465).

genotype_phenotype_challenges.label: Genotype-Phenotype Association Challenges
genotype_phenotype_challenges.summary: Difficulties in moving from a identified genomic region to a causative mutation.

fact_ld_problem.label: Linkage Disequilibrium (LD)
fact_ld_problem.summary: Causative mutations are hard to pinpoint because multiple mutations in linkage disequilibrium are typically found in associated intervals (p. 465).

fact_functional_studies_necessity.label: Role of Functional Studies
fact_functional_studies_necessity.summary: Functional studies are ultimately needed to identify causative mutations, regardless of variant prioritization (coding vs noncoding, conservation, biochemical effects) (p. 465).

adaptation_genomics.label: Searching for Adaptation in the Genome
adaptation_genomics.summary: Using population and comparative genomics to detect signatures of natural selection.

adaptation_glossary.label: Adaptation Glossary
adaptation_glossary.summary: Core technical definitions for population genomics.

fact_def_adaptation.label: Adaptation
fact_def_adaptation.summary: The process by which a population evolves to having greater fitness in a given environment (p. 466).

fact_def_ne.label: Effective Population Size (Ne)
fact_def_ne.summary: The size of an idealized population that models the evolutionary dynamics of a real population N(t); generally smaller than census size. Short-term Ne affects rapid adaptation, long-term Ne affects slow neutral processes (p. 466).

fact_def_fixation.label: Fixation
fact_def_fixation.summary: Process where a new mutation becomes present in all individuals in a species (p. 466).

fact_def_hitchhiking.label: Hitchhiking
fact_def_hitchhiking.summary: Change of allele frequency of a polymorphism allele due to linkage to selected alleles in the genomic vicinity (p. 466).

fact_def_mutation.label: Mutation
fact_def_mutation.summary: DNA sequence change ranging from single nucleotides to structural changes (insertions, deletions, translocations, inversions) or whole genome polyploidization (p. 466).

fact_def_polymorphism.label: Polymorphism
fact_def_polymorphism.summary: A genetic variant (allele) present in some but not all individuals in a species (p. 466).

fact_def_substitution.label: Substitution
fact_def_substitution.summary: The outcome of fixation of a new mutation, observed by comparing DNA sequences of different species (p. 466).

fact_def_synonymous.label: Synonymous Mutation
fact_def_synonymous.summary: Mutation in protein-coding sequence that does not change the amino acid sequence (p. 466).

evolution_phases.label: Phases of Evolution
evolution_phases.summary: The two-step process of evolutionary change.

fact_phase_1_origination.label: Phase 1: Origination
fact_phase_1_origination.summary: The creation of new alleles by mutation, appearing in a single individual or few siblings (p. 467).

fact_phase_2_frequency_change.label: Phase 2: Allele Frequency Change
fact_phase_2_frequency_change.summary: The process by which new variants become established as polymorphisms or substitutions; this is where natural selection acts (p. 467).

fact_purifying_selection.label: Purifying Selection
fact_purifying_selection.summary: Natural selection that acts against deleterious alleles, purging them and preserving ancestral states (p. 467).

fact_positive_selection.label: Positive Selection
fact_positive_selection.summary: Natural selection that promotes the increase and eventual fixation of advantageous alleles, speeding up divergence (p. 467).

fact_neutral_postulate.label: Neutral Postulate
fact_neutral_postulate.summary: Postulates that practically all mutations are either deleterious or neutral, and all detectable polymorphisms and substitutions are neutral (p. 468).

fact_fixation_probability_neutral.label: Neutral Fixation Probability
fact_fixation_probability_neutral.summary: The probability of fixation of a neutral mutation is the reciprocal of the long-term effective population size (1/Ne) (p. 468).

fact_fixation_probability_adaptive.label: Adaptive Fixation Probability
fact_fixation_probability_adaptive.summary: The probability of fixation for a strongly advantageous mutation is roughly equal to its selective benefit (p. 468).

mk_test.label: McDonald-Kreitman (MK) Test
mk_test.summary: A test to detect adaptive substitutions by comparing polymorphism and divergence ratios.

fact_mk_variables.label: MK Test Variables
fact_mk_variables.summary: Pn: nonsynonymous polymorphism; Ps: synonymous polymorphism; Dn: nonsynonymous divergence; Ds: synonymous divergence (p. 468).

fact_mk_neutral_expectation.label: MK Neutral Expectation
fact_mk_neutral_expectation.summary: Under neutral theory, the ratio of functional to nonfunctional polymorphisms (Pn/Ps) should equal the ratio of functional to nonfunctional substitutions (Dn/Ds) (p. 469).

fact_mk_adaptive_signature.label: MK Adaptive Signature
fact_mk_adaptive_signature.summary: Adaptive substitutions are identified as the excess of divergence at functional sites relative to neutral expectations: Dn - Ds * (Pn/Ps) (p. 469).

fact_mk_biases.label: MK Test Biases
fact_mk_biases.summary: Slightly deleterious mutations can bias results; if mistaken for neutral polymorphisms, they can cause an underestimation of adaptive evolution (p. 470).

selective_sweeps.label: Selective Sweeps
selective_sweeps.summary: The reduction of polymorphism around an adaptive mutation due to hitchhiking.

hard_sweeps.label: Hard Sweeps
hard_sweeps.summary: A single de novo adaptive mutation rises to fixation, dragging linked neutral variants with it and creating a dearth of polymorphism (p. 471).

fact_sweep_range.label: Detection Range of Sweeps
fact_sweep_range.summary: The distance over which a sweep is detected is roughly 0.1 s/r, where s is selection strength and r is recombination rate (p. 471).

soft_sweeps.label: Soft Sweeps
soft_sweeps.summary: Adaptation driven by multiple adaptive mutations on multiple haplotypes rising simultaneously (p. 472).

fact_soft_sweep_standing_variation.label: Standing Variation
fact_soft_sweep_standing_variation.summary: Occurs when a neutral or slightly deleterious allele becomes adaptive due to environmental change (p. 472).

fact_soft_sweep_multiple_origin.label: Multiple-Origin De Novo Mutations
fact_soft_sweep_multiple_origin.summary: Occurs when independent adaptive mutations arise at the same site in large populations (p. 472).

sweep_statistics.label: Statistics for Sweep Detection
sweep_statistics.summary: Quantitative methods to identify selective sweeps.

fact_ehh.label: Extended Haplotype Homozygosity (EHH)
fact_ehh.summary: Detects partial sweeps by comparing the lengths of haplotypes linked to alternative states of a SNP (p. 472).

fact_tajimas_d.label: Tajima's D
fact_tajimas_d.summary: Detects complete sweeps; negative values indicate a bias toward rare variants compared to neutral expectations (p. 472).

ancient_dna.label: Ancient DNA (aDNA)
ancient_dna.summary: Study of DNA sequence data recovered from decayed organisms.

adna_challenges.label: aDNA Technical Challenges
adna_challenges.summary: Issues regarding the degradation and contamination of old samples.

fact_adna_deamination.label: Cytosine Deamination
fact_adna_deamination.summary: Most common hydrolytic damage where cytosine converts to uracil, read as thymine, leading to A-T substitutions in the sequence (p. 476).

fact_adna_contamination.label: Contaminating DNA
fact_adna_contamination.summary: Modern DNA introduced from the environment or handler; managed by separate extraction and post-PCR facilities (p. 476).

fact_adna_dark_days.label: The Dark Days
fact_adna_dark_days.summary: A period in the 1990s featuring false claims of dinosaur DNA and million-year-old plant DNA caused by contamination (p. 476).

adna_applications.label: aDNA Applications
adna_applications.summary: Uses of ancient DNA in phylogeny and population genetics.

fact_adna_phylogeny.label: Phylogenetic Resolution
fact_adna_phylogeny.summary: Used to clarify relationships, such as showing mammoths are closer to Asian than African elephants (p. 477).

fact_adna_popgen.label: Ancient Population Genetics
fact_adna_popgen.summary: Allows estimation of demographic history, such as the peak and decline of North American bison diversity (p. 479).

fact_adna_sedimentary.label: Sedimentary DNA
fact_adna_sedimentary.summary: DNA from soil used to characterize ancient communities without macrofossil remains (p. 477).

adna_genomics.label: Ancient Genomics
adna_genomics.summary: Application of high-throughput sequencing to ancient samples.

fact_shotgun_sequencing.label: Shotgun Sequencing
fact_shotgun_sequencing.summary: Sequencing all DNA in an extract, including target and contaminating organisms (p. 480).

fact_neanderthal_genome.label: Neanderthal Genomic Insight
fact_neanderthal_genome.summary: Revealed positive selection in regions associated with autism and type 2 diabetes and evidence of interbreeding with modern humans (p. 480, 481).

speciation_macroevolution.label: Speciation and Macroevolution
speciation_macroevolution.summary: The process of species origin and the resulting large-scale patterns of biodiversity.

fact_bsc.label: Biological Species Concept (BSC)
fact_bsc.summary: Defines species as groups of actually or potentially interbreeding populations reproductively isolated from others (p. 484, 490).

fact_phylogenetic_concept.label: Phylogenetic/Genealogical Concept
fact_phylogenetic_concept.summary: Defines species as monophyletic or exclusive groups (all members more closely related to each other than to any outside the group) (p. 491).

fact_evolutionary_concept.label: Evolutionary Species Concept
fact_evolutionary_concept.summary: A lineage of ancestor-descendant populations maintaining its identity and having its own evolutionary trajectory (p. 492).

fact_character_based_concept.label: Character-Based Concept
fact_character_based_concept.summary: Species defined by diagnosability; fixed differences in one or more characters (p. 490).

premating_barriers.label: Premating Barriers
premating_barriers.summary: Traits that prevent mating from occurring.

fact_temporal_isolation.label: Temporal Isolation
fact_temporal_isolation.summary: Seasonal or diurnal differences in sexual activity or presence (p. 493).

fact_habitat_isolation.label: Habitat/Resource Isolation
fact_habitat_isolation.summary: Association with specific habitats or host plants; includes ecogeographic isolation (p. 493).

fact_behavioral_isolation.label: Behavioral Isolation
fact_behavioral_isolation.summary: Differences in communication systems (visual, acoustical, chemical) and mate preferences (p. 493).

fact_mechanical_isolation.label: Mechanical Isolation
fact_mechanical_isolation.summary: Genitalic mismatch preventing successful sperm transfer (p. 493).

postmating_prezygotic_barriers.label: Postmating, Prezygotic Barriers
postmating_prezygotic_barriers.summary: Barriers acting after mating but before the formation of a zygote.

fact_sperm_competition.label: Sperm/Pollen Competition
fact_sperm_competition.summary: Conspecific sperm precedence where offspring are sired by conspecific males despite multiple inseminations (p. 494).

fact_gametic_incompatibility.label: Gametic Incompatibility
fact_gametic_incompatibility.summary: Failure of sperm-egg interaction mediated by evolving recognition proteins (e.g., lysin-VERL in abalone) (p. 494).

fact_dobzhansky_muller_model.label: Dobzhansky-Muller Model
fact_dobzhansky_muller_model.summary: Hybrid incompatibility caused by the interaction of mutations fixed at two different loci in separate populations (p. 494).

fact_haldanes_rule.label: Haldane's Rule
fact_haldanes_rule.summary: In hybrid offspring, the heterogametic sex (XY or ZW) is more likely to be absent, sterile, or rare (p. 494).

fact_extrinsic_postzygotic.label: Extrinsic Postzygotic Isolation
fact_extrinsic_postzygotic.summary: Hybrid reduced fitness due to lack of ecological niche or failure to attract mates (p. 494).

fact_ecological_speciation.label: Ecological Speciation
fact_ecological_speciation.summary: Reproductive isolation evolves as a by-product of adaptation to different environments (p. 485).

fact_mutation_order_speciation.label: Mutation-Order Speciation
fact_mutation_order_speciation.summary: Populations accumulate different sets of advantageous mutations despite similar selection pressures (p. 485).

fact_reinforcement.label: Reinforcement
fact_reinforcement.summary: Natural selection directly favors stronger prezygotic isolation to avoid low-fitness hybrid offspring (p. 485).

macroevolution_trends.label: Macroevolutionary Trends
macroevolution_trends.summary: Large-scale patterns of biodiversity over geological time.

fact_punctuated_equilibrium.label: Punctuated Equilibrium
fact_punctuated_equilibrium.summary: Hypothesis that evolution consists of brief periods of rapid change during speciation followed by long periods of stasis (p. 486).

fact_species_selection.label: Species Selection
fact_species_selection.summary: Macroevolutionary analogue of natural selection; traits that influence speciation or extinction rates determine the prevalence of those traits across lineages (p. 487).

fact_species_drift.label: Species Drift
fact_species_drift.summary: Chance-based changes in the frequency distribution of traits during mass extinctions (p. 487).

asexual_speciation.label: Speciation in Asexual Organisms
asexual_speciation.summary: The process of divergence and reproductive isolation in organisms that do not undergo sexual reproduction.

asexual_divergence_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Asexual Divergence
asexual_divergence_mechanisms.summary: Conditions that promote the evolution of distinct clusters in asexual lineages.

fact_asexual_drivers.label: Drivers of Asexual Divergence
fact_asexual_drivers.summary: Geographic isolation or adaptation to distinct ecological niches cause divergence in asexuals similar to sexuals. (p. 499)

fact_asexual_clustering.label: Genotypic Clustering Balance
fact_asexual_clustering.summary: Asexuals may show stronger clustering due to lack of interbreeding, but weaker clustering if they adapt more slowly to new niches than sexuals. (p. 499)

asexual_variation_patterns.label: Patterns of Variation
asexual_variation_patterns.summary: Distinctions in how traits are distributed within sexual vs asexual populations.

fact_sexual_variation.label: Sexual Variation Distribution
fact_sexual_variation.summary: Sexuals inherit genes from many ancestors; traits like body size display normal distributions due to averaging of multiple genes. (p. 499)

fact_asexual_variation.label: Asexual Variation Distribution
fact_asexual_variation.summary: Asexuals inherit genes from a single mother; traits exhibit a hierarchical pattern reflecting maternal ancestry. (p. 499)

bdelloid_rotifers_case.label: Bdelloid Rotifers Case Study
bdelloid_rotifers_case.summary: A celebrated clade of long-lived asexuals used to evaluate divergence patterns.

fact_bdelloid_clusters.label: Bdelloid Genetic Clusters
fact_bdelloid_clusters.summary: Bdelloids have diversified into distinct and independently evolving clusters broadly equivalent to sexual species. (p. 500)

fact_bdelloid_morphology.label: Divergent Selection in Bdelloids
fact_bdelloid_morphology.summary: Divergent selection on feeding morphology was a primary cause of bdelloid diversification. (p. 500)

fact_bdelloid_horizontal_transfer.label: Horizontal Gene Transfer in Bdelloids
fact_bdelloid_horizontal_transfer.summary: Bdelloids can acquire genes from bacterial, plant, fungal, and protist environments to compensate for reduced adaptive abilities of strict asexuality. (p. 500)

prokaryotic_speciation.label: Speciation in Prokaryotes
prokaryotic_speciation.summary: The challenge of applying biological species concepts to clonal organisms that exchange genes via non-sexual mechanisms.

prokaryotic_genetic_exchange.label: Mechanisms of Genetic Exchange
prokaryotic_genetic_exchange.summary: Non-sexual methods by which prokaryotes incorporate new genetic material.

fact_homologous_recombination.label: Homologous Recombination
fact_homologous_recombination.summary: Naked DNA is taken up from the environment; the probability of recombination declines exponentially with increasing sequence divergence. (p. 501)

fact_plasmid_transfer.label: Plasmid Transfer
fact_plasmid_transfer.summary: Independently replicating DNA molecules (plasmids) can transfer functionally related genes, such as antibiotic resistance, across distantly related taxa. (p. 501)

prokaryotic_taxonomy_methods.label: Taxonomic Approaches in Prokaryotes
prokaryotic_taxonomy_methods.summary: Methods used to classify prokaryotic 'species' in the absence of sexual reproduction.

fact_16S_threshold.label: 16S rRNA Gene Threshold
fact_16S_threshold.summary: Species richness is often calculated by counting groups differing by more than 1 percent in their 16S ribosomal RNA sequences. (p. 501)

prokaryotic_evolutionary_models.label: Evolutionary Models of Prokaryotic Diversity
prokaryotic_evolutionary_models.summary: Theoretical frameworks predicting how recombination rates affect speciation.

prokaryotic_ecotypes.label: Ecotypes (Cohan Model)
prokaryotic_ecotypes.summary: Genetic clusters of individuals that emerge due to specialization to different ecological niches. (p. 501)

fact_ecotype_recombination.label: Recombination and Ecotypes
fact_ecotype_recombination.summary: Ecotype clustering at neutral DNA markers requires rare recombination, unless a barrier to recombination evolves with ecological divergence. (p. 501)

recombination_threshold_model.label: Recombination Rate Threshold (Fraser et al.)
recombination_threshold_model.summary: The behavior of bacterial populations depends on the ratio of recombination rate to mutation rate per gene. (p. 501)

fact_low_recombination.label: Low Recombination Behavior
fact_low_recombination.summary: When recombination < mutation rate, populations behave as asexuals (similar to asexual eukaryotes). (p. 501)

fact_high_recombination.label: High Recombination Behavior
fact_high_recombination.summary: When recombination >= mutation rate, populations behave as 'sexual' organisms; reproductive isolation arises from the decline in homologous recombination with genetic distance. (p. 501)

global_diversity.label: Speciation and Global Diversity Patterns
global_diversity.summary: The relationship between speciation, extinction, and the resulting species richness in geographic regions.

diversity_determinants.label: Determinants of Species Number
diversity_determinants.summary: Factors that influence the total number of species in a group.

fact_diversity_balance.label: Net Diversity Balance
fact_diversity_balance.summary: Species number depends on the balance between origin (speciation) and loss (extinction), the age of the group, and available space/resources. (p. 502)

fact_ecological_divergence_impact.label: Ecological Shifts and Relatives
fact_ecological_divergence_impact.summary: If speciation involves ecological shifts, close relatives differ in traits; if driven by geographic isolation in identical habitats, they share traits. (p. 502)

latitudinal_diversity_gradient.label: Latitudinal Diversity Gradient (LDG)
latitudinal_diversity_gradient.summary: The tendency for species richness to be highest at the equator and decline toward the poles.

ldg_ecological_limit_hypothesis.label: Ecological Limit Hypothesis
ldg_ecological_limit_hypothesis.summary: Tropics receive more energy, supporting more productivity and more species in more niches (higher carrying capacity). (p. 505)

ldg_diversification_rate_hypothesis.label: Diversification Rate Hypothesis
ldg_diversification_rate_hypothesis.summary: The net contribution of speciation minus extinction is higher in the tropics. (p. 505)

fact_cradle_hypothesis.label: Cradle Hypothesis
fact_cradle_hypothesis.summary: Tropics are sites of faster speciation due to geographic variation in biotic conditions or higher mutation rates in ectotherms/plants. (p. 505)

fact_museum_hypothesis.label: Museum Hypothesis
fact_museum_hypothesis.summary: Tropics are sites of slower extinction due to climatic stability or larger population sizes. (p. 505)

ldg_time_hypothesis.label: Time Hypothesis
ldg_time_hypothesis.summary: Tropical biomes have been climatically stable and expansive for more time, providing more opportunity for diversification. (p. 506)

diversity_paradoxes.label: Diversity Paradoxes
diversity_paradoxes.summary: Unexpected patterns of species richness among different groups.

fact_protist_poverty.label: The Poverty of Protists
fact_protist_poverty.summary: Single-celled eukaryotes (protists) have lower diversity than bacteria or multicellular eukaryotes, potentially due to higher dispersal rates (reducing geographic isolation) or high recombination rates limiting genetic divergence. (p. 503)

geography_speciation.label: Geography, Range Evolution, and Speciation
geography_speciation.summary: How geographic distributions and spatial barriers influence the mode and rate of speciation.

geographic_modes_of_speciation.label: Geographic Modes of Speciation
geographic_modes_of_speciation.summary: Classifications based on the level of gene flow and spatial relationship between diverging populations.

vicariant_speciation.label: Vicariant Speciation
vicariant_speciation.summary: A mode of allopatry where a physical barrier (e.g., mountain range) subdivides a range and prevents gene flow. (p. 504)

peripatric_speciation.label: Peripatric Speciation
peripatric_speciation.summary: A mode of allopatry where individuals disperse beyond a preexisting barrier to establish a new, remote population. (p. 504)

fact_sympatric_requirements.label: Requirements for Sympatry
fact_sympatric_requirements.summary: Easiest when a single trait is subject to both disruptive selection and assortative mating, or when genes are physically linked on a chromosome. (p. 506)

island_biogeography.label: Island Biogeography
island_biogeography.summary: The study of islands as 'natural laboratories' to test speciation and diversity hypotheses.

theory_island_biogeography.label: Theory of Island Biogeography (MacArthur & Wilson)
theory_island_biogeography.summary: Species richness is a dynamic equilibrium between immigration rates (which decline as richness increases) and extinction rates (which increase as richness increases). (p. 508)

island_endemism.label: Island Endemism
island_endemism.summary: Types of species unique to an island based on phylogenetic relationships.

fact_anagenetic_species.label: Anagenetic Species
fact_anagenetic_species.summary: Closest relatives are not confined to the island; often found on islands of intermediate isolation. (p. 508)

fact_cladogenetic_species.label: Cladogenetic Species
fact_cladogenetic_species.summary: Closest relatives are endemic to the same island; indicative of within-island speciation. (p. 508)

area_speciation_relationship.label: Relationship between Area and Speciation
area_speciation_relationship.summary: How the geographic size of a region influences the probability and mode of speciation.

fact_area_vicariance_prob.label: Area and Barrier Probability
fact_area_vicariance_prob.summary: Larger ranges increase the probability that a random barrier will bisect a population, promoting vicariant speciation. (p. 509)

fact_area_cladogenesis_threshold.label: Cladogenetic Size Threshold
fact_area_cladogenesis_threshold.summary: Within-island speciation typically only occurs above certain area thresholds (e.g., >11,189 km2 for birds, >3000 km2 for anoles). (p. 509)

natural_selection_speciation.label: Speciation and Natural Selection
natural_selection_speciation.summary: The role of selective pressures in creating reproductive isolating barriers.

selection_types_speciation.label: Types of Selection in Speciation
selection_types_speciation.summary: How different forms of selection drive or maintain divergence.

disruptive_selection_speciation.label: Disruptive Selection
disruptive_selection_speciation.summary: Selection favoring extreme phenotypes over intermediates; can divide a population if paired with assortative mating. (p. 513)

directional_selection_speciation.label: Directional Selection
directional_selection_speciation.summary: Selection favoring one end of the phenotypic spectrum; promotes speciation when operating differentially across habitats. (p. 513)

stabilizing_selection_speciation.label: Stabilizing Selection
stabilizing_selection_speciation.summary: Favors intermediate phenotypes; typically maintains existing differences rather than initiating speciation. (p. 513)

reproductive_barriers_selection.label: Reproductive Barriers and Selection
reproductive_barriers_selection.summary: The specific mechanisms through which selection creates isolation.

habitat_isolation.label: Habitat Isolation
habitat_isolation.summary: Reduced gene flow because populations are adapted to different habitats, making immigrants less viable. (p. 515)

temporal_isolation.label: Temporal Isolation
temporal_isolation.summary: Reproductive isolation due to populations mating at different times (e.g., flowering-time divergence in plants). (p. 515)

pollinator_isolation.label: Pollinator Isolation
pollinator_isolation.summary: Isolation resulting from pollinator behavior and preferences for different flower morphologies. (p. 515)

behavioral_isolation.label: Behavioral Isolation
behavioral_isolation.summary: Isolation caused by changes in mating preferences or communication (e.g., apple maggot fly host preference). (p. 515)

extrinsic_postzygotic_isolation.label: Extrinsic Postzygotic Isolation
extrinsic_postzygotic_isolation.summary: Hybrids have reduced fitness because they are maladapted to either parental niche. (p. 515)

intrinsic_postzygotic_isolation.label: Intrinsic Postzygotic Isolation
intrinsic_postzygotic_isolation.summary: Hybrid lethality, inviability, or sterility resulting from genic incompatibilities or chromosomal rearrangements. (p. 515)

reinforcement_mechanism.label: Mechanism of Reinforcement
reinforcement_mechanism.summary: Steps: 1. Allopatric divergence. 2. Secondary contact and hybridization. 3. Selection against hybrids drives evolution of prezygotic barriers. (p. 517)

reinforcement_genetic_models.label: Genetic Models of Reinforcement
reinforcement_genetic_models.summary: Theoretical approaches to how assortative mating alleles spread despite recombination.

two_allele_mechanism.label: Two-Allele Mechanism
two_allele_mechanism.summary: Alternative alleles at a single locus result in assortative mating (e.g., Red prefers Red, Blue prefers Blue). (p. 518)

one_allele_mechanism.label: One-Allele Mechanism
one_allele_mechanism.summary: The same allele increases assortative mating in both diverging taxa. (p. 518)

sexual_selection_speciation.label: Speciation and Sexual Selection
sexual_selection_speciation.summary: How variation in mating success and mate preference drive reproductive isolation.

sexual_selection_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Sexual Selection
sexual_selection_mechanisms.summary: Processes that cause mating traits and preferences to diverge.

sensory_drive.label: Sensory Drive
sensory_drive.summary: Mate preferences evolve as a by-product of communication systems adapting to local environmental conditions. (p. 523)

fact_sensory_drive_cichlids.label: Cichlid Opsin Evolution
fact_sensory_drive_cichlids.summary: Evolution in genes controlling color vision (opsins) based on water clarity/depth leads to divergent female preferences for male color. (p. 524)

good_genes_selection.label: Good Genes Sexual Selection
good_genes_selection.summary: Females prefer traits that honestly indicate genetic quality (e.g., disease resistance). (p. 524)

fact_context_dependent_benefits.label: Context-Dependent Benefits
fact_context_dependent_benefits.summary: Benefits of a mate trait depend on the environment (e.g., gray tree frogs in low- vs high-density habitats). (p. 524)

fact_locally_good_genes.label: Locally Good Genes
fact_locally_good_genes.summary: Locally adapted males express condition-dependent traits; females preferring these traits reject non-local males. (p. 524)

fisherian_runaway.label: Fisherian Runaway
fisherian_runaway.summary: Positive feedback loop where male display traits and female preferences coevolve and exaggerate independently of survival benefits. (p. 525)

sexual_conflict.label: Sexual Conflict
sexual_conflict.summary: Antagonistic coevolution where the sexes have different optimal reproductive strategies, leading to an 'arms race' of adaptations and counter-adaptations. (p. 526)

sexual_isolation_types.label: Sexual Isolation
sexual_isolation_types.summary: A form of premating isolation where the choosy sex refuses to mate with members of another population. (p. 521)

gene_flow_hybridization.label: Gene Flow, Hybridization, and Speciation
gene_flow_hybridization.summary: The movement of genetic material between diverging lineages and its effect on species cohesion.

fact_gene_flow_cohesion.label: Gene Flow and Cohesion
fact_gene_flow_cohesion.summary: High gene flow causes homogenization and evolutionary cohesion; low gene flow permits divergence. (p. 529)

fact_hybrid_novelty.label: Hybridization Outcomes
fact_hybrid_novelty.summary: Hybridization can erode differences, create stable hybrid zones, or produce evolutionary novelty and new species. (p. 529)

concept_gene_flow_hybridization.label: Gene Flow and Hybridization
concept_gene_flow_hybridization.summary: Processes involving the movement of genetic material between populations and the production of offspring from divergent parents.

subconcept_gene_flow.label: Gene Flow
subconcept_gene_flow.summary: The movement of genetic variants (alleles) among geographic locations and populations.

fact_gene_flow_definition.label: Gene Flow Definition
fact_gene_flow_definition.summary: The movement of any genomic material, not just protein-coding regions; genes constitute only about 1 percent of eukaryotic genomes (p. 530).

fact_gene_flow_effect.label: Effects of Gene Flow
fact_gene_flow_effect.summary: Homogenizes differences arising from genetic drift or natural selection; makes populations more genetically similar and exports adaptive mutations broadly (p. 530).

fact_gene_flow_vs_dispersal.label: Gene Flow vs. Dispersal
fact_gene_flow_vs_dispersal.summary: Dispersal is the movement of individuals; gene flow requires dispersal PLUS successful establishment and reproduction in the new location (p. 530).

fact_gene_flow_modes.label: Modes of Gene Flow
fact_gene_flow_modes.summary: Includes sexual reproduction (union of gametes), asexual reproduction (immigration of clonal lineages, e.g., Taraxacum officinale), and horizontal gene transfer (bacteria and eukaryotes like grasses and ferns) (p. 530).

subconcept_hybridization.label: Hybridization
subconcept_hybridization.summary: The production of progeny from matings between genetically divergent parents, including different species.

fact_hybridization_definition.label: Hybridization Definition
fact_hybridization_definition.summary: Process by which progeny are produced from matings between genetically divergent parents (p. 530).

fact_hybrid_zone.label: Hybrid Zone
fact_hybrid_zone.summary: A geographic region where two species come into contact and hybridize. Can be structured at range margins or as a mosaic patchwork (p. 530, 532).

fact_introgression.label: Introgression
fact_introgression.summary: Gene flow between species or lineages that moves foreign alleles into the native genetic background (p. 530).

subconcept_hybrid_speciation.label: Hybrid Speciation
subconcept_hybrid_speciation.summary: The formation of an independent evolutionary lineage through hybridization.

fact_homoploid_speciation.label: Homoploid Hybrid Speciation
fact_homoploid_speciation.summary: Genomes merge without an increase in chromosome number; resulting genome is a mosaic of parental genetic material (p. 530, 532).

fact_allopolyploid_speciation.label: Allopolyploid Speciation
fact_allopolyploid_speciation.summary: Involves doubling or multiplying chromosome number (polyploidy); genomes of both parents are retained (p. 530, 532).

subconcept_hybrid_outcomes.label: Outcomes of Hybridization
subconcept_hybrid_outcomes.summary: The evolutionary results depending on hybrid fitness and ecological context.

fact_outcome_homogenization.label: Homogenization
fact_outcome_homogenization.summary: Loss of evolutionary genetic novelty as divergent lineages merge and cease to evolve independently (p. 532).

fact_outcome_hybrid_zones.label: Persistence of Hybrid Zones
fact_outcome_hybrid_zones.summary: Hybrids persist adjacent to parents. Dynamics affected by parental allele input, dispersal, and extrinsic/intrinsic fitness factors (p. 532).

fact_outcome_speciation.label: Speciation via Hybridization
fact_outcome_speciation.summary: Hybrids become reproductively isolated from parents. Success is more likely if the hybrid is spatially or ecologically isolated (p. 532).

concept_reproductive_isolation.label: Reproductive Isolation
concept_reproductive_isolation.summary: The lowered probability that members of different populations will mate or produce fit progeny.

subconcept_prezygotic_isolation.label: Prezygotic Isolating Mechanisms
subconcept_prezygotic_isolation.summary: Barriers that function prior to the formation of a zygote.

fact_prezygotic_ecological.label: Ecological Isolation
fact_prezygotic_ecological.summary: Includes habitat isolation (e.g., Helianthus paradoxus in salt marshes) and temporal isolation (differences in breeding timing) (p. 531, 544).

fact_prezygotic_behavioral.label: Behavioral/Sexual Isolation
fact_prezygotic_behavioral.summary: Differences in courtship signals, pheromones (e.g., Drosophila), color patterns (e.g., Lake Victoria cichlids), or songs (e.g., Laupala crickets) (p. 531, 544).

fact_prezygotic_gametic.label: Gametic Isolation
fact_prezygotic_gametic.summary: Post-mating prezygotic isolation where gametes fail to fuse, such as lysin-VERL interaction in abalones or bindin in sea urchins (p. 545).

subconcept_postzygotic_isolation.label: Postzygotic Isolating Mechanisms
subconcept_postzygotic_isolation.summary: Barriers that function after the formation of a zygote, affecting viability or fertility.

fact_postzygotic_extrinsic.label: Extrinsic Postzygotic Isolation
fact_postzygotic_extrinsic.summary: Hybrids are intrinsically healthy but possess intermediate phenotypes that fall between parental ecological niches, reducing fitness (e.g., benthic/limnetic sticklebacks) (p. 531, 546).

fact_postzygotic_intrinsic.label: Intrinsic Postzygotic Isolation
fact_postzygotic_intrinsic.summary: Hybrids suffer from developmental defects, sterility, or inviability regardless of environment (p. 531, 546).

concept_coevolution.label: Coevolution
concept_coevolution.summary: Reciprocal evolutionary change among interacting species driven by natural selection.

subconcept_geographic_mosaic.label: Geographic Mosaic of Coevolution
subconcept_geographic_mosaic.summary: Variation among environments in the structure and strength of selection on interspecific interactions.

fact_selection_mosaic.label: Selection Mosaic
fact_selection_mosaic.summary: Divergent natural selection on interspecific interactions driven by differences in gene expression or ecological outcomes across environments (p. 536).

fact_coevolutionary_hot_spots.label: Coevolutionary Hot/Cold Spots
fact_coevolutionary_hot_spots.summary: Hot spots are environments where reciprocal selection is strong; cold spots are where selection is nonreciprocal (p. 536).

fact_trait_remixing.label: Trait Remixing
fact_trait_remixing.summary: The continual shifting in occurrence and frequency of traits due to new mutations, gene flow, genetic drift, and metapopulation dynamics (p. 536).

subconcept_character_displacement.label: Character Displacement
subconcept_character_displacement.summary: Evolutionary shifts of ecological traits of competing species in environments where they co-occur to reduce competition.

fact_character_displacement_sticklebacks.label: Stickleback Character Displacement
fact_character_displacement_sticklebacks.summary: Sequential colonization of lakes led to divergence into benthic (broad morphology) and limnetic (slender morphology) forms (p. 537).

fact_character_displacement_anolis.label: Anolis Lizard Ecomorphs
fact_character_displacement_anolis.summary: Repeated divergence into predictable ecomorphs (ground, trunk, canopy) across different Caribbean islands (p. 537).

subconcept_trophic_interactions.label: Trophic Interactions
subconcept_trophic_interactions.summary: Interactions between different trophic levels (predator-prey, parasite-host) as drivers of speciation.

fact_host_races.label: Host Races
fact_host_races.summary: Plant-feeding insect populations that adapt to different plant species, sometimes leading directly to speciation (p. 538).

fact_trophic_mosaic_example.label: Conifer-Squirrel-Crossbill Mosaic
fact_trophic_mosaic_example.summary: Conifer cone structures evolve differently based on whether the primary predator is a squirrel or a crossbill, creating a geographic mosaic of coevolution (p. 538).

fact_free_living_mutualisms.label: Free-living Mutualisms
fact_free_living_mutualisms.summary: Typically form multispecies webs rather than pairwise interactions (e.g., plants and pollinators) (p. 538).

fact_symbiotic_mutualisms.label: Symbiotic Mutualisms
fact_symbiotic_mutualisms.summary: Intimate contact over extended periods; often involves symbionts adapted to a single host, which can drive host speciation (e.g., Wolbachia distorting sex ratios) (p. 539).

fact_mullerian_mimicry.label: Müllerian Mimicry
fact_mullerian_mimicry.summary: Distasteful species converge on a common warning color pattern; regional differences in these patterns can foster speciation through selection against non-matching hybrids (p. 539).

subconcept_escape_and_radiate.label: Escape-and-Radiate Coevolution
subconcept_escape_and_radiate.summary: A macroevolutionary process of alternating starbursts of speciation.

fact_escape_radiate_process.label: Escape-and-Radiate Process
fact_escape_radiate_process.summary: 1. Mutation allows host to escape enemy. 2. Host radiates into new environments. 3. Parasite evolves counter-defense and radiates to specialize on new hosts (p. 540).

subconcept_cospeciation.label: Cospeciation
subconcept_cospeciation.summary: Parallel cladogenesis where speciation events in interacting lineages are matched.

fact_cospeciation_conditions.label: Conditions for Cospeciation
fact_cospeciation_conditions.summary: Favored by maternally inherited symbionts, host-tracking by commensals, or highly host-specific pollinating seed parasites (e.g., Epicephala moths and Glochidion plants) (p. 540, 541).

concept_genetics_of_speciation.label: Genetics of Speciation
concept_genetics_of_speciation.summary: The molecular and chromosomal basis of reproductive barriers.

subconcept_genetics_prezygotic.label: Genetics of Prezygotic Isolation
subconcept_genetics_prezygotic.summary: Genes controlling traits that prevent mating or fertilization.

fact_mimulus_genetics.label: Mimulus Genetics
fact_mimulus_genetics.summary: Different pollinators drive divergence; the YUP locus regulates flower color and pollinator visitation (p. 544).

fact_drosophila_pheromones.label: Drosophila Pheromones
fact_drosophila_pheromones.summary: Sexual isolation driven by pheromone differences; mapped to multiple chromosomal regions including the 3rd chromosome and X chromosome (p. 544).

fact_cichlid_opsins.label: Cichlid Opsins
fact_cichlid_opsins.summary: Female preference for male color is linked to long-wavelength-sensitive opsin genes adapted to local light environments (p. 544).

fact_flycatcher_mc1r.label: Flycatcher MC1R
fact_flycatcher_mc1r.summary: Single amino acid change in the MC1R gene is associated with plumage color differences used in species recognition (p. 544).

subconcept_genetics_postzygotic.label: Genetics of Postzygotic Isolation
subconcept_genetics_postzygotic.summary: Genes causing hybrid inviability or sterility.

fact_large_x_effect.label: Large-X Effect
fact_large_x_effect.summary: Postzygotic isolation genes are disproportionately concentrated on the X chromosome (p. 547).

concept_genome_evolution.label: Speciation and Genome Evolution
concept_genome_evolution.summary: How the physical architecture of the genome facilitates or impedes speciation.

subconcept_selection_recombination.label: Selection-Recombination Antagonism
subconcept_selection_recombination.summary: The conflict between divergent selection (building associations between loci) and recombination/gene flow (breaking them apart).

fact_selection_recombination_def.label: Selection-Recombination Mechanism
fact_selection_recombination_def.summary: Speciation with gene flow is constrained unless genes for assortative mating and local adaptation are tightly linked (p. 551).

subconcept_genomic_heterogeneity.label: Genomic Heterogeneity
subconcept_genomic_heterogeneity.summary: Variation in genetic divergence across different regions of the genome.

fact_genomic_islands.label: Genomic Islands of Divergence
fact_genomic_islands.summary: Regions with divergence exceeding neutral expectations; contain selected loci and linked hitchhiking genes (p. 551).

fact_genomic_continents.label: Genomic Continents
fact_genomic_continents.summary: Widespread genetic divergence across the genome, often driven by multifarious selection acting on many loci (p. 552, 554).

subconcept_divergence_hitchhiking.label: Hitchhiking Mechanisms
subconcept_divergence_hitchhiking.summary: Processes by which neutral regions diverge due to proximity to selected genes.

fact_divergence_hitchhiking_def.label: Divergence Hitchhiking
fact_divergence_hitchhiking_def.summary: A selected gene creates a local window of reduced gene flow, causing linked neutral genes to diverge as well (p. 554).

fact_genome_hitchhiking_def.label: Genome Hitchhiking
fact_genome_hitchhiking_def.summary: Global reduction in gene flow across the entire genome once several strong selection loci are established, allowing less-favored mutations to persist (p. 554).

fact_isolation_by_adaptation.label: Isolation by Adaptation (IBA)
fact_isolation_by_adaptation.summary: Positive correlation between adaptive phenotypic divergence and molecular genetic differentiation, independent of distance (p. 554).

subconcept_chromosomal_rearrangements.label: Chromosomal Rearrangements
subconcept_chromosomal_rearrangements.summary: Structural changes in chromosomes that affect recombination.

fact_chromosomal_inversions.label: Chromosomal Inversions
fact_chromosomal_inversions.summary: Reverse orientation of a segment; suppresses recombination, protecting adaptive gene blocks from being broken up by gene flow (p. 555).

subconcept_polyploidy_genomics.label: Polyploidy and Speciation
subconcept_polyploidy_genomics.summary: Numerical increase in whole chromosome sets.

fact_autopolyploidy.label: Autopolyploidy
fact_autopolyploidy.summary: Increase in ploidy within a single species (p. 556).

fact_allopolyploidy.label: Allopolyploidy
fact_allopolyploidy.summary: Increase in ploidy resulting from hybridization between two distinct species (p. 556).

fact_polyploidy_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Polyploidy
fact_polyploidy_mechanisms.summary: Includes somatic doubling (mitotic failure), meiotic nonreduction (unreduced gametes), and polyspermy (two sperm fertilizing one egg) (p. 556).

concept_adaptive_radiation.label: Adaptive Radiation
concept_adaptive_radiation.summary: Rapid diversification of a common ancestor into an array of species exploiting different ecological niches.

subconcept_ecological_theory_radiation.label: Ecological Theory of Radiation
subconcept_ecological_theory_radiation.summary: The pattern of species multiplication followed by a slowdown as niches are filled.

fact_ecological_barrel.label: Filling the Ecological Barrel
fact_ecological_barrel.summary: Metaphor for limited environment: highest opportunity for occupancy exists when the environment is empty; difficulty increases as it fills (p. 560).

fact_radiation_pattern.label: Adaptive Radiation Pattern
fact_radiation_pattern.summary: Rapid multiplication and morphological diversification early on, followed by a decline in rates as competition increases (p. 560).

fact_ecological_opportunity.label: Ecological Opportunity
fact_ecological_opportunity.summary: Availability of underexploited resources (niches) that allow species to multiply and diversify (p. 561).

fact_key_innovations.label: Key Innovations
fact_key_innovations.summary: Intrinsic traits that increase a taxon's evolvability and potential to diversify (p. 560).

fact_ecomorphs.label: Ecomorphs
fact_ecomorphs.summary: Recognizable association between the morphology of a species and its specific use of the environment (p. 559).

core_adaptive_radiation.label: Adaptive Radiation
core_adaptive_radiation.summary: The rapid evolution of ecological differences among species in a diversifying lineage, often triggered by ecological opportunity.

sub_ecological_opportunity.label: Ecological Opportunity
sub_ecological_opportunity.summary: The presence of unexploited niche space experienced by an evolving lineage, which facilitates diversification.

fact_adaptive_landscape.label: Adaptive Landscape
fact_adaptive_landscape.summary: A conceptual model where mean fitness for a phenotype is indicated by the height of a surface; organisms move toward 'peaks' of steepest fitness ascent. Landscapes are dynamic, with hills changing height, shape, and position over time. (p. 561-562)

fact_gaussian_principle.label: Gaussian Principle
fact_gaussian_principle.summary: The principle that no two species can occupy the same ecological niche (or adaptive peak) due to competitive inequality. (p. 562)

fact_character_displacement.label: Character Displacement
fact_character_displacement.summary: Evolutionary adjustments in body size or shape to reduce competition. Example: Medium ground finches evolved smaller beaks when outcompeted by large ground finches for large seeds during drought. (p. 562)

fact_anolis_parallelism.label: Anolis Lizard Parallelism
fact_anolis_parallelism.summary: Different species colonizing Greater Antilles islands underwent parallel evolution into the same four ecotypes: ground, tree trunk, branches, and twigs. (p. 562)

sub_intrinsic_factors.label: Intrinsic Factors
sub_intrinsic_factors.summary: Genetic, developmental, or physiological factors that potentiate or constrain a lineage's ability to radiate.

fact_intrinsic_evolvability.label: Intrinsic Evolvability
fact_intrinsic_evolvability.summary: Variations in speciation speed among taxa; e.g., lacustrine fish speciate faster (15k-300k years) than terrestrial birds/arthropods (0.5-1M years). (p. 563)

fact_pharyngeal_jaws.label: Pharyngeal Jaws
fact_pharyngeal_jaws.summary: A key innovation in cichlid fish: toothlike plates in the roof of the mouth that separate food procurement (oral jaws) from processing (pharyngeal jaws). (p. 563)

sub_hybridization.label: Hybridization in Radiation
sub_hybridization.summary: The role of introgressive hybridization in increasing genetic variation and facilitating radiation.

fact_hybrid_swarm.label: Hybrid Swarm
fact_hybrid_swarm.summary: Gene mixing through hybridization that creates a 'swarm' of genetic variation, facilitating rapid radiation. (p. 564)

fact_introgression_patterns.label: Introgression Patterns
fact_introgression_patterns.summary: Introgressive hybridization is common in young radiations (e.g., Darwin's finches, African cichlids) but nearly absent in older ones (e.g., Hawaiian honeycreepers). (p. 563)

sub_experimental_radiation.label: Experimental Adaptive Radiations
sub_experimental_radiation.summary: Laboratory tests of radiation theory using microorganisms to observe diversification in real-time.

fact_pseudomonas_ecotypes.label: Pseudomonas fluorescens Ecotypes
fact_pseudomonas_ecotypes.summary: Asexual bacteria diversify into three morphological types: 'smooth' (colonizer), 'wrinkly spreader' (biofilm producer), and 'fuzzy spreader', specialized for different spatial niches. (p. 565)

fact_microbe_disparity.label: Microbe Richness vs Disparity
fact_microbe_disparity.summary: In P. fluorescens, richness (number of clones) peaks then declines, but disparity (range of morphological variation) rises to a maximum and remains stable. (p. 565)

core_evolutionary_rates.label: Evolutionary Rates
core_evolutionary_rates.summary: The measurement and comparison of the speed of speciation, extinction, and trait change.

sub_diversification_rates.label: Diversification Rates
sub_diversification_rates.summary: Rates at which new species form (speciation) and disappear (extinction).

fact_birth_death_model.label: Birth-Death Model
fact_birth_death_model.summary: A mathematical model where lineages have constant probabilities of speciation (birth) or extinction (death). Predicts exponential increase if speciation > extinction. (p. 568)

fact_taphonomy.label: Taphonomy
fact_taphonomy.summary: The study of the process of fossilization and its variation across lineages and time, critical for correcting biases in extinction rate estimates. (p. 568)

fact_tree_balance.label: Tree Balance
fact_tree_balance.summary: A measure of relative sizes of sister clades in a phylogeny. Most natural phylogenies are more imbalanced than birth-death models predict, suggesting varying diversification rates. (p. 569)

sub_trait_evolution_rates.label: Trait Evolution Rates
sub_trait_evolution_rates.summary: Quantitative measures of how fast phenotypes change over time.

fact_darwins_unit.label: Darwin (Unit)
fact_darwins_unit.summary: Rate of evolutionary change = difference in log-transformed trait values divided by elapsed time in millions of years. (p. 570)

fact_haldanes_unit.label: Haldane (Unit)
fact_haldanes_unit.summary: Rate of evolutionary change = difference in mean trait values divided by the pooled standard deviation and number of generations. Relates more to population genetics. (p. 570)

fact_brownian_motion.label: Brownian Motion Model
fact_brownian_motion.summary: A statistical process where trait evolution mimics a 'random walk', described by a rate parameter s2. (p. 570)

fact_paradox_of_stasis.label: Paradox of Stasis
fact_paradox_of_stasis.summary: Observation that fastest rates of evolution occur over the shortest intervals; long-term rates are slow because rapid changes are often reversed or balanced over time. (p. 571)

core_macroevolutionary_trends.label: Macroevolutionary Trends
core_macroevolutionary_trends.summary: Persistent temporal changes in characteristics of lineages or clades over geologic time.

sub_trend_scope.label: Scope of Trends
sub_trend_scope.summary: The biological level at which a trend operates.

fact_species_level_trend.label: Species-Level Trend
fact_species_level_trend.summary: Directional change within a single species. Often rare in fossil records; most species show fluctuating/meandering change. (p. 574)

fact_clade_level_trend.label: Clade-Level Trend
fact_clade_level_trend.summary: Change in the mean trait value of a group of related species over time. Example: Human brain size increase. (p. 574)

fact_whole_fauna_trend.label: Whole-Fauna Trend
fact_whole_fauna_trend.summary: Large-scale patterns across multiple distantly related clades, such as the general increase in species richness since the early Paleozoic. (p. 574)

sub_trend_mechanisms.label: Trend Mechanisms
sub_trend_mechanisms.summary: The processes that generate directional change over time.

fact_active_vs_passive_trends.label: Active vs Passive Trends
fact_active_vs_passive_trends.summary: Active (driven) trends result from uniform bias in the direction of evolution. Passive trends arise from diffusion-like evolution in the presence of a lower boundary (e.g., a minimum body size). (p. 575)

fact_copes_rule.label: Cope's Rule
fact_copes_rule.summary: The hypothesis that animal body size tends to increase within lineages and clades over time. (p. 575)

fact_escalation_hypothesis.label: Escalation Hypothesis
fact_escalation_hypothesis.summary: An overarching ecological trend where organisms increase their ability to acquire resources, leading to a biological 'arms race' between predators and prey. (p. 577)

core_extinction_dynamics.label: Extinction Dynamics
core_extinction_dynamics.summary: The patterns, causes, and consequences of the disappearance of species and taxa.

fact_background_extinction.label: Background Extinction
fact_background_extinction.summary: The sum of all normal species terminations during a defined time interval, treated as a stochastic process. (p. 581)

fact_pseudoextinction.label: Pseudoextinction
fact_pseudoextinction.summary: The 'extinction' of a species when it evolves sufficiently into another species that it is renamed by taxonomists. (p. 581)

sub_mass_extinctions.label: Mass Extinctions
sub_mass_extinctions.summary: Sudden, worldwide losses of many species of diverse ecologies.

fact_big_five.label: The Big Five
fact_big_five.summary: The primary mass extinction events: End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, and End-Cretaceous. (p. 581)

fact_extinction_victims.label: Extinction Victims
fact_extinction_victims.summary: During mass extinctions, selectivity often shifts from 'bad genes' (fitness) to 'bad luck'. Survival is often linked to wide geographic range and broad dietary/physiological requirements. (p. 583)

fact_recovery_dynamics.label: Recovery Dynamics
fact_recovery_dynamics.summary: Post-extinction recovery involves initial filling of ecospace by 'disaster taxa' (e.g., Lystrosaurus) before long-term ecosystem stabilization. (p. 583)

sub_extinction_models.label: Extinction Models
sub_extinction_models.summary: Theories regarding the primary drivers of macroevolutionary change.

fact_red_queen_model.label: Red Queen Model
fact_red_queen_model.summary: Macroevolution driven primarily by biotic interactions (competition, predation); species must constantly evolve just to survive in a changing biological environment. (p. 585)

fact_court_jester_model.label: Court Jester Model
fact_court_jester_model.summary: Macroevolution driven primarily by unpredictable abiotic changes in the physical environment (climate, tectonics). (p. 585)

core_species_selection.label: Species Selection
core_species_selection.summary: Selection acting at the level of the species, where traits affect speciation and extinction rates.

sub_species_traits.label: Species-Level Traits
sub_species_traits.summary: Characteristics that can be measured at the species level rather than the individual level.

fact_emergent_trait.label: Emergent Trait
fact_emergent_trait.summary: A trait not defined by individuals, such as geographic range size or population density. (p. 586)

fact_aggregate_trait.label: Aggregate Trait
fact_aggregate_trait.summary: A species-level summary of a trait present in individuals, such as average body size or generation time. (p. 586)

sub_species_fitness.label: Species Fitness
sub_species_fitness.summary: The ability of a species to persist and diversify.

fact_emergent_fitness.label: Emergent Fitness
fact_emergent_fitness.summary: The net diversification rate of a species (speciation rate minus extinction rate). (p. 586)

fact_species_heritability.label: Species Heritability
fact_species_heritability.summary: The fidelity with which a species' trait is passed to its daughter lineages during speciation. (p. 586)

sub_species_sorting.label: Species Sorting
sub_species_sorting.summary: Any process where speciation and extinction rates differ among lineages.

fact_effect_macroevolution.label: Effect Macroevolution
fact_effect_macroevolution.summary: Species sorting specifically driven by aggregate traits (traits expressed at the organismal level). (p. 588)

fact_price_equation.label: Price Equation (Macroevolutionary)
fact_price_equation.summary: A framework used to separate overall trait changes into two components: the correlation between trait and fitness (species selection) and within-lineage evolution. (p. 590)

core_key_innovations.label: Key Evolutionary Innovations
core_key_innovations.summary: Traits of outstanding ecological significance that contribute to the species richness or diversity of a lineage.

sub_innovation_effects.label: Effects of Key Innovations
sub_innovation_effects.summary: How novel traits lead to diversification.

fact_adaptive_zone.label: Adaptive Zone
fact_adaptive_zone.summary: A set of closely related niches exploited in a similar manner by a lineage that has evolved a key trait. (p. 592)

fact_exaptation.label: Exaptation
fact_exaptation.summary: A trait that evolved for one function but was later co-opted for a new function. (p. 592)

sub_innovation_concepts.label: Innovation Concepts
sub_innovation_concepts.summary: The theoretical framework for identifying key traits.

fact_comparative_method.label: Comparative Method
fact_comparative_method.summary: A statistical method for comparing traits of lineages that incorporates phylogenetic relatedness to test if a trait drove diversification. (p. 592)

ki_success_metrics.label: Metrics of Evolutionary Success
ki_success_metrics.summary: The criteria used to determine if a trait has contributed to the success of a lineage.

metric_species_richness.label: Species Richness
metric_species_richness.summary: Measuring success by the absolute number of species evolved within a lineage.

metric_diversity.label: Morphological and Ecological Diversity
metric_diversity.summary: Measuring success by the degree of phenotypic and niche variation within a lineage.

ki_origins.label: Origins of Key Innovations
ki_origins.summary: The nature of the genetic and structural changes that constitute an innovation.

origin_simple.label: Simple Changes
origin_simple.summary: Small changes, such as a single amino acid substitution, that allow a lineage to cross a functional or ecological threshold (e.g., toxin resistance).

origin_complex.label: Complex Changes
origin_complex.summary: Suites of functionally related characters involving multiple evolutionary steps (e.g., powered flight involving wings, feathers, and skeletal modifications).

origin_exaptation.label: Exaptations
origin_exaptation.summary: Traits that evolved under selection for one function but were later co-opted for a new use (e.g., feathers evolving for insulation/display before being used for flight).

ki_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Diversity Production
ki_mechanisms.summary: The pathways through which a key innovation translates into macroevolutionary success.

mech_adaptive_zone.label: Exploitation of New Adaptive Zones
mech_adaptive_zone.summary: Accessing a set of related niches that can only be filled by species possessing the novelty (e.g., wings).

mech_competitive_advantage.label: Competitive Advantage
mech_competitive_advantage.summary: Traits that allow a lineage to drive competitors to extinction, reducing extinction rates for the innovative lineage (e.g., protrusible jaws for suction feeding).

mech_reproductive_isolation.label: Increased Reproductive Isolation
mech_reproductive_isolation.summary: Innovations that directly increase the potential for speciation, such as complex mating behaviors or nectar spurs in Aquilegia affecting pollinator specificity.

mech_ecological_opportunity.label: Ecological Opportunity
mech_ecological_opportunity.summary: The potential to diversify into new niches along an ecological axis, often granted by a key innovation (e.g., algal grazing jaws in fish).

ki_testing.label: Testing Key Innovation Hypotheses
ki_testing.summary: Methodologies used to empirically validate the role of a trait in diversification.

test_sister_clade.label: Sister Clade Comparison
test_sister_clade.summary: Comparing the number of species in a lineage with the trait against its most closely related lineage lacking the trait.

test_stochastic_models.label: Stochastic Diversification Models
test_stochastic_models.summary: Using birth-death models to treat speciation and extinction as random events to determine if differences in richness are statistically significant.

test_phylogenetics.label: Molecular Phylogenetic Analysis
test_phylogenetics.summary: Using DNA data to infer time of origin, track tempo of speciation events post-innovation, and measure rates of evolution of related ecological traits.

ki_critiques.label: Problems and Critiques
ki_critiques.summary: Limitations and common failures of the key innovation framework.

critique_just_so.label: Just-So Stories
critique_just_so.summary: The tendency to propose plausible but untested explanations for the success of a trait without rigorous data.

critique_codistribution.label: Trait Co-distribution
critique_codistribution.summary: Difficulty in isolating one causal trait when multiple innovations evolve in the same ancestor.

critique_lag_time.label: Diversification Lag
critique_lag_time.summary: Observations where diversification bursts occur millions of years after the innovation (e.g., weevils and angiosperms, teleosts and genome duplication).

critique_context.label: Context Dependence
critique_context.summary: Success depends on ecological, historical, and geographic context, not just the trait itself.

community_evolution.label: Evolution of Communities
community_evolution.summary: The study of how species interactions and macroevolutionary processes shape the distribution and abundance of species.

comm_interactions.label: Species Interactions
comm_interactions.summary: Mechanisms by which species affect each other's population growth rates.

int_predation.label: Predation and Parasitism
int_predation.summary: Interactions such as predator-prey or pathogen-host relationships.

int_competition.label: Competition
int_competition.summary: Struggle for limiting resources like light, water, or food.

int_mutualism.label: Mutualism
int_mutualism.summary: Interactions where both species benefit, such as plants and pollinators.

int_facilitation.label: Facilitation
int_facilitation.summary: One species altering the environment to benefit another (e.g., nutrient recycling from detritus).

comm_microevolution.label: Microevolutionary Community Change
comm_microevolution.summary: How changes in phenotypes within species alter community dynamics.

micro_genetic_diversity.label: Intra-specific Genetic Diversity
micro_genetic_diversity.summary: Genetic variation (e.g., secondary compounds in plants) that affects which herbivores can feed on a genotype, impacting higher trophic levels.

micro_natural_selection.label: Adaptive Responses
micro_natural_selection.summary: Rapid evolutionary changes in response to interactions, such as guppies evolving size and reproductive effort based on predation regimes.

comm_macroevolution.label: Macroevolutionary Community Change
comm_macroevolution.summary: The impact of speciation and extinction on community structure.

macro_ecological_speciation.label: Ecological Speciation
macro_ecological_speciation.summary: Reproductive isolation resulting from adaptation to different environments; introduces new functional groups into a community.

macro_nonecological_speciation.label: Non-ecological Speciation
macro_nonecological_speciation.summary: Isolation via mate recognition or sexual selection; adds ecologically equivalent species, leading to neutral community dynamics.

macro_hybridization.label: Hybridization and Polyploidization
macro_hybridization.summary: Production of new species that may be ecologically different from progenitors but not necessarily aligned with available niches.

comm_geography.label: Geography of Speciation and Extinction
comm_geography.summary: The spatial scale at which new species are added or lost.

geo_allopatric.label: Allopatric/Parapatric/Peripatric
geo_allopatric.summary: Speciation occurring in spatially segregated lineages; increases regional richness but not local richness until range expansion.

geo_sympatric.label: Sympatric Speciation
geo_sympatric.summary: Speciation occurring within the same geographic area; directly increases local community species richness (e.g., Rhagoletis flies).

geo_extinction.label: Spatial Dimensions of Extinction
geo_extinction.summary: Local extinction occurs when a species is lost from a specific area; total extinction occurs when it is lost from all local communities.

behavioral_evolution.label: Evolution of Behavior
behavioral_evolution.summary: The genetic, hormonal, and evolutionary basis of animal actions and social systems.

beh_genetics.label: Behavioral Genetics
beh_genetics.summary: The study of how DNA and gene expression influence behavioral phenotypes.

gen_nature_nurture.label: Nature versus Nurture
gen_nature_nurture.summary: Modern view: DNA determines behavioral phenotypic boundaries, while environment determines specific values within those boundaries.

gen_analysis_methods.label: Genetic Analysis Methods
gen_analysis_methods.summary: Techniques used to identify genes associated with behavior.

meth_qtl.label: Quantitative Trait Loci (QTL)
meth_qtl.summary: Identifying multiple independent genes that each contribute a fraction of behavioral variation (e.g., Hirsch's geotaxis studies in flies).

meth_forward_genetics.label: Forward Genetics / Mutagenesis
meth_forward_genetics.summary: Using mutations to identify single genes that have measurable effects on behavior (e.g., Benzer's phototaxis screens).

gen_systems_genetics.label: Systems Genetics
gen_systems_genetics.summary: A holistic approach analyzing emergent properties of complex networks rather than individual genes (e.g., Drosophila Genome Reference Panel).

gen_epigenetics.label: Behavioral Epigenetics
gen_epigenetics.summary: Heritable changes in gene expression via DNA methylation or histone acetylation without changing DNA sequence (e.g., rat maternal grooming affecting stress responses).

beh_hormones.label: Evolution of Hormones and Behavior
beh_hormones.summary: The role of chemical messengers in coordinating physiological and behavioral responses.

horm_types.label: Hormone Types
horm_types.summary: Peptides (protein-based, membrane receptors, second messengers) and Steroids (cholesterol-based, intracellular receptors, gene regulation).

horm_effects.label: Organizational vs Activational Effects
horm_effects.summary: Organizational: Early-life, usually irreversible developmental changes. Activational: Fluctuating, reversible changes based on circulating levels.

horm_cascades.label: Hormonal Cascades
horm_cascades.summary: Multi-step pathways like the HPG axis: Hypothalamus (GnRH) -> Pituitary (LH/FSH) -> Gonads (Steroids).

horm_integration.label: Phenotypic Integration and Pleiotropy
horm_integration.summary: Hormonal pleiotropy allows one hormone to coordinate a suite of correlated traits (e.g., testosterone affecting aggression, plumage, and immune function).

beh_sexual_selection.label: Sexual Selection
beh_sexual_selection.summary: Evolutionary forces based on competition for mates, distinct from survival-based natural selection.

sex_male_competition.label: Male-Male Competition
sex_male_competition.summary: Selection for traits that enhance ability to compete with other males for access to mates.

sex_female_choice.label: Female Mate Choice
sex_female_choice.summary: Selection for traits that are preferred by females, often leading to elaborate ornaments.

concept_endocrinology.label: Evolutionary Endocrinology
concept_endocrinology.summary: The study of how hormonal systems inform microevolutionary processes, phenotypic plasticity, and responses to global change.

concept_hormonal_mechanisms.label: Hormonal Mechanisms and Evolution
concept_hormonal_mechanisms.summary: The role of hormones in mediating trade-offs and trait integration.

fact_endo_global_change.label: Endocrinology and Global Change
fact_endo_global_change.summary: Endocrinology is critical for understanding how organisms respond to global change (p. 623).

fact_testosterone_tradeoffs.label: Testosterone-Mediated Trade-offs
fact_testosterone_tradeoffs.summary: Organismal and evolutionary mechanisms relate testosterone signaling to life history and behavioral trade-offs (p. 623).

fact_hormonal_pleiotropy.label: Hormonal Pleiotropy
fact_hormonal_pleiotropy.summary: Hormonal pleiotropy can either constrain or facilitate the evolution of traits (p. 623).

fact_phenotypic_integration.label: Phenotypic Integration
fact_phenotypic_integration.summary: Suites of traits mediated by hormones may respond developmentally or evolutionarily as integrated or independent units (p. 623).

concept_game_theory.label: Evolutionary Game Theory
concept_game_theory.summary: A theoretical framework used to analyze the outcome of natural selection in settings where fitness is frequency-dependent.

concept_frequency_dependence.label: Frequency Dependence
concept_frequency_dependence.summary: The phenomenon where the fitness of a given strategy depends on the frequency of other strategies in the population.

fact_freq_dep_definition.label: Frequency Dependence Definition
fact_freq_dep_definition.summary: Fitness, and hence the action of selection, is dependent on the frequency of strategies (e.g., aggressive vs nonaggressive) within the population (p. 624).

fact_freq_dep_environment.label: Dynamic Environment
fact_freq_dep_environment.summary: Under frequency-dependent selection, the 'environment' changes over evolutionary time as strategies evolve, altering the fitness landscape (p. 624).

concept_evolutionary_endpoints.label: Evolutionary End Points
concept_evolutionary_endpoints.summary: The characterization of stable outcomes in frequency-dependent evolutionary processes.

concept_nash_equilibrium.label: Nash Equilibrium
concept_nash_equilibrium.summary: A state where no individual can increase their fitness by unilaterally changing their strategy.

fact_nash_condition.label: Nash Equilibrium Condition
fact_nash_condition.summary: A resident strategy p# is a Nash equilibrium if for all possible mutants p, W(p, p#) <= W(p#, p#) (p. 624).

concept_ess.label: Evolutionarily Stable Strategy (ESS)
concept_ess.summary: A strategy that, if adopted by a population, cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy.

fact_ess_definition.label: ESS Definition
fact_ess_definition.summary: A resident strategy such that any mutant strategy (different from that of the resident) is selected against while rare and so cannot increase in frequency (p. 624).

fact_ess_condition_1.label: ESS Condition ES1
fact_ess_condition_1.summary: W(p#, p#) > W(p, p#) for every mutant strategy p (p. 628).

fact_ess_condition_2.label: ESS Condition ES2
fact_ess_condition_2.summary: If W(p, p#) = W(p#, p#), then W(p#, p) > W(p, p) must hold (p. 628).

concept_convergence_stability.label: Convergence Stability
concept_convergence_stability.summary: The property of a strategy being a local attractor under evolutionary dynamics.

fact_conv_stable_definition.label: Convergence Stability Definition
fact_conv_stable_definition.summary: A strategy is convergence stable if a population strategy will evolve toward it if initially close to it (p. 624).

concept_game_examples.label: Classic Game Examples
concept_game_examples.summary: Models used to illustrate fundamental game theory principles.

concept_hawk_dove.label: Hawk-Dove Game
concept_hawk_dove.summary: A model of resource contest between two individuals.

fact_hawk_strategy.label: Hawk Strategy
fact_hawk_strategy.summary: Hawks attack their opponent; if two hawks fight, the winner gets V, the loser pays cost C (p. 625).

fact_dove_strategy.label: Dove Strategy
fact_dove_strategy.summary: Doves display and run away if attacked; two doves share the resource (p. 625).

fact_hawk_dove_payoffs.label: Hawk-Dove Payoffs
fact_hawk_dove_payoffs.summary: Payoff matrix: Hawk vs Hawk = (V-C)/2; Hawk vs Dove = V; Dove vs Hawk = 0; Dove vs Dove = V/2 (p. 625).

fact_hawk_dove_equilibrium.label: Hawk-Dove Nash Equilibrium
fact_hawk_dove_equilibrium.summary: The Nash equilibrium and unique ESS is to play hawk with probability p# = V/C (p. 626).

concept_sex_ratio_game.label: Sex-Ratio Game
concept_sex_ratio_game.summary: A game concerning the proportion of sons vs daughters produced by females.

fact_sex_ratio_equilibrium.label: Sex-Ratio Nash Equilibrium
fact_sex_ratio_equilibrium.summary: The strategy of producing equal numbers of sons and daughters (p# = 1/2) is a Nash equilibrium (p. 626).

concept_game_issues.label: Issues for Consideration in Game Theory
concept_game_issues.summary: Nuances regarding strategies, payoffs, fitness, and population dynamics.

concept_gt_strategies.label: Game Theory Strategies
concept_gt_strategies.summary: Rules for choosing actions, which can be deterministic, probabilistic, or contingent.

fact_mixed_strategy.label: Mixed Strategy
fact_mixed_strategy.summary: A strategy in which actions are chosen probabilistically (p. 624).

fact_contingent_strategy.label: Contingent Strategy
fact_contingent_strategy.summary: Decisions based on an underlying state (e.g., fighting ability) rather than probability (p. 627).

concept_gt_payoffs.label: Payoffs in Game Theory
concept_gt_payoffs.summary: Representations of changes in fitness as a result of playing a game.

fact_payoff_matrix_def.label: Payoff Matrix Definition
fact_payoff_matrix_def.summary: A table specifying how the increment to fitness depends on the action of the individual and its opponent(s) (p. 624).

fact_payoff_holistic_view.label: Holistic Payoff View
fact_payoff_holistic_view.summary: Payoffs may not be specifiable in advance but emerge from a holistic view of the breeding season (p. 627).

concept_gt_fitness.label: Fitness in Game Theory
concept_gt_fitness.summary: The measure of average reproductive success used to determine the change in frequency of strategies.

fact_fitness_measures.label: Fitness Measures
fact_fitness_measures.summary: Fitness can be the mean number of surviving offspring, grandchildren, or great-grandchildren depending on the system (p. 627).

concept_gt_role_asymmetries.label: Role Asymmetries
concept_gt_role_asymmetries.summary: Differences in possible actions or payoffs based on role (e.g., owner vs intruder).

fact_asymmetry_impact.label: Impact of Asymmetry
fact_asymmetry_impact.summary: The presence of asymmetry, even without payoff effects, can completely alter the predicted evolutionary outcome (p. 628).

concept_adaptive_dynamics.label: Adaptive Dynamics
concept_adaptive_dynamics.summary: A simplified approach to evolutionary dynamics that ignores genetic detail and assumes selection acts to locally hill climb.

fact_adaptive_dynamics_branching.label: Evolutionary Branching
fact_adaptive_dynamics_branching.summary: Occurs when a strategy is convergence stable but not an ESS, leading to disruptive selection (p. 628).

concept_mating_systems.label: Mating Systems and Sexual Selection
concept_mating_systems.summary: The study of who mates with whom, when, and the evolutionary forces (sexual selection) driving these patterns.

concept_sexual_selection.label: Sexual Selection
concept_sexual_selection.summary: Selection arising from differential access to reproductive opportunities.

concept_intrasexual_selection.label: Intrasexual Selection
concept_intrasexual_selection.summary: Competition between members of the same sex for access to the opposite sex.

concept_weapon_evolution.label: Weapon Evolution
concept_weapon_evolution.summary: The evolution of morphological traits used in intrasexual competition.

fact_weapon_signaling.label: Weapons as Signals
fact_weapon_signaling.summary: Weapons may evolve initially as small dangerous traits and later serve as visual signals of quality (p. 643).

fact_weapon_ritualization.label: Ritualized Combat
fact_weapon_ritualization.summary: Complex weapons can facilitate ritualized contests with low lethality (e.g., elk pushing contests) (p. 643).

concept_alternative_mating_strategies.label: Alternative Mating Strategies
concept_alternative_mating_strategies.summary: Non-conventional behavioral and morphological tactics to achieve mating success.

fact_sneaking_behavior.label: Sneaking Behavior
fact_sneaking_behavior.summary: Males may evade dominant males by resembling females or using sneaking tactics (e.g., Pacific salmon) (p. 643).

fact_mating_niche.label: Mating Niche
fact_mating_niche.summary: Polygyny can create a 'mating niche' for unconventional males who avoid direct confrontation but still sire offspring (p. 644).

concept_sperm_competition.label: Sperm Competition
concept_sperm_competition.summary: Postcopulatory competition between the ejaculates of different males to fertilize the ova of a female.

fact_sperm_competition_adaptations.label: Adaptations to Sperm Competition
fact_sperm_competition_adaptations.summary: Include larger testes, accessory glands producing copulatory plugs, and chemicals that manipulate female reproduction (p. 644).

fact_cryptic_female_choice.label: Cryptic Female Choice
fact_cryptic_female_choice.summary: The ability of females to discriminate in their reproductive tract among the sperm of different males (p. 644).

concept_intersexual_selection.label: Intersexual Selection (Mate Choice)
concept_intersexual_selection.summary: Selection based on the nonrandom choice of mates by one sex.

concept_costs_of_choosiness.label: Costs of Choosiness
concept_costs_of_choosiness.summary: Factors that reduce the fitness of an individual that is selective about mates.

fact_cost_breeding_rate.label: Reduced Breeding Rate
fact_cost_breeding_rate.summary: Choosiness lowers lifetime reproductive output by increasing the interval between breeding events (p. 647).

fact_convenience_polyandry.label: Convenience Polyandry
fact_convenience_polyandry.summary: Females may acquiesce to superfluous matings to avoid the costs of resisting sexually coercive males (p. 637).

concept_rewards_of_choosiness.label: Rewards of Choosiness
concept_rewards_of_choosiness.summary: Benefits that offset the costs of being selective.

concept_direct_benefits.label: Direct Benefits
concept_direct_benefits.summary: Increases in offspring number or female longevity due to resources provided by the mate.

fact_direct_benefit_examples.label: Direct Benefit Examples
fact_direct_benefit_examples.summary: Include parental care, nuptial gifts, or access to high-quality breeding territories (p. 651).

concept_indirect_benefits.label: Indirect Benefits
