concept_indirect_benefits.summary: Increases in mean offspring fitness due to the genetic quality of the mate.

fact_good_genes_hypothesis.label: Good Genes Hypothesis
fact_good_genes_hypothesis.summary: Females choose males with traits that signal heritable variation in fitness or condition (p. 652).

fact_genetic_compatibility.label: Genetic Compatibility
fact_genetic_compatibility.summary: Choice based on avoiding inbreeding to increase heterozygosity in offspring, improving immune defense and performance (p. 652).

concept_cryptic_choice.label: Cryptic Choice
concept_cryptic_choice.summary: Strategic adjustment of reproductive effort (sperm or eggs) after mating or during courtship.

fact_cryptic_male_choice.label: Cryptic Male Choice
fact_cryptic_male_choice.summary: Strategic allocation of sperm based on female fecundity or mating status to maximize fertilization success (p. 649).

fact_cryptic_female_choice_mech.label: Cryptic Female Choice Mechanism
fact_cryptic_female_choice_mech.summary: Active sperm selection or reproductive tract design that biases paternity toward preferred males (p. 649).

concept_sexual_conflict.label: Sexual Conflict
concept_sexual_conflict.summary: Divergence in evolutionary interests between males and females.

fact_intralocus_conflict.label: Intralocus Sexual Conflict
fact_intralocus_conflict.summary: Occurs when each sex has a different fitness optimum for a shared trait, potentially resolved by sex-specific alleles (p. 638).

fact_interlocus_conflict.label: Interlocus Sexual Conflict
fact_interlocus_conflict.summary: Occurs when sexes differ in fitness outcomes of interactions, leading to a coevolutionary arms race (p. 638).

concept_mating_system_measures.label: Measures of Mating Systems
concept_mating_system_measures.summary: Quantitative tools to assess the strength of sexual selection and the nature of the mating system.

fact_osr_definition.label: Operational Sex Ratio (OSR)
fact_osr_definition.summary: Average ratio of fertilizable females to sexually active males at any given time (p. 632).

fact_epp_definition.label: Environmental Potential for Polygamy (EPP)
fact_epp_definition.summary: The degree to which multiple mates or critical resources are economically defendable (p. 632).

fact_prr_definition.label: Potential Reproductive Rate (PRR)
fact_prr_definition.summary: The maximum number of independent offspring parents can produce per unit time when partners are freely available (p. 632).

fact_batemans_gradient.label: Bateman's Gradient (bss)
fact_batemans_gradient.summary: A selection differential describing the covariance between a particular trait (mating success) and fitness (p. 635).

fact_opportunity_sexual_selection.label: Opportunity for Sexual Selection (Is)
fact_opportunity_sexual_selection.summary: Measures the standardized variance in mating success and represents an upper limit of the strength of sexual selection (p. 635).

concept_mating_system_categories.label: Mating System Categories
concept_mating_system_categories.summary: Classifications based on the number of mates and monopolization ability.

fact_monogamy.label: Monogamy
fact_monogamy.summary: A system where each sex has only one partner; limited opportunity for monopolization (p. 634).

fact_polygyny.label: Polygyny
fact_polygyny.summary: A system where one male mates with multiple females; high variance in male reproductive success (p. 634).

fact_polyandry.label: Polyandry
fact_polyandry.summary: A system where one female mates with multiple males (p. 634).

concept_evolutionary_potential.label: Mating Systems and Evolutionary Potential
concept_evolutionary_potential.summary: How mating structures influence the rate and direction of evolutionary change.

fact_ige_definition.label: Indirect Genetic Effects (IGEs)
fact_ige_definition.summary: Occurs when the phenotype of one individual is affected by genes expressed in interacting partners (p. 638).

fact_between_sex_correlation.label: Between-Sex Genetic Correlation
fact_between_sex_correlation.summary: Correlation in traits expressed in both sexes due to a shared genome, which can constrain evolutionary trajectories (p. 638).

fact_x_chromosome_influence.label: X Chromosome Influence
fact_x_chromosome_influence.summary: The X chromosome facilitates the evolution of sex-linked genes related to sexual antagonism due to its hemizygous state in males (p. 638).

comm_ev.label: Evolution of Communication
comm_ev.summary: The study of how animals send, receive, and interpret messages and how these systems evolve over time.

comm_elements.label: Elements of Animal Communication
comm_elements.summary: The four fundamental components required for communication to occur.

fact_comm_4_elements.label: Four Elements of Communication
fact_comm_4_elements.summary: Communication comprises: (1) the signaler, (2) the signal, (3) the receiver, and (4) the channel. (Page 656)

comm_modalities.label: Signaling Modalities
comm_modalities.summary: The physical or chemical mediums used to transmit communication signals.

fact_modality_types.label: Types of Modalities
fact_modality_types.summary: Signals include chemical, mechanical (sound and vibration), visual, and electrostatic messages. (Page 656)

fact_modality_requirement.label: Modality Requirement
fact_modality_requirement.summary: Communication signals must be a modification of the physical or chemical environment that stands out against background noise. (Page 656)

comm_constraints.label: Constraints on Signaling Modalities
comm_constraints.summary: Factors that favor one modality over another based on environment, target, and biology.

cons_environmental.label: Environmental Constraints
cons_environmental.summary: Physical conditions that limit signal effectiveness.

fact_nocturnal_visual.label: Nocturnal Visual Constraints
fact_nocturnal_visual.summary: Nocturnal species cannot rely on visual signals unless they generate bioluminescence (e.g., fireflies). (Page 656)

fact_alarm_speed.label: Alarm Signal Constraints
fact_alarm_speed.summary: Alarm signals require speed, often precluding chemical messages (which rely on slow diffusion or uncontrolled convection) in favor of visual, acoustic, or vibrational signals. (Page 656)

cons_privacy.label: Privacy and Control Constraints
cons_privacy.summary: The need to reach intended receivers while avoiding eavesdroppers (predators/rivals).

fact_private_channels.label: Private Channels
fact_private_channels.summary: Selection for signals that the signaler can control to avoid unintended receivers. (Page 656)

fact_substrate_vibration.label: Substrate Vibration
fact_substrate_vibration.summary: Shift from airborne sound to substrate vibration (e.g., in katydids) to avoid bat predation. (Page 656)

cons_size.label: Body Size Constraints
cons_size.summary: Physical limitations on signal production and perception based on organism dimensions.

fact_size_acoustic.label: Acoustic Size Constraint
fact_size_acoustic.summary: Animals below minimum dimensions cannot radiate sound waves or bear tympana; smallest insects (ants) rarely use acoustic communication. (Page 656)

fact_size_visual.label: Visual Size Constraint
fact_size_visual.summary: Eyes capable of forming images must exceed a minimum diameter; smallest insects extract only crude movement patterns. (Page 656)

fact_size_chemical.label: Chemical Size Ubiquity
fact_size_chemical.summary: Chemical communication has no fundamental size constraints and is found even in single-celled organisms. (Page 656)

comm_evolution_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Communication Evolution
comm_evolution_mechanisms.summary: The processes by which communication signals originate and modify.

def_pheromone.label: Pheromone
def_pheromone.summary: A chemical substance emitted outside the body that influences the behavior or physiology of another individual of the same species. (Page 656)

def_phylogenetic_analysis.label: Phylogenetic Analysis
def_phylogenetic_analysis.summary: Using evolutionary models (trees) based on independent traits to infer the evolutionary trajectory of a particular trait. (Page 656)

def_sensory_bias.label: Sensory Bias
def_sensory_bias.summary: A perceptual trait evolved in a non-communicative context that is later exploited by the evolution of specific communication signals. (Page 656)

def_signal_intensity.label: Signal Intensity
def_signal_intensity.summary: The energy transmitted (mechanical/visual) or matter disseminated (chemical) measured relative to the source. (Page 656)

def_snr.label: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
def_snr.summary: The intensity of a signal divided by the intensity of its modality in the local environment when the signal is not transmitted. (Page 656)

mech_fisherian.label: Fisherian/Coevolutionary Mechanism
mech_fisherian.summary: Evolutionary changes occur in both the signaler and the receiver in a reciprocal, alternating fashion. (Page 657)

mech_sensory_exploitation.label: Sensory Bias Exploitation
mech_sensory_exploitation.summary: Evolutionary change occurs initially only in the signaler, who exploits a preexisting perceptual capability in the receiver. (Page 657)

mech_genetic_coupling.label: Genetic Coupling
mech_genetic_coupling.summary: The hypothesis that same or linked genetic elements control both signaler and receiver traits. (Page 657)

mech_ritualization.label: Ritualization
mech_ritualization.summary: A process where a postural movement or displacement activity (initially serving physiological functions) becomes standardized as a message. (Page 658)

comm_reliability.label: Reliability of Communication
comm_reliability.summary: The degree to which a signal accurately represents the signaler's identity, quality, or intent.

fact_honesty_economics.label: Economics of Honesty
fact_honesty_economics.summary: Signals tend to be honest because receivers who ignore unreliable signals reduce their own fitness cost, forcing signalers to be reliable to be heard. (Page 660)

fact_intensity_proxy.label: Intensity as Quality Proxy
fact_intensity_proxy.summary: High-intensity signals often demand high energy; therefore, only high-quality individuals can afford to signal strongly. (Page 661)

parental_care.label: Evolution of Parental Care
parental_care.summary: Traits that increase the fitness of offspring, often at a cost to the parents.

care_definitions.label: Parental Care Definitions
care_definitions.summary: Technical terms used to measure the costs and effects of parental investment.

def_parental_care.label: Parental Care
def_parental_care.summary: Any parental trait (behavioral or other) that increases offspring fitness and originated/is maintained for this function. (Page 663)

def_parental_effect.label: Parental Effect
def_parental_effect.summary: Causal effects of parent phenotype on offspring phenotype (growth, survival) beyond inherited genes. (Page 663)

def_parental_effort.label: Parental Effort
def_parental_effort.summary: Combined fitness costs (reduced mating/somatic effort) incurred by parents due to producing and caring for offspring. (Page 663)

def_parental_expenditure.label: Parental Expenditure
def_parental_expenditure.summary: Proximate measure of cost: time, energy, and food spent on care. (Page 663)

def_parental_investment.label: Parental Investment
def_parental_investment.summary: Investment in an individual offspring that increases its survival chance at the cost of investment in other offspring. (Page 663)

def_parent_offspring_conflict.label: Parent-Offspring Conflict
def_parent_offspring_conflict.summary: Difference between optima for parental investment from the perspective of the parent's gene vs. the offspring's gene. (Page 663)

care_forms.label: Forms of Parental Care
care_forms.summary: The diversity of parental strategies across taxa.

fact_gamete_provisioning.label: Gamete Provisioning
fact_gamete_provisioning.summary: Providing eggs with extra nutrients (proteins, lipids). Most basal form of care. (Page 664)

fact_nesting_behavior.label: Nesting and Burrowing
fact_nesting_behavior.summary: Choosing oviposition sites or building nests/burrows to protect from predators or infanticide. (Page 664)

fact_attendance_brooding.label: Attendance and Brooding
fact_attendance_brooding.summary: Remaining with eggs at a fixed location or carrying them in specialized pouches. (Page 664)

fact_viviparity.label: Viviparity
fact_viviparity.summary: Retention of fertilized eggs within the female reproductive tract during development. (Page 665)

fact_food_provisioning.label: Food Provisioning
fact_food_provisioning.summary: ranges from placental transfer and mass provisioning to progressive provisioning of prey or secretions (milk). (Page 665)

care_origins.label: Origins of Parental Care
care_origins.summary: Conditions that promote the evolutionary emergence of care.

fact_spatial_aggregation.label: Spatial Aggregation
fact_spatial_aggregation.summary: Clutches or litters remaining near parents ensure mutations for care benefit the parent's own carriers. (Page 666)

fact_life_history_origin.label: Life History Influence
fact_life_history_origin.summary: Care evolves more readily in species with slow development or low prospects for future reproduction. (Page 666)

fact_ecological_hazard.label: Ecological Hazard Differential
fact_ecological_hazard.summary: Care is favored when environment harshness (predation, parasites) affects juveniles more severely than parents. (Page 666)

care_maintenance.label: Maintenance of Parental Care
care_maintenance.summary: Forces that sustain care and shape coevolution.

care_sexual_conflict.label: Sexual Conflict in Care
care_sexual_conflict.summary: Disagreement between parents over who provides care and the amount provided.

fact_sex_roles.label: Sex Roles
fact_sex_roles.summary: Most common: female-only care (mammals). Male-only care occurs in some fish/amphibians. Biparental care common in birds. (Page 667)

fact_paternal_care_drivers.label: Drivers of Paternal Care
fact_paternal_care_drivers.summary: Male care is favored when mating pool is male-biased (low mating success) or when certainty of parentage is high. (Page 667)

care_sibling_conflict.label: Sibling Conflict
care_sibling_conflict.summary: Competition among offspring for limited parental resources.

fact_sibling_aggression.label: Sibling Aggression
fact_sibling_aggression.summary: Competition can be lethal, e.g., cattle egrets where older chicks kill younger siblings. (Page 668)

fact_begging_manipulation.label: Begging Manipulation
fact_begging_manipulation.summary: Offspring may exaggerate demands to manipulate parents; resolution occurs when begging becomes costly to the offspring. (Page 668)

care_social_parasitism.label: Social Parasitism
care_social_parasitism.summary: Exploitation of parental care by non-related individuals.

fact_egg_dumping.label: Egg Dumping
fact_egg_dumping.summary: Subordinate females lay eggs in the nests of breeding conspecifics (e.g., starlings). (Page 668)

fact_brood_parasitism.label: Brood Parasitism
fact_brood_parasitism.summary: Obligate parasites like the cuckoo use acoustic trickery to stimulate foster parents to provide food for a whole brood. (Page 668)

care_genetics.label: Genetics and Epigenetics of Care
care_genetics.summary: The heritable and developmental basis of care traits.

fact_correlational_selection.label: Correlational Selection
fact_correlational_selection.summary: Selection favoring particular combinations of parent and offspring traits (e.g., good providers having offspring that beg intensely). (Page 669)

fact_genomic_imprinting.label: Genomic Imprinting
fact_genomic_imprinting.summary: Parent-of-origin specific gene expression; e.g., Igf2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is paternally expressed to enhance fetal growth. (Page 669)

coop_conflict.label: Cooperation and Conflict
coop_conflict.summary: Analysis of interactions that benefit both the actor and the recipient.

coop_definitions.label: Cooperation Definitions
coop_definitions.summary: Terminology for different types of cooperative interactions.

def_cooperation.label: Cooperation
def_cooperation.summary: An interaction that benefits the recipient and the actor either directly or indirectly. (Page 671)

def_cheating.label: Cheating
def_cheating.summary: Behavior that benefits oneself at a cost to others within a cooperative framework. (Page 671)

def_direct_benefit.label: Direct Benefit
def_direct_benefit.summary: A benefit that accrues to the actor's personal fitness. (Page 671)

def_indirect_benefit.label: Indirect Benefit
def_indirect_benefit.summary: Benefit of actions toward nondescendant kin who share the actor's genes. (Page 671)

def_inclusive_fitness.label: Inclusive Fitness
def_inclusive_fitness.summary: Total fitness including direct reproduction and the share contributed to nondescendant kin. (Page 671)

def_hamiltons_rule.label: Hamilton's Rule
def_hamiltons_rule.summary: rB - C > 0, where r = relatedness, B = benefit to beneficiary, C = cost to altruist. (Page 671)

coop_fraternal.label: Fraternal Cooperation
coop_fraternal.summary: Cooperation between relatives; can be altruistic as payoff can be indirect. (Page 672)

fact_kin_selection.label: Kin Selection
fact_kin_selection.summary: Mechanism where genes for fraternal cooperation spread because they are present in the recipient. (Page 673)

fact_division_of_labor_fraternal.label: Fraternal Division of Labor
fact_division_of_labor_fraternal.summary: Different participants perform different tasks, often resulting in specialized castes (e.g., soldiers in ants). (Page 673)

fact_social_insect_lifestyles.label: Social Insect Lifestyles
fact_social_insect_lifestyles.summary: Life insurance (adults take over young if others die) vs. Fortress defense (defensible nesting sites). (Page 673)

coop_egalitarian.label: Egalitarian Cooperation
coop_egalitarian.summary: Cooperation between unrelated individuals; requires direct benefits to the actor. (Page 672)

fact_mutualism_theory.label: Mutualism Theory
fact_mutualism_theory.summary: Cooperation between nonrelatives where different goods or services are exchanged. (Page 671)

fact_complementary_talents.label: Complementary Talents
fact_complementary_talents.summary: Egalitarian cooperation often succeeds because partners have different skills (e.g., pollinators and plants). (Page 674)

coop_conflict_control.label: Control of Cooperation Conflict
coop_conflict_control.summary: Mechanisms to prevent cheating and maintain cooperative alliances.

ctrl_fraternal.label: Fraternal Conflict Control
ctrl_fraternal.summary: Control through power asymmetries and policing.

fact_power_asymmetry.label: Power Asymmetry
fact_power_asymmetry.summary: Conflict resolved by the relative power of parties; e.g., age asymmetry (parent-child). (Page 674)

fact_policing.label: Policing
fact_policing.summary: Group enforcement of common good; e.g., honey bee workers suppressing other workers from laying eggs. (Page 675)

ctrl_egalitarian.label: Egalitarian Conflict Control
ctrl_egalitarian.summary: Control through partner selection and shared fates.

fact_partner_choice.label: Partner Choice
fact_partner_choice.summary: Under-performers are punished or rejected (e.g., plants rejecting nitrogen-poor rhizobia). (Page 675)

fact_partner_fidelity.label: Partner Fidelity Feedback
fact_partner_fidelity.summary: Fates of partners are so commingled that sanctions would hurt both; common in vertically transmitted symbionts. (Page 675)

def_organismality.label: Organismality
def_organismality.summary: A living unit characterized by high cooperation and very low conflict among its parts. (Page 671)

coop_breeding.label: Cooperative Breeding
coop_breeding.summary: Social system where adult helpers rear offspring that are not their own.

cb_ecology.label: Ecology of Cooperative Breeding
cb_ecology.summary: Environmental factors favoring delayed dispersal and helping.

fact_habitat_saturation.label: Habitat Saturation
fact_habitat_saturation.summary: Intense competition for breeding territories leads offspring to remain as helpers (e.g., Seychelles warbler). (Page 678)

fact_benefits_philopatry.label: Benefits of Philopatry
fact_benefits_philopatry.summary: Fitness benefits of remaining at home rather than dispersing to low-quality habitats. (Page 678)

fact_insect_nest_insurance.label: Nest Insurance
fact_insect_nest_insurance.summary: In insects, helping protects the nest from failure if the breeding female dies. (Page 678)

mech_indiscriminate.label: Indiscriminate Helping
mech_indiscriminate.summary: Helping occurs because population viscosity ensures recipients are more related than average. (Page 679)

mech_discriminate.label: Discriminate Helping
mech_discriminate.summary: Helpers use cues (often learned during development) to identify and preferentially aid close kin. (Page 679)

mech_direct_fitness.label: Direct Fitness Benefits
mech_direct_fitness.summary: Helping for personal gain: Skills hypothesis (learning), Group augmentation (larger group), Prestige hypothesis (status). (Page 679)

mech_enforced.label: Enforced Helping
mech_enforced.summary: Pay-to-stay hypothesis (threat of eviction) or active punishment (aggression) to induce help. (Page 679)

cb_individual_diff.label: Individual Differences in Helping
cb_individual_diff.summary: Variation in effort among helpers within a group.

fact_cost_variation.label: Cost Variation
fact_cost_variation.summary: Helping effort correlates with nutritional state (e.g., meerkats feed more when they have more food). (Page 680)

fact_future_fitness_impact.label: Future Fitness Impact
fact_future_fitness_impact.summary: Individuals with higher expected future direct fitness (e.g., higher in the inheritance queue) may work less. (Page 680)

fact_behavioral_plasticity.label: Behavioral Plasticity
fact_behavioral_plasticity.summary: Early life conditions interact with genotype to create consistent individual 'personalities' in helping. (Page 680)

cb_repro_conflict.label: Reproductive Conflict
cb_repro_conflict.summary: Competition for breeding status and distribution of reproduction (skew).

model_transactional.label: Transactional Models
model_transactional.summary: Reproductive skew is determined by threats to exercise outside options (e.g., leaving the group). (Page 681)

model_incomplete_control.label: Incomplete Control Models
model_incomplete_control.summary: Skew depends on the relative strength/efficiency of players to exert costly control over reproduction. (Page 682)

human_beh_eco.label: Human Behavioral Ecology
human_beh_eco.summary: Application of behavioral ecology theories to human populations.

hbe_approach.label: Human Behavioral Ecology Approach
hbe_approach.summary: Using optimality models to study how behavioral strategies maximize fitness in varying environments.

fact_optimality_tradeoffs.label: Optimality Trade-offs
fact_optimality_tradeoffs.summary: Analysis of birth intervals as a trade-off between number of offspring and maternal/infant mortality risks. (Page 684)

hbe_methodology.label: Methodology in HBE
hbe_methodology.summary: Data sources used to test evolutionary predictions in humans.

fact_traditional_societies.label: Traditional Society Study
fact_traditional_societies.summary: Focus on hunter-gatherer or agro-pastoral groups (e.g., !Kung San, Hadza) as proxies for Pleistocene environments. (Page 684)

fact_cohort_studies.label: Cohort Studies
fact_cohort_studies.summary: Longitudinal designs recording life events of groups sharing common characteristics. (Page 683)

fact_twin_registers.label: Twin Registers
fact_twin_registers.summary: Comparing identical and fraternal twins to estimate relative genetic and environmental influences. (Page 683)

hbe_case_menopause.label: The Case of Menopause
hbe_case_menopause.summary: An evolutionary puzzle explained by the Grandmother Hypothesis.

fact_grandmother_hypothesis.label: Grandmother Hypothesis
fact_grandmother_hypothesis.summary: Post-reproductive women increase their inclusive fitness by helping rear grandchildren, increasing grandchild survival. (Page 685)

hbe.label: Human Behavioral Ecology (HBE)
hbe.summary: The study of how environmental conditions and ecological pressures influence human fitness and life history traits.

hbe_menopause.label: Evolution of Menopause
hbe_menopause.summary: Investigation into why humans experience a post-reproductive lifespan and its fitness benefits.

fact_grandmother_effect.label: The Grandmother Effect
fact_grandmother_effect.summary: Mothers gain extra grandchildren by surviving beyond menopause until their mid-seventies because offspring with living post-reproductive mothers bred earlier, more frequently, and more successfully (p. 685).

fact_menopause_selection.label: Selection for Lifespan
fact_menopause_selection.summary: Life span can be under positive selection at least until the mid-seventies, provided the grandmother lives close to her adult offspring (p. 685).

hbe_environmental_fitness.label: Environmental Conditions and Fitness
hbe_environmental_fitness.summary: The analysis of how energy budgets and resource availability affect the costs of reproduction and selection on life history.

fact_reproduction_costs.label: Reproduction Energy Budget
fact_reproduction_costs.summary: High costs of reproduction have different effects depending on a woman's diet and physical activity levels (p. 685).

fact_fecundity_longevity_poor.label: Fecundity in Poor Women
fact_fecundity_longevity_poor.summary: There is a negative relationship between the number of offspring and postmenopausal life span among poor landless women due to high costs of reproduction (multiple pregnancies, breastfeeding) that cannot be compensated by diet (p. 685).

fact_fecundity_longevity_wealthy.label: Fecundity in Wealthy Women
fact_fecundity_longevity_wealthy.summary: Wealthier women often show a positive relationship between fecundity and postmenopausal life span because they can afford both large family size and long life span (p. 685).

hbe_criticisms.label: Problems and Criticisms of HBE
hbe_criticisms.summary: Critiques regarding the focus on traditional populations and the application of adaptive explanations.

hbe_crit_traditional.label: Limitations of Traditional Population Focus
hbe_crit_traditional.summary: Focusing on hunter-gatherers leads to limited sample sizes, disappearing groups, estimated ages, and ignoring rapid evolution since agriculture (p. 686).

hbe_crit_modern_selection.label: Modern Selection Validity
hbe_crit_modern_selection.summary: Claims that natural selection stopped with agriculture are contradicted by genomic evidence showing positive selection in the past 10,000 years (p. 686).

hbe_crit_genetic_role.label: The Role of Genes
hbe_crit_genetic_role.summary: Modern HBE should move past Social Darwinism to study mating patterns, reproductive patterns on genetic variation, and genetic constraints on evolvability (p. 686).

hbe_crit_adaptationism.label: Over-application of Adaptationism
hbe_crit_adaptationism.summary: Critics argue HBE seeks adaptive explanations where unlikely; however, HBE also studies environmental constraints (e.g., birth season) and non-beneficial cultural practices (p. 686-687).

hbe_modern_evolution.label: Evolution in Modern Societies
hbe_modern_evolution.summary: The shift toward measuring current selection and microevolution in contemporary human populations.

hbe_mod_data.label: Modern Data Sources
hbe_mod_data.summary: Use of historical population records, cohort studies, twin registers, medical intervention studies, and noninvasive manipulations (p. 687).

hbe_mod_heritability.label: Heritability and Genetic Constraints
hbe_mod_heritability.summary: Many life history traits (age at first reproduction, weight, height) have measurable heritability. Genetic correlations can constrain evolution, such as the negative correlation between reproduction rates and longevity seen in Finnish pedigrees (p. 687-688).

hbe_mod_strength.label: Selection Strength in Modernity
hbe_mod_strength.summary: Studies show significant selection in the US (predicting descendants to be shorter, stouter, with lower cholesterol) and preindustrial French-Canadians (selection for earlier age at first reproduction) (p. 688).

hbe_contributions.label: Contributions to General Evolution
hbe_contributions.summary: How human-specific data enhances the study of general evolutionary biology.

fact_human_data_advantage.label: Human Data Advantages
fact_human_data_advantage.summary: Humans provide unique lifetime vital records, medical histories, and genomic data. Fitness can be measured more reliably via the number of grandchildren rather than just offspring (p. 688-689).

fact_natural_experiments.label: Natural Experiments
fact_natural_experiments.summary: Events like the Dutch Hunger Winter, wars creating sex-ratio biases, and crop variations allow for testing evolutionary questions (p. 689).

fact_mating_systems_utah.label: Mating System Impacts
fact_mating_systems_utah.summary: Reductions in polygamy among Utahans (1830-1894) corresponded to a 58% reduction in sexual selection strength (p. 689).

ep.label: Evolutionary Psychology (EP)
ep.summary: A field integrating cognitive psychology with evolutionary biology to explain human psychological mechanisms as adaptations to ancestral environments.

ep_glossary.label: EP Key Terms
ep_glossary.summary: Definitions of fundamental concepts used in Evolutionary Psychology.

def_comp_mechanisms.label: Computational Mechanisms
def_comp_mechanisms.summary: Algorithms that compute determinate input-output functions, dependent only on the structure of representations involved (p. 690).

def_eco_rationality.label: Ecological Rationality
def_eco_rationality.summary: The hypothesis that rationality is relative to the ecological context in which a procedure is applied (p. 690).

def_eea.label: Environment Of Evolutionary Adaptedness (EEA)
def_eea.summary: The physical and social environment characteristic of human evolution, often associated with the Pleistocene African savanna or a statistical composite of ancestral environments (p. 690).

def_incest_taboos.label: Incest Taboos
def_incest_taboos.summary: Social prohibitions against sexual relations among closely related individuals, often considered a human universal (p. 690).

def_modules.label: Modules
def_modules.summary: Cognitive mechanisms that operate in relative independence from other mechanisms governing other domains (p. 690).

def_social_exchange.label: Social Exchange
def_social_exchange.summary: Any exchange of value among individuals with attached costs and benefits, often involving reciprocal altruism (p. 690).

ep_core_claims.label: Core Commitments of EP
ep_core_claims.summary: The foundational assumptions of the modern Evolutionary Psychology program.

claim_selection.label: Selection Basis
claim_selection.summary: Psychological mechanisms are results of natural and sexual selection to solve problems like mating, hunting, and offspring rearing (p. 692).

claim_computation.label: Computational Nature
claim_computation.summary: Psychological mechanisms (cognitive processes and emotional responses) are thought of as computational mechanisms or genetically specified behavioral strategies (p. 692).

claim_eea_focus.label: EEA Influence
claim_eea_focus.summary: Mechanisms evolved in response to stable features of ancestral environments (Pleistocene), not contemporary ones (p. 692).

claim_non_modern_adaptation.label: Modern Mismatch
claim_non_modern_adaptation.summary: Ancestral adaptations (e.g., preference for sweets) may be nonadaptive or maladaptive in contemporary environments (p. 692).

claim_mosaic_mind.label: Mosaic Mind
claim_mosaic_mind.summary: The mind is a collection of domain-specific mechanisms (modules) rather than a general-purpose learning machine (p. 692).

ep_evidence.label: Psychological Evidence in EP
ep_evidence.summary: Methods used to test EP hypotheses and examples of findings.

fact_ep_methods.label: EP Methodology
fact_ep_methods.summary: Use of questionnaires, controlled experiments, observational methods, and brain imaging (fMRI/PET) (p. 693).

fact_survival_memory.label: Survival-Oriented Memory
fact_survival_memory.summary: Experimental probes show that recall for survival-oriented terms is significantly better than for neutral words (p. 693).

fact_jealousy_patterns.label: Gender-Specific Jealousy
fact_jealousy_patterns.summary: Females are predicted to be more sensitive to emotional infidelity (risk of abandonment), while males are more sensitive to sexual infidelity (risk to paternity) (p. 693).

ep_application.label: Application of Evolutionary Models
ep_application.summary: The use of reverse engineering and ancestral scenarios to explain current behavior.

ep_app_ancestral.label: Ancestral Social Life Portrait
ep_app_ancestral.summary: EP assumes ancestral hominids lived in compact kin-based groups (<100 members) with sexual division of labor and biparental care (p. 693).

ep_app_incest.label: Incest Avoidance and the Westermark Hypothesis
ep_app_incest.summary: The Westermark hypothesis suggests children raised together develop sexual aversion to avoid inbreeding depression. However, this is criticized as emigration patterns in early Homo might have made incest avoidance unnecessary (p. 694-695).

ep_alternatives.label: Evolutionary Alternatives to EP
ep_alternatives.summary: Perspectives from broader evolutionary biology that challenge EP's constraints.

alt_phylogeny.label: Phylogeny and Comparative Biology
alt_phylogeny.summary: EP often ignores primate kinship; incorporating comparative biology provides testable alternative hypotheses for social patterns (p. 695).

alt_recent_genomics.label: Recent Genomic Changes
alt_recent_genomics.summary: Contrary to EP's 'Pleistocene relic' view, substantial genomic changes occurred in the last 10,000 years due to agriculture and animal domestication (p. 695).

alt_plasticity.label: Epigenetics and Plasticity
alt_plasticity.summary: Interplay between genetic factors, epigenetic influences, and learning makes universals less likely than EP assumes (p. 695).

alt_gene_culture.label: Gene-Culture Coevolution
alt_gene_culture.summary: Cultural practices can modify the human brain and accelerate evolutionary rates (p. 695).

eusoc_glossary.label: Eusociality Key Terms
eusoc_glossary.summary: Technical definitions related to eusocial systems.

def_eusociality.label: Eusociality
def_eusociality.summary: A social organization including reproductive division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlap of generations (p. 697).

def_haplodiploidy.label: Haplodiploidy
def_haplodiploidy.summary: Sex determination where males are from unfertilized haploid eggs and females from fertilized diploid eggs (p. 697).

def_kin_selection.label: Kin Selection
def_kin_selection.summary: Selection on genes for social traits that affect the fitness of relatives (p. 697).

def_philopatry.label: Philopatry
def_philopatry.summary: The tendency to stay close or return to the natal site (p. 697).

def_relatedness.label: Relatedness
def_relatedness.summary: The probability that individuals share identical alleles inherited from recent common ancestors (p. 697).

def_repro_altruism.label: Reproductive Altruism
def_repro_altruism.summary: An action by which an individual decreases its own reproduction to help others reproduce (p. 697).

def_self_org.label: Self-organization
def_self_org.summary: Spontaneous organization arising from local interactions among individuals without central control (p. 697).

eusoc_drivers.label: Drivers of Eusociality
eusoc_drivers.summary: The evolutionary mechanisms that resolve the paradox of sterile workers.

fact_hamilton_rule.label: Hamilton's Rule
fact_hamilton_rule.summary: Reproductive altruism is favored when the loss in personal fitness (c) is smaller than the gain in recipient fitness (b) multiplied by relatedness (r): rb > c (p. 699).

fact_inclusive_fitness.label: Inclusive Fitness
fact_inclusive_fitness.summary: Includes direct reproductive output plus the indirect effects of genes on the fitness of other individuals carrying the same genes (p. 699).

eusoc_eco_factors.label: Ecological and Life History Factors
eusoc_eco_factors.summary: Environmental conditions that promote the evolution of eusociality.

fact_shelter_food_coincidence.label: Shelter and Food Coincidence
fact_shelter_food_coincidence.summary: Living in cavities/burrows (e.g., mole rats, termites) promotes sociality via colony defense, inheritability of the colony, and proximity of relatives (p. 699).

fact_life_insurance.label: Life Insurance Effect
fact_life_insurance.summary: High mortality risk during brood rearing favors helping because if one helper dies, the investment is not lost, as others finish rearing the brood (p. 699).

eusoc_family_structure.label: Role of Family Structure
eusoc_family_structure.summary: How genetic relatedness patterns in families facilitate reproductive altruism.

fact_mother_daughter_asymmetry.label: Mother-Daughter Asymmetry
fact_mother_daughter_asymmetry.summary: Daughters are as related to mother's offspring (r=0.5) as to their own, while mothers are more related to their own (r=0.5) than daughters' offspring (r=0.25), stabilizing reproductive monopolization by mothers (p. 699).

fact_monoandry_ancestral.label: Monoandry
fact_monoandry_ancestral.summary: A queen mating with a single male was ancestral in eusocial Hymenoptera, ensuring high relatedness of offspring (p. 700).

eusoc_castes.label: Caste Differentiation
eusoc_castes.summary: The development of morphological and behavioral specializations.

fact_dimorphism_colony_size.label: Dimorphism and Colony Size
fact_dimorphism_colony_size.summary: Morphological differences between queens and workers are more pronounced in larger colonies because the probability of workers becoming replacement reproductives decreases (p. 700).

eusoc_working.label: Collective Work in Eusociality
eusoc_working.summary: How division of labor increases colony performance.

eusoc_work_benefits.label: Efficiency, Robustness, and Flexibility
eusoc_work_benefits.summary: Concurrent task performance, synergy (e.g., mole rat burrows), redundancy against failure, and behavioral flexibility to match environmental needs (p. 701).

eusoc_work_reg.label: Regulation of Division of Labor
eusoc_work_reg.summary: Mechanisms for allocating workers to tasks, specifically the response threshold model where workers act when a stimulus exceeds their individual threshold (p. 701).

eusoc_conflict.label: Intragroup Conflicts and Resolution
eusoc_conflict.summary: The persistence of divergent genetic interests and their management.

fact_hymenoptera_sex_conflict.label: Hymenoptera Sex Allocation
fact_hymenoptera_sex_conflict.summary: Workers may kill brothers to favor more related sisters, while queens bias sex ratio toward males (p. 702).

fact_conflict_resolution.label: Conflict Resolution Mechanisms
fact_conflict_resolution.summary: Resolution occurs through genetic homogeneity, synergistic fitness benefits, and social enforcement like policing (e.g., workers suppressing each other's eggs) or aggression (p. 702).

cognition.label: Cognitive Evolution
cognition.summary: The study of the phylogenetic similarities and discontinuities between human and nonhuman minds.

cog_decomp.label: Cognitive Decomposition Approach
cog_decomp.summary: The method of dissecting complex cognitive phenotypes (language, music, math) into component mechanisms to study their evolutionary history (p. 704-705).

fact_co_option.label: Cognitive Co-option
fact_co_option.summary: Mechanisms evolved for specific functions are co-opted for others; e.g., the temporal lobe evolved for object recognition but is used for reading in humans (p. 706).

cog_space.label: The Space of Possibilities
cog_space.summary: The theory that organisms have a space of potential anatomical, behavioral, and cognitive forms not yet realized (p. 706).

cog_domestication.label: Domestication and Cognitive Change
cog_domestication.summary: Using artificial selection to reveal hidden cognitive potential.

fact_dog_pointing.label: Pointing in Dogs vs. Wolves
fact_dog_pointing.summary: Dogs understand human pointing gestures; wolves raised by humans can do so, but feral dogs cannot, indicating a combination of selection and experience (p. 707).

fact_belyaev_foxes.label: Belyaev's Silver Foxes
fact_belyaev_foxes.summary: Selecting for tameness produced by-products including floppier ears, curly tails, and 'social cleverness' (ability to read human gestures) (p. 707).

cog_human_uniqueness.label: Uniquely Human Cognitive Mechanisms
cog_human_uniqueness.summary: Four mechanisms that drive human generativity and distinguish humans from other primates.

def_generative_comp.label: Generative Computation
def_generative_comp.summary: Includes recursive operations (infinite hierarchical expressions) and combinatorial operations (mixing discrete elements for new meanings) (p. 708).

def_cog_promiscuity.label: Cognitive Promiscuity
def_cog_promiscuity.summary: The capacity to combine thoughts and feelings from disparate domains to create novel solutions (p. 708).

def_abstract_thought.label: Abstract Thought
def_abstract_thought.summary: The ability to represent things detached from primary sensory/perceptual inputs (p. 708).

def_symbolic_expression.label: Symbolic Expression
def_symbolic_expression.summary: Representing thoughts with discrete symbols (words, icons), facilitating lossless transfer and reduced memory load (p. 708).

nonadaptive_behavior.label: Apparently Nonadaptive Behavior
nonadaptive_behavior.summary: Behavior that appears to impose a fitness cost on the actor with no immediate compensating benefit.

nonad_glossary.label: Nonadaptive Behavior Key Terms
nonad_glossary.summary: Definitions of terms related to fitness costs and nonadaptive traits.

def_altricial.label: Altricial
def_altricial.summary: Offspring unable to feed or fend for themselves without significant parental assistance (p. 710).

def_arms_race.label: Arms Race
def_arms_race.summary: Cycles of adaptations and counteradaptations between interacting species or sexes (p. 710).

def_brood_parasite.label: Brood Parasite
def_brood_parasite.summary: Species that exploit others' reproductive behavior by laying eggs in host nests (p. 710).

def_filial_cannibalism.label: Filial Cannibalism
def_filial_cannibalism.summary: The eating of offspring by their parents (p. 710).

def_overdominance.label: Overdominance
def_overdominance.summary: Heterozygote advantage where alleles in heterozygous condition increase fitness but decrease it in homozygous condition (p. 710).

def_parasite_manipulation.label: Parasite Manipulation
def_parasite_manipulation.summary: Changes induced in a host by a parasite to increase transmission likelihood (p. 710).

def_phenotypic_plasticity.label: Phenotypic Plasticity
def_phenotypic_plasticity.summary: Production of different phenotypes by a single genotype depending on environment (p. 710).

def_sexual_antagonism.label: Sexual Antagonism
def_sexual_antagonism.summary: Genes conferring advantage in one sex but disadvantage in the other (p. 710).

def_sexual_cannibalism.label: Sexual Cannibalism
def_sexual_cannibalism.summary: The killing and consumption of a mate during or after copulation (p. 710).

nonad_explanations.label: Explanations for Nonadaptive Behavior
nonad_explanations.summary: Ways to understand behaviors that seem to decrease fitness.

fact_tokyo_mice.label: Tokyo Strain Mice
fact_tokyo_mice.summary: A mutant VDR receptor causes females to cannibalize pups, showing how a maladaptive mutation is not evolutionarily maintained (p. 712).

fact_adaptive_infanticide.label: Adaptive Filial Infanticide
fact_adaptive_infanticide.summary: Parents may kill some offspring to ensure others have enough food (e.g., burying beetles) or because costs of rearing outweigh benefits during stress (p. 712).

nonad_manipulation.label: Behavioral Manipulation
nonad_manipulation.summary: Hosts manipulated by other agents to serve the agent's fitness.

fact_cuckoo_parasitism.label: Cuckoo Parasitism
fact_cuckoo_parasitism.summary: Cuckoo chicks push host eggs out of the nest; hosts feed the cuckoo due to mimicry, creating an evolutionary arms race (p. 713).

fact_snail_trematodes.label: Snail and Trematode Interaction
fact_snail_trematodes.summary: Leucochloridium paradoxum induces pulsating brood sacs in snail eyes and positive phototaxis to increase bird predation (p. 713).

fact_redback_spiders.label: Redback Spider Sexual Cannibalism
fact_redback_spiders.summary: Males flip into female mandibles; while this increases cannibalism, it increases the male's paternity share because females are less likely to remate after eating a male (p. 714-715).

nonad_ssb.label: Same-Sex Sexual Behavior (SSB)
nonad_ssb.summary: Sexual behavior between individuals of the same sex, present across many species (e.g., Laysan albatross, Octopoteuthis deletron), used as a case study for deductive evolutionary reasoning (p. 716).

nonadaptive_categories.label: Categories of Nonadaptive Behavior
nonadaptive_categories.summary: The spectrum of behaviors that seem fitness-reducing.

fact_perspective_adaptive.label: Perspective-based Adaptations
fact_perspective_adaptive.summary: Behaviors that seem detrimental but are actually adaptive upon closer inspection, such as in red-back spiders (p. 717).

fact_fitness_reducing_mutations.label: True Fitness-Reducing Mutations
fact_fitness_reducing_mutations.summary: Behaviors resulting from new mutations that have not yet been eliminated from the population (p. 717).

fact_evolutionary_gray_area.label: Evolutionary Gray Area
fact_evolutionary_gray_area.summary: Behaviors maintained despite perceived heavy costs, including sexual cannibalism, brood parasitism, parasite manipulation, and same-sex sexual behavior (p. 717).

ssb.label: Same-Sex Sexual Behavior (SSB)
ssb.summary: Sexual interactions between members of the same sex, studied as a vehicle for understanding nonadaptive evolutionary mechanisms.

ssb_genetic_models.label: Genetic Models for SSB Maintenance
ssb_genetic_models.summary: Theoretical frameworks proposed by Gavrilets and Rice to explain the persistence of SSB (p. 717).

ssb_overdominance.label: Overdominance
ssb_overdominance.summary: Heterozygote advantage where genes providing fitness benefits in heterozygous conditions induce SSB in homozygous conditions (p. 717).

ssb_sexual_antagonism.label: Sexual Antagonism
ssb_sexual_antagonism.summary: Genes providing a fitness advantage in one sex cause the expression of SSB in the other sex. Supported by evidence that female relatives of male homosexuals produce more offspring (p. 717).

ssb_social_functions.label: Social Functions of SSB
ssb_social_functions.summary: The hypothesis that SSB provides social cohesion or acts as a 'currency' in group interactions.

fact_dolphin_alliances.label: Bottlenose Dolphin Alliances
fact_dolphin_alliances.summary: Male-male SSB represents approx. half of sexual encounters and facilitates social alliances in small male groups (p. 717).

fact_macaque_uncertainty.label: Japanese Macaque Uncertainty
fact_macaque_uncertainty.summary: The social functions of SSB in Japanese macaques remain unclear (p. 717).

ssb_intrasexual_competition.label: Intrasexual Competition in Insects
ssb_intrasexual_competition.summary: Examination of SSB as a mediator of competition, specifically in flour beetles (Tribolium castaneum).

fact_fertilization_by_proxy.label: Fertilization by Proxy
fact_fertilization_by_proxy.summary: Hypothesis that males transfer sperm to other males, which then fertilizes females' eggs; found to be too infrequent to explain SSB maintenance (p. 717).

aging_senescence.label: Senescence and Aging
aging_senescence.summary: The age-related decline in fitness components, including survival, fertility, physiology, and morphological traits (p. 719).

aging_definitions.label: Aging Terminology
aging_definitions.summary: Technical definitions related to the study of senescence.

def_demographic_senescence.label: Demographic Senescence
def_demographic_senescence.summary: Age-related decrease in the frequency of survival and mean reproductive output of same-age groups (p. 719).

def_iteroparous.label: Iteroparous
def_iteroparous.summary: Capable of reproducing multiple times throughout life (p. 719).

def_semelparous.label: Semelparous
def_semelparous.summary: Reproducing just once, then dying; e.g., spawning salmon (p. 719).

aging_theories.label: Theories for the Evolution of Aging
aging_theories.summary: Frameworks explaining why natural selection permits the decline of organisms over time.

theory_programmed_death.label: Programmed Death Hypothesis
theory_programmed_death.summary: Proposed by August Weismann (1881); suggests death in late age is adaptive to make room for the young. Generally rejected due to reliance on group selection over individual selection (p. 721).

theory_mutation_accumulation.label: Mutation Accumulation (MA) Theory
theory_mutation_accumulation.summary: Proposed by Peter Medawar (1946); suggests the strength of selection declines with age, allowing late-acting deleterious mutations to accumulate (p. 721).

theory_antagonistic_pleiotropy.label: Antagonistic Pleiotropy (AP) Theory
theory_antagonistic_pleiotropy.summary: Proposed by George Williams (1957); suggests alleles with beneficial effects early in life have deleterious effects late in life. Selection favors early benefits, leading to senescence as a constraint (p. 721).

fact_tp53_gene.label: TP53 Gene Trade-off
fact_tp53_gene.summary: Human gene example of AP: R72 variant reduces cancer risk but decreases longevity; P72 has the opposite effect (p. 722).

theory_disposable_soma.label: Disposable Soma Theory
theory_disposable_soma.summary: Proposed by Tom Kirkwood (1977); suggests senescence evolves from trade-offs between energy investment in reproduction vs. somatic maintenance and repair (p. 722).

menopause.label: Menopause
menopause.summary: The late-onset, irreversible cessation of reproductive capability in human females, typically around age 50 (p. 719).

menopause_adaptive_hypotheses.label: Adaptive Hypotheses for Menopause
menopause_adaptive_hypotheses.summary: Theories suggesting that menopause increases fitness for descendants.

hyp_mother.label: The Mother Hypothesis
hyp_mother.summary: Menopause mitigates the high risk of mortality from pregnancy/delivery complications in older women, allowing them to continue providing care for existing descendants (p. 723).

hyp_grandmother.label: The Grandmother Hypothesis
hyp_grandmother.summary: At a certain age, the benefits of helping daughters care for grandchildren outweigh the benefits of producing more offspring (p. 723).

menopause_reproductive_competition.label: Reproductive Competition Hypothesis
menopause_reproductive_competition.summary: Proposed by Cant and Johnstone; cessation of fertility is favored in older females to reduce the social cost of reproduction borne by close relatives in small groups (p. 724).

evolutionary_medicine.label: Evolutionary Medicine
evolutionary_medicine.summary: The use of modern evolutionary methods and theory to understand human health and improve disease treatment.

evo_med_foundations.label: Foundations of Evolutionary Medicine
evo_med_foundations.summary: Focuses on why natural selection left bodies vulnerable to disease, shifting from proximate causes to ultimate causes (p. 733).

evo_med_pathogens.label: Evolution of Pathogens
evo_med_pathogens.summary: The study of how parasites and pathogens evolve to exploit hosts and how this affects virulence.

parasite_virulence.label: Evolution of Parasite Virulence
parasite_virulence.summary: Analysis of parasite-induced morbidity and mortality of a host as an evolutionary trait.

virulence_phase_model.label: Phase Model of Virulence
virulence_phase_model.summary: Distinguishes three stages of disease evolution (p. 742).

phase_1_accidental.label: Phase 1: Accidental Infections
phase_1_accidental.summary: First contact with a host usually not infected; often highly virulent or avirulent; transmission chains are short (e.g., Ebola) (p. 742).

phase_2_invasion.label: Phase 2: Successful Invasion
phase_2_invasion.summary: Parasite established in new host; virulence is not yet adaptive. Example: Myxoma virus in Australia evolved lower virulence over time (p. 742).

phase_3_optimal.label: Phase 3: Optimal Virulence
phase_3_optimal.summary: Parasite has evolved to a level where fitness is maximal, typically governed by trade-offs (p. 743).

virulence_tradeoff_model.label: The Trade-off Model of Virulence
virulence_tradeoff_model.summary: Parasite fitness is maximized by balancing the benefit of higher transmission (b) against the cost of host death (a).

fact_r0_formula.label: Basic Reproductive Number (R0)
fact_r0_formula.summary: Formula: R0 = bN / (a + r + m), where b=transmission rate, N=population density, a=virulence, r=clearance rate, m=background mortality (p. 744).

fact_multiple_infections.label: Multiple Infections and Virulence
fact_multiple_infections.summary: Within-host competition among different parasite variants often favors higher replication rates, increasing overall virulence (p. 744).

virulence_transmission.label: Transmission Mode and Virulence
virulence_transmission.summary: How the mode of transmission influences the evolved level of virulence.

trans_horizontal.label: Horizontal Transmission
trans_horizontal.summary: Passing between unrelated hosts; can support higher virulence if transmission is decoupled from host viability (e.g., via vectors) (p. 745).

trans_vertical.label: Vertical Transmission
trans_vertical.summary: Passing from parent to offspring; generally favors avirulence or reproductive manipulation (e.g., Wolbachia) to ensure parasite survival (p. 745).

antibiotic_resistance.label: Evolution of Antibiotic Resistance
antibiotic_resistance.summary: The process by which bacteria acquire genetic mechanisms to survive antimicrobial drugs.

ab_resistance_mechanisms.label: Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance
ab_resistance_mechanisms.summary: Biochemical strategies bacteria use to nullify antibiotics (p. 749).

mech_enzymatic.label: Enzymatic Inactivation
mech_enzymatic.summary: Hydrolysis (e.g., beta-lactamases) or modification (acetylation) of the drug (p. 749).

mech_uptake.label: Reduced Uptake
mech_uptake.summary: Changes in the cell wall or porin channels to prevent the drug from entering (p. 749).

mech_efflux.label: Efflux Systems
mech_efflux.summary: Active pumping of antibiotics out of the cell (p. 749).

mech_target_mod.label: Target Modification
mech_target_mod.summary: Altering the structure of the target molecule (e.g., ribosomal proteins) so the drug cannot bind (p. 749).

mech_bypass.label: Bypass Mechanism
mech_bypass.summary: Providing an alternative target or pathway to replace the inhibited one (p. 749).

ab_resistance_transmission.label: Transmission of Resistance
ab_resistance_transmission.summary: Ways resistance genes spread through bacterial populations.

hgt_conjugation.label: Conjugation
hgt_conjugation.summary: Transfer of genetic material (e.g., plasmids) via direct cell-to-cell contact (p. 749).

hgt_transduction.label: Transduction
hgt_transduction.summary: Injection of DNA into bacteria by a bacteriophage (p. 749).

hgt_transformation.label: Transformation
hgt_transformation.summary: Uptake of exogenous naked DNA from the environment (p. 749).

ab_resistome.label: The Resistome
ab_resistome.summary: The collective set of all resistance genes and precursors present in all bacterial species (p. 749).

evo_med_defense.label: Immune Defense Mechanisms
evo_med_defense.summary: The coevolutionary arms race between human immunity and pathogens.

autoimmune_disease.label: Autoimmune and Allergic Diseases
autoimmune_disease.summary: Malfunctions where the immune system attacks the body's own cells or overreacts to harmless stimuli (p. 737).

fact_hla_b27.label: HLA-B27 Allele
fact_hla_b27.summary: Allele associated with increased risk of ankylosing spondylitis, possibly due to aberrant response to Klebsiella bacteria (p. 737).

hygiene_hypothesis.label: The Hygiene Hypothesis
hygiene_hypothesis.summary: Suggests that lack of early childhood exposure to microbes and parasites increases susceptibility to allergic and autoimmune diseases by modulating immune development (p. 733, 737).

evo_med_tradeoffs.label: Evolutionary Trade-offs in Health
evo_med_tradeoffs.summary: The concept that no trait is perfect; improving one trait may compromise another (p. 737).

fact_estrogen_cancer_tradeoff.label: Estrogen and Cancer Trade-off
fact_estrogen_cancer_tradeoff.summary: Increased menses (due to contraceptive use/low birth intervals) leads to prolonged estrogen exposure, potentially fueling breast and ovarian cancers (p. 738).

fact_reproduction_repair_tradeoff.label: Reproduction vs. Repair
fact_reproduction_repair_tradeoff.summary: Resources deployed toward peak reproductive performance are traded off against post-reproductive reparative functions, leading to age-related chronic diseases (p. 738).

evo_med_mismatch.label: Mismatch to Modernity
evo_med_mismatch.summary: Maladaptation produced by the inability of human biological evolution to keep pace with rapid cultural and environmental changes (p. 733, 738).

mismatch_metabolic.label: Metabolic Mismatch
mismatch_metabolic.summary: Excess energy intake relative to expenditure in modern lifestyles leads to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (p. 738).

mismatch_nutritional.label: Nutritional Mismatch
mismatch_nutritional.summary: Diseases resulting from deficiencies in novel environments, such as scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) or goiter (iodine deficiency) (p. 739).

human_cultural_evolution.label: Human and Cultural Evolution
human_cultural_evolution.summary: The interaction between genetic evolution and the rapid transmission of cultural information.

cultural_evolution_traits.label: Traits of Cultural Evolution
cultural_evolution_traits.summary: How culture differs from biological evolution in information transmission.

fact_compositional_language.label: Compositional Language
fact_compositional_language.summary: Unique human capacity allowing an infinite variety of ways for ideas to be combined and expressed (p. 730).

fact_horizontal_cultural_transmission.label: Horizontal Cultural Transmission
fact_horizontal_cultural_transmission.summary: Unlike genes (vertical), cultural info can be disseminated broadly across a generation from many sources (p. 730).

human_biological_variation.label: Human Biological Variation
human_biological_variation.summary: Analysis of genetic differences and the concept of race.

fact_race_genetic_diversity.label: Race and Genetic Diversity
fact_race_genetic_diversity.summary: Studies do not support biologically defined races in humans; racial categories account for only a few percent of total human genetic variation (p. 730).

evolution_public_sphere.label: Evolution in the Public Sphere
evolution_public_sphere.summary: The conflict and interaction between evolutionary science and religious narratives, particularly in the US (p. 731).

fact_intelligent_design.label: Intelligent Design
fact_intelligent_design.summary: An attempt to present religious opposition to evolution under a scientific gloss, disallowed in US public schools (p. 731).

resistance_transmission.label: Transmission of Resistant Bacteria
resistance_transmission.summary: Factors influencing the spread of resistant strains from origin into human or animal populations.

transmission_factors_fact.label: Factors Influencing Transmission
transmission_factors_fact.summary: Transmission rates depend on host density, travel/migration patterns, hygienic factors (hospitals, food prep), host immunity (vaccination), and intrinsic transmissibility. (p. 750)

resistance_persistence.label: Persistence and Reversibility of Resistance
resistance_persistence.summary: The balance of selective forces that determine if resistance remains in a population after antibiotic exposure ceases.

selective_forces.label: Selective Forces
selective_forces.summary: Opposing forces acting on resistant bacterial populations.

direct_advantage_fact.label: Direct Advantage
direct_advantage_fact.summary: Advantage gained by resistant bacteria when exposed to antibiotic concentrations lethal or inhibitory to sensitive strains. (p. 750)

fitness_cost_def.label: Fitness Cost of Resistance
fitness_cost_def.summary: Any effect of a resistance mechanism that reduces the pathogen's ability to grow, persist, or spread in the host population. (p. 750)

sub_mic_selection.label: Sub-MIC Selection
sub_mic_selection.summary: Selection for resistance occurring at antibiotic concentrations below the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC).

sub_mic_threshold_fact.label: Selection Threshold
sub_mic_threshold_fact.summary: Selection for resistant bacteria can occur at concentrations less than 1% of the MIC of susceptible bacteria. (p. 750)

environmental_source_fact.label: Environmental Antibiotic Sources
environmental_source_fact.summary: Roughly half of antibiotics consumed by humans/animals enter sewage systems via urine; several hundred thousand tons are released annually. (p. 750)

coselection.label: Coselection of Resistance Genes
coselection.summary: Increase in frequency of a resistance gene due to its genetic linkage to another gene under selection.

hgt_elements_fact.label: HGT Elements in Coselection
hgt_elements_fact.summary: Coselection is common in determinants acquired by Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT), including plasmids, transposons, and integrons. (p. 750)

linkage_targets_fact.label: Linked Genes
linkage_targets_fact.summary: The linked gene sustaining unselected resistance can be another antibiotic resistance gene, a heavy metal resistance gene, a disinfectant resistance gene, or a virulence-associated function. (p. 750)

fitness_costs.label: Variability of Fitness Costs
fitness_costs.summary: The cost of resistance is not uniform and depends on environmental and genetic contexts.

epistatic_interactions_fact.label: Epistatic Interactions
epistatic_interactions_fact.summary: The cost of resistance often depends on the bacterial strain due to epistatic interactions between the resistance gene and other genes. (p. 751)

cost_free_resistance_fact.label: Cost-Free Resistance
cost_free_resistance_fact.summary: Some resistance genes show no measurable fitness cost in specific environments/strains; measuring differences below 0.3% per generation is difficult in labs. (p. 751)

fitness_enhancing_fact.label: Fitness-Enhancing Resistance
fitness_enhancing_fact.summary: In some cases, resistance is advantageous even in drug-free environments. Example: fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli and C. jejuni. (p. 751)

compensatory_evolution.label: Compensatory Evolution
compensatory_evolution.summary: Process where selection favors mutations that restore cellular balance and reduce/eliminate the cost of resistance without losing the resistance itself.

compensation_mechanisms_fact.label: Compensation Mechanisms
compensation_mechanisms_fact.summary: May include mutations in the resistance gene itself or mutations altering the expression of the resistance gene or other genes. (p. 751)

plasmid_persistence.label: Plasmid Persistence
plasmid_persistence.summary: Mechanisms that ensure plasmids are maintained in bacterial populations even without antibiotic selection.

persistence_mechanisms_fact.label: Persistence Mechanisms
persistence_mechanisms_fact.summary: Includes resolution/partitioning systems, toxin-antitoxin systems (killing cells that lose the plasmid), and conjugation-mediated horizontal transfer. (p. 751)

resistance_mitigation.label: Slowing or Stopping Resistance
resistance_mitigation.summary: Strategies to reduce the emergence and spread of resistant bacteria.

usage_reduction_strategies.label: Antibiotic Use Reduction
usage_reduction_strategies.summary: Reducing the strength of selection by limiting antibiotic consumption.

reduction_tactics_fact.label: Specific Reduction Tactics
reduction_tactics_fact.summary: Avoiding use for viruses, discontinuing growth promoters in animal husbandry, stopping use in crop production/aquaculture, regulating marketing, and prohibiting non-prescription internet sales. (p. 752)

hygienic_measures.label: Hygienic and Infection Control
hygienic_measures.summary: Reducing transmission to decrease the need for antibiotics.

hygiene_examples_fact.label: Examples of Effective Hygiene
hygiene_examples_fact.summary: Successful against food-borne pathogens (Salmonella) and nosocomial infections (MRSA) through screening and isolation. (p. 752)

pharmacological_approaches.label: Pharmacological and Design Strategies
pharmacological_approaches.summary: Using drug combinations and rational drug design to minimize resistance risk.

design_principles_fact.label: Rational Drug Design Principles
design_principles_fact.summary: Developing antibiotics where: 1) resistance is difficult to acquire by mutation/HGT, 2) resistance confers high fitness cost, and 3) compensatory adaptation opportunities are limited. (p. 752)

microbial_forensics.label: Microbial Forensics and Molecular Epidemiology
microbial_forensics.summary: The use of genomic and evolutionary analysis to identify the source of infective material in biological crimes or outbreaks.

forensic_technologies.label: Forensic Technologies
forensic_technologies.summary: Methods used to characterize bacterial strains and identify matches or relationships.

pfge_details.label: Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE)
pfge_details.summary: A method generating restriction fragment patterns (DNA fingerprints).

pfge_limitations_fact.label: PFGE Limitations
pfge_limitations_fact.summary: Generates yes/no outcomes based on matching algorithms; precludes thorough evolutionary analysis and probabilistic confidence estimates. (p. 754)

mlva_details.label: Multiple Loci VNTR Analysis (MLVA)
mlva_details.summary: A DNA fingerprinting method screening multiple loci with variable number of tandem repeats.

mlva_utility_fact.label: MLVA Utility
mlva_utility_fact.summary: Used for differentiating bacterial types, such as in B. anthracis investigations, though less precise than whole-genome sequencing. (p. 757)

whole_genome_sequencing_details.label: Whole-Genome Sequencing (WGS)
whole_genome_sequencing_details.summary: The analysis of the entire DNA sequence of a bacterial isolate.

wgs_advantages_fact.label: WGS Advantages
wgs_advantages_fact.summary: Allows identification of SNPs and distinguishes between convergent (homoplastic) and vertically inherited matches. (p. 756)

forensic_concepts.label: Core Forensic Concepts
forensic_concepts.summary: Theoretical frameworks for interpreting genetic data in microbes vs humans.

inheritance_modes.label: Modes of Genetic Inheritance
inheritance_modes.summary: Comparison of how genes are passed in bacteria vs humans.

vertical_inheritance_fact.label: Vertical Inheritance
vertical_inheritance_fact.summary: Primary mode in bacteria (mother cell to daughter cell), creating clonal lineages. (p. 755)

hgt_forensics_fact.label: Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) in Forensics
hgt_forensics_fact.summary: Movement of genes between cells/species; can leave conspicuous genetic evidence when occurring between distantly related species. (p. 755)

match_vs_membership.label: Match vs Membership
match_vs_membership.summary: Distinction between identical genotypic profiles and phylogenetic grouping.

match_definition_fact.label: Genetic Match
match_definition_fact.summary: An identical genotypic profile based on a particular technology; problematic in microbes due to high resolution revealing mutations even in colonies. (p. 756)

membership_definition_fact.label: Phylogenetic Membership
membership_definition_fact.summary: The concept of belonging to a clade based on shared derived states; more meaningful for epidemiology than a 'match'. (p. 756)

snp_utility_fact.label: Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs)
snp_utility_fact.summary: Single base-pair differences used to define membership in clades because they are produced by rare mutation events and are stable. (p. 756)

anthrax_case_studies.label: B. anthracis Case Studies
anthrax_case_studies.summary: Application of microbial forensics to bioterrorism events.

kameido_attack.label: Kameido Aum Shinrikyo Attack (1993)
kameido_attack.summary: A failed biological attack in Tokyo.

kameido_strain_fact.label: Sterne Strain Analysis
kameido_strain_fact.summary: Attack failed because the cult used the Sterne strain (vaccine strain), which lacks the pXO2 plasmid and is therefore non-virulent. (p. 757)

anthrax_letters_2001.label: 2001 Anthrax Letters
anthrax_letters_2001.summary: A deadly biological attack involving spores sent through the US Postal Service.

ames_strain_fact.label: Ames Strain Identification
ames_strain_fact.summary: Initial MLVA showed spores matched the virulent Ames strain, which is used in several US government laboratories. (p. 758)

iraqi_strain_exclusion_fact.label: Iraqi Strain Exclusion
iraqi_strain_exclusion_fact.summary: The Iraqi weapon strain matched the Vollum strain, not the Ames strain, allowing the Iraqi source to be excluded with high confidence. (p. 758)

rmr1029_flask_fact.label: RMR-1029 Flask
rmr1029_flask_fact.summary: WGS and mutation screening of colony morphology identified the specific source as the RMR-1029 flask. (p. 758)

domestication_agriculture.label: Domestication and the Evolution of Agriculture
domestication_agriculture.summary: The process of acquiring wild species for breeding and the resulting coevolutionary mutualisms.

domestication_process.label: The Process of Domestication
domestication_process.summary: The acquisition and breeding of species in captivity, altering their genetic makeup.

artificial_selection_def.label: Artificial Selection
artificial_selection_def.summary: Evolutionary change caused by human breeding in populations of domesticated plants and animals. (p. 761)

domestication_syndrome.label: Domestication Syndrome
domestication_syndrome.summary: A suite of traits characteristic of domesticated species.

plant_syndrome_fact.label: Plant Domestication Traits
plant_syndrome_fact.summary: Increased size of reproductive organs, seeds remaining on plant (non-shattering), faster/synchronized germination, changed biomass allocation, and reduced defenses. (p. 762)

animal_syndrome_fact.label: Animal Domestication Traits
animal_syndrome_fact.summary: Variation in body size, changes in coloration (white/spotted), and altered behavioral traits (reduced aggression/panic). (p. 762)

species_suitability_traits.label: Traits Predisposing Species to Domestication
species_suitability_traits.summary: Characteristics that make a wild species a candidate for agriculture.

plant_suitability_fact.label: Plant Suitability Factors
plant_suitability_fact.summary: Edibility, fast growth, storability, and self-fertilization (crucial for passing traits unchanged). (p. 762)

animal_suitability_fact.label: Animal Suitability Factors
animal_suitability_fact.summary: Herbivorous diet (energy efficiency), fast growth, ability to breed in captivity, pleasant disposition, lack of panic, and herd hierarchy. (p. 762)

agricultural_mutualism.label: Agriculture as a Mutualism
agricultural_mutualism.summary: A coevolved interaction where both the agriculturalist and the domesticate benefit.

domesticate_benefits.label: Benefits to Domesticates
domesticate_benefits.summary: Three general categories of benefits provided by humans.

domesticate_benefit_details_fact.label: Specific Domesticate Benefits
domesticate_benefit_details_fact.summary: 1) Protection (reduced competition, predation, herbivory), 2) Increased reproduction (higher germination/birth rates), and 3) Dispersal (expanded range). (p. 763)

human_evolution_agriculture.label: Human Evolution in Response to Agriculture
human_evolution_agriculture.summary: Genetic changes in humans resulting from an agricultural lifestyle.

lactase_persistence_fact.label: Lactase Persistence
lactase_persistence_fact.summary: Mutation in the promoter region of the lactase gene allowing adults to digest milk; strongly correlated with pastoralism. (p. 763)

amylase_evolution_fact.label: Amylase Evolution
amylase_evolution_fact.summary: Populations with starch-heavy agricultural diets evolved extra copies of the salivary amylase gene. (p. 763)

ant_agriculture.label: Agriculture in Ants
ant_agriculture.summary: Fungus-farming mutualisms in ants, paralleling human agriculture.

ant_fungus_details.label: Ant Fungus Cultivation
ant_fungus_details.summary: The symbiotic relationship between fungus-growing ants and their fungal cultivars.

gongylidia_fact.label: Gongylidia
gongylidia_fact.summary: Specialized fungal structures rich in lipids and carbohydrates, optimized as a nutrient source for ants via artificial selection. (p. 764)

ant_genetic_loss_fact.label: Genetic Dependence
ant_genetic_loss_fact.summary: Fungus-growing ants have lost the ability to synthesize an essential amino acid, obtaining it instead from the fungus. (p. 764)

ant_crop_protection.label: Ant Crop Protection Mechanisms
ant_crop_protection.summary: Behaviors and symbioses used to protect fungus gardens from pathogens.

escovopsis_pathogen_fact.label: Escovopsis Pathogen
escovopsis_pathogen_fact.summary: A specialized microfungus that consumes ant fungal cultivars; managed via grooming and weeding. (p. 764)

actinobacteria_symbiosis_fact.label: Actinobacteria Symbiosis
actinobacteria_symbiosis_fact.summary: Ants harbor antibiotic-producing Actinobacteria on their cuticle to inhibit Escovopsis. (p. 764)

evolution_conservation.label: Evolution and Conservation
evolution_conservation.summary: The application of evolutionary biology and genomics to preserve biodiversity and manage endangered species.

conservation_triage.label: Conservation Triage
conservation_triage.summary: Using evolutionary history to prioritize species for protection.

phylogenetic_uniqueness_fact.label: Phylogenetic Uniqueness
phylogenetic_uniqueness_fact.summary: Prioritizing lineages with long branches (e.g., Tuatara) because they represent a greater amount of unique evolutionary history. (p. 767)

conservation_metrics.label: Population Genetics Metrics in Conservation
conservation_metrics.summary: Quantitative tools for assessing population health and viability.

ne_vs_nc.label: Effective vs Census Population Size
ne_vs_nc.summary: Distinction between total population and those contributing to genetic variation.

nc_definition_fact.label: Census Population Size (Nc)
nc_definition_fact.summary: The total number of individuals in a population. (p. 772)

ne_definition_fact.label: Effective Population Size (Ne)
ne_definition_fact.summary: The number of individuals who actually breed and contribute to the genetic variation of the species. (p. 772)

basic_rule_of_conservation_genetics_fact.label: Basic Rule of Conservation Genetics
basic_rule_of_conservation_genetics_fact.summary: An inbreeding coefficient (DF) greater than 1% is considered a threshold above which fitness relentlessly declines. (p. 768)

frankel_50_500_rule_fact.label: Frankel's 50/500 Rule
frankel_50_500_rule_fact.summary: Populations with Ne < 50 may face immediate extinction; Ne < 500 may lack sufficient variation to adapt over the long term. (p. 768)

conservation_strategies.label: Conservation Strategies
conservation_strategies.summary: Different approaches based on whether one conserves past history or future potential.

conserving_history.label: Conserving Evolutionary History
conserving_history.summary: Focusing on preserving the outcomes of the evolutionary process.

branch_length_fact.label: Phylogenetic Branch Length
branch_length_fact.summary: Conserving the sum of the branches of a phylogeny in units of time to prevent loss of unique evolutionary history. (p. 769)

phylogenetic_diversity_def.label: Phylogenetic Diversity (PD)
phylogenetic_diversity_def.summary: A character-based approach prioritizing taxa that have evolved the most unique features. (p. 769)

conserving_potential.label: Conserving Potential for Future Evolution
conserving_potential.summary: Focusing on preserving the processes that generate diversity.

ecotone_conservation_fact.label: Ecotone Conservation
ecotone_conservation_fact.summary: Preserving transition areas (ecotones) between habitats because they can select for different morphologies and generate diversity. (p. 770)

landscape_genetics_def.label: Landscape Genetics/Genomics
landscape_genetics_def.summary: Integrating population genetics data with landscape features (GIS) to study gene flow and identify migration corridors. (p. 770)

conservation_threats.label: Genetic Threats in Conservation
conservation_threats.summary: Evolutionary processes that can jeopardize the survival of at-risk species.

hybridization_threats.label: Hybridization and Genetic Rescue
hybridization_threats.summary: The impact of interbreeding between different species or subspecies.

genetic_rescue_example_fact.label: Florida Panther Genetic Rescue
genetic_rescue_example_fact.summary: Supplementing the inbred Florida panther (P. c. coryi) with Texas panthers (P. c. stanleyana) to reverse inbreeding depression. (p. 771)

bottleneck_threats.label: Population Bottlenecks and Isolation
bottleneck_threats.summary: The effect of small, isolated populations on genetic health.

genetic_drift_isolation_fact.label: Genetic Drift and Isolation
genetic_drift_isolation_fact.summary: In small isolated populations, genetic drift can overcome natural selection, allowing low-fitness genotypes to rise in frequency. (p. 771)

directed_evolution.label: Directed Evolution
directed_evolution.summary: An engineering process using iterative selection and amplification to push molecular or cellular systems toward a specific goal.

directed_evolution_requirements.label: Requirements for Directed Evolution
directed_evolution_requirements.summary: The three fundamental components needed for the process.

de_reqs_fact.label: Core Requirements
de_reqs_fact.summary: 1) A genetic system (encoded, heritable, mutable), 2) A means of selection (sieving based on function/fitness), and 3) An amplification method. (p. 774)

nucleic_acid_evolution.label: Directed Evolution of Nucleic Acids
nucleic_acid_evolution.summary: The selection of functional RNA or DNA molecules from random pools.

in_vitro_selection.label: In Vitro Selection
in_vitro_selection.summary: Iterative cycles of selection and PCR amplification to isolate functional nucleic acids.

ivs_process_fact.label: The Selection Process
ivs_process_fact.summary: Functional molecules are bound/selected from a random pool, eluted, and then exponentially amplified by PCR. (p. 775)

aptamers_ribozymes.label: Aptamers and Ribozymes
aptamers_ribozymes.summary: Functional nucleic acids resulting from directed evolution.

aptamer_def_fact.label: Aptamer
aptamer_def_fact.summary: A short nucleic acid molecule that binds to a specific target molecule. (p. 775)

macugen_fact.label: Macugen
macugen_fact.summary: An experimentally evolved RNA aptamer used clinically to inhibit vascular endothelial growth factor in treating macular degeneration. (p. 776)

ribozyme_def_fact.label: Ribozyme
ribozyme_def_fact.summary: An RNA molecule with a tertiary structure enabling it to catalyze a chemical reaction. (p. 775)
