bartel_ligase_fact.label: Class I Bartel Ligase
bartel_ligase_fact.summary: A complex ribozyme isolated from a random pool, demonstrating that functional complexity can emerge from random sequences. (p. 776)

protein_evolution.label: Directed Evolution of Proteins
protein_evolution.summary: The engineering of proteins with novel binding or catalytic properties.

protein_display_methods.label: Protein Display Methods
protein_display_methods.summary: Methods that link a protein's phenotype to its encoding genotype.

phage_display_fact.label: Phage Display
phage_display_fact.summary: Peptides are expressed on the coat protein of a bacteriophage; selected variants are amplified by infecting host cells. (p. 776)

cell_surface_display_fact.label: Cell Surface Display and FACS
cell_surface_display_fact.summary: Proteins are expressed on E. coli surfaces and sorted using Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) based on activity (e.g., substrate cleavage). (p. 777)

in_vitro_protein_synthesis.label: In Vitro Protein Evolution
in_vitro_protein_synthesis.summary: Evolution of proteins without living cells.

ribosome_display_fact.label: Ribosome Display
ribosome_display_fact.summary: Stalling ribosomes to connect mRNA information with the protein function being translated. (p. 777)

water_oil_emulsion_fact.label: Water-in-Oil Emulsions
water_oil_emulsion_fact.summary: Creating cell-like bubbles with transcription/translation components; proteins are coupled to nucleic acids for selection. (p. 777)

cellular_evolution.label: Directed Evolution of Cells
cellular_evolution.summary: The adaptation of whole microorganisms for industrial or research purposes.

strain_improvement.label: Strain Improvement
strain_improvement.summary: Using random mutagenesis and screening to increase product yield.

penicillin_example_fact.label: Penicillin Production
penicillin_example_fact.summary: P. notatum was subjected to X-ray radiation to accelerate mutation and then screened for high penicillin yields. (p. 778)

genome_shuffling.label: Genome Shuffling
genome_shuffling.summary: A multiparent mating process to create mosaic genomes.

shuffling_process_fact.label: Genome Shuffling Process
shuffling_process_fact.summary: Cells are turned into protoplasts and fused; recombination machinery resolves the genetic material into a single unit, amplifying diversity. (p. 778)

mage_technology.label: Multiplex Automated Genome Engineering (MAGE)
mage_technology.summary: A technique for precise, targeted mutations in multiple genomic sites.

mage_mechanism_fact.label: MAGE Mechanism
mage_mechanism_fact.summary: Synthesizing single-stranded DNA oligonucleotides that are incorporated into the genome through recombination. (p. 778)

evolution_computing.label: Evolution and Computing
evolution_computing.summary: The convergence of evolutionary biology and computer science through shared principles of code, information, and function.

shared_principles_ec.label: Shared Principles (Biology & Computing)
shared_principles_ec.summary: Deep conceptual linkages focusing on processes rather than products.

fact_coded_functions.label: Coded Functions
fact_coded_functions.summary: Both fields rely on coded instructions (software in computers, genetic code in organisms) to execute functions; errors in either result in functional failure (e.g., software bugs or genetic mutations).

fact_information_theory.label: Information Processing
fact_information_theory.summary: Both fields view their subject matter as information processing. Computer science is increasingly identified as information science, and genomes are viewed as carrying biological information via informational molecules (DNA/RNA).

fact_bcsp_nsf.label: Biological and Computing Shared Principles (BCSP)
fact_bcsp_nsf.summary: A 2011 NSF initiative highlighting the convergence of central ideas requiring competencies from both biology and computing, focusing on adaptation, self-repair, coevolution, and robustness.

evolutionary_computation_field.label: Evolutionary Computation
evolutionary_computation_field.summary: Computer science research utilizing insights from evolutionary biology to solve problems.

genetic_algorithms.label: Genetic Algorithms
genetic_algorithms.summary: Pioneered by John Holland; uses binary strings of 0s and 1s that recombine and mutate, subject to selection.

evolutionary_strategies.label: Evolutionary Strategies
evolutionary_strategies.summary: Developed by Ingo Rechenberg and Hans-Paul Schwefel in Germany.

digital_evolution.label: Digital Evolution
digital_evolution.summary: The causal instantiation of the evolutionary mechanism within a computer system.

darwinian_causal_principle.label: Darwinian Causal Principle
darwinian_causal_principle.summary: Evolution by natural selection requires three conditions: 1) Random production of variations, 2) Heritability of variations, and 3) Natural selection by the environment.

avida_platform.label: Avida Platform
avida_platform.summary: A model system for digital evolution where digital organisms (Avidians) evolve computational functions as phenotypes to gain energy (digital metabolism).

fact_avida_complexity.label: Evolution of Complex Features
fact_avida_complexity.summary: Lenski et al. (2003) used Avida to show that complex functions evolve via incremental changes and that functions often depend on sequences evolved for previous tasks.

fact_avida_deleterious_mutations.label: Role of Deleterious Mutations
fact_avida_deleterious_mutations.summary: Research showed that occasional highly deleterious mutations (reducing fitness by >50%) can persist if they become beneficial in combination with subsequent mutations.

evolutionary_engineering.label: Evolutionary Engineering
evolutionary_engineering.summary: Applying evolutionary computation to solve design problems in applied engineering.

nasa_evolved_antenna.label: NASA Evolved Antenna
nasa_evolved_antenna.summary: An X-band antenna for the Space Technology 5 mission evolved in a virtual world using tree-structured encoding. It outperformed human-designed prototypes in power efficiency and coverage.

humies_award.label: Humies (Human-Competitive Results)
humies_award.summary: GECCO awards for evolved designs that produce patentable results or peer-reviewed publications, equal to or surpassing human intelligence.

evolution_linguistics.label: Linguistics and Human Language
evolution_linguistics.summary: The study of the origin, evolution, and structure of human language as a biological and cultural replicator.

language_definition.label: Definition of Human Language
language_definition.summary: A unique form of communication characterized by compositionality: the use of discrete words in sentences with subjects, objects, and verbs.

language_origins.label: Origins of Language
language_origins.summary: The timing and biological markers of language evolution in the Homo lineage.

fact_language_timeline.label: Evolutionary Timeline
fact_language_timeline.summary: Language evolved between 6-7 million years ago (common ancestor with chimps) and 160-200k years ago (modern humans). Evidence of symbolic thinking increases sharply around 70-100k years ago.

fact_brain_areas.label: Neurological Markers
fact_brain_areas.summary: Broca's and Wernicke's areas are involved in speech; they are present in Homo erectus and some apes, but the expanded neocortex in Homo sapiens is critical for symbolic thinking.

fact_foxp2.label: FOXP2 Segment
fact_foxp2.summary: A segment of DNA (not a gene) that influences the fine motor control of facial muscles. Found in both modern humans and Neanderthals, though its effect may differ due to neocortex differences.

language_social_theory.label: Social Evolution of Language
language_social_theory.summary: The theory that language evolved to facilitate cooperation among unrelated members of the species, managing the risk of 'cheating' through reputation and coordination.

linguistic_evolution_mechanisms.label: Linguistic Evolution Mechanisms
linguistic_evolution_mechanisms.summary: Parallels between genetic and linguistic evolution.

cognates.label: Cognates
cognates.summary: Words derived from a common ancestral word, analogous to biological homology (e.g., English 'water' and German 'wasser').

regular_sound_correspondences.label: Regular Sound Correspondences
regular_sound_correspondences.summary: Statistical regularities in sound changes over time (e.g., Latin 'p' becoming Germanic 'f', such as 'pater' to 'father').

phylogenetic_inference_methods.label: Phylogenetic Inference Methods
phylogenetic_inference_methods.summary: Formal methods to reconstruct language trees.

parsimony_method.label: Parsimony Method
parsimony_method.summary: Seeks the tree that minimizes the total number of evolutionary events.

distance_method.label: Distance Method
distance_method.summary: Defines genetic/linguistic distance between pairs to construct a tree.

likelihood_method.label: Likelihood Method
likelihood_method.summary: Uses statistical models to estimate the probability of changes through time.

indo_european_phylogeny.label: Indo-European Language Family
indo_european_phylogeny.summary: A family originating 8,000-9,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, encompassing Germanic, Romance, Slavic, and Indo-Iranian branches.

lexical_replacement.label: Lexical Replacement
lexical_replacement.summary: The process by which words are replaced by unrelated words over time.

fact_linguistic_half_life.label: Linguistic Half-Life
fact_linguistic_half_life.summary: The expected time before a word has a 50% chance of being replaced. Average is 5,300 years, with a median of 2,500 years.

fact_word_stability.label: Frequency and Stability
fact_word_stability.summary: Words used most frequently (e.g., top 25 words) are often shorter, monosyllabic, and more stable over time because they are highly adapted to the human mind.

cultural_evolution.label: Cultural Evolution
cultural_evolution.summary: The process of change in population traits explained by social learning and nongenetic inheritance.

gene_culture_coevolution.label: Gene-Culture Coevolution
gene_culture_coevolution.summary: The bidirectional influence where cultural changes create selective pressures that affect genetic evolution (e.g., dairy farming leading to lactose tolerance).

memetics.label: Memetics
memetics.summary: A theory proposed by Richard Dawkins treating cultural entities (memes) as replicators analogous to genes.

fact_meme_definition.label: Meme Definition
fact_meme_definition.summary: A cultural entity (tunes, ideas, techniques) capable of being replicated and transmitted between individuals.

meme_criticisms.label: Criticisms of Memetics
meme_criticisms.summary: Major objections to the gene-meme analogy.

fact_imitation_error.label: Imitation Error
fact_imitation_error.summary: Cultural transmission is often error-prone and lacks the faithful copying found in genetic replication.

fact_lack_of_discrete_units.label: Holism vs. Discrete Units
fact_lack_of_discrete_units.summary: Unlike genes, ideas are often interdependent; it is difficult to isolate a single 'meme' without its required logical context.

fact_horizontal_transmission_risk.label: Horizontal Transmission
fact_horizontal_transmission_risk.summary: Transmission within a generation is much faster than vertical transmission, potentially undermining the longevity required for cumulative natural selection.

population_cultural_evolution.label: Population-Level Cultural Evolution
population_cultural_evolution.summary: Models by Boyd, Richerson, and others focusing on population-level consequences of social learning rather than discrete replicators.

conformist_bias.label: Conformist Bias
conformist_bias.summary: The tendency to imitate the most common traits in a population, which helps dampen the spread of individual errors.

prestige_bias.label: Prestige Bias
prestige_bias.summary: The tendency to imitate traits possessed by successful individuals, increasing the likelihood of inheriting adaptive traits.

nonhuman_cultural_evolution.label: Nonhuman Animal Culture
nonhuman_cultural_evolution.summary: The existence of traditions in nonhuman species, though often lacking cumulative evolution.

fact_koshima_macaques.label: Koshima Island Macaques
fact_koshima_macaques.summary: Example of cultural innovation: macaques learned to wash sweet potatoes in streams and later the sea, and to eat discarded fish.

fact_blue_tits_learning.label: Blue Tits and Milk Bottles
fact_blue_tits_learning.summary: Demonstrates that social learning (attention) without observational learning (imitation of technique) prevents cumulative evolution.

human_race_biology.label: Biological Notions of Human Race
human_race_biology.summary: The application of objective, culture-free biological criteria to determine the existence of races in humans.

biological_race_criteria.label: Biological Race Criteria
biological_race_criteria.summary: Criteria used in conservation biology for vertebrates to define subspecies/races.

quantitative_fst_threshold.label: Quantitative Fst Threshold
quantitative_fst_threshold.summary: Races are defined if 25% or more of the total genetic variability is found between populations. Fst = (Ht - Hs) / Ht.

qualitative_lineage_definition.label: Qualitative Lineage Definition
qualitative_lineage_definition.summary: Races are defined as separate evolutionary lineages resulting from splits with limited genetic interchange, forming a treelike structure.

chimpanzee_race_study.label: Race in Chimpanzees
chimpanzee_race_study.summary: Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) satisfy both race definitions, with three distinct lineages: Upper Guinea, Gulf of Guinea, and Equatorial Africa.

human_race_analysis.label: Race in Humans
human_race_analysis.summary: Analysis showing humans do not meet biological race criteria.

fact_human_fst_value.label: Human Genetic Variation
fact_human_fst_value.summary: Only 4.3% of human genetic variation is between the five major geographic groups, far below the 25% threshold. 93.2% of variation is among individuals.

fact_ml_ncpa_results.label: ML-NCPA Findings
fact_ml_ncpa_results.summary: Multilocus Nested-Clade Phylogeographic Analysis shows humans as a single evolutionary lineage with continuous gene flow and admixture throughout the Pleistocene.

adaptive_traits_discordance.label: Adaptive Traits Discordance
adaptive_traits_discordance.summary: Local adaptations do not define races because different traits are distributed discordantly. Skin color (UV adaptation) does not correlate with other traits like sleeping sickness or malaria resistance.

future_human_evolution.label: The Future of Human Evolution
future_human_evolution.summary: Speculation on the future of human biological change given random processes and cultural influence.

evolutionary_predictability.label: Evolutionary Predictability
evolutionary_predictability.summary: Future evolution is unpredictable due to mutation, recombination, genetic drift, and rapidly changing cultural environments.

evolution_stoppage_debate.label: The Evolution Stoppage Debate
evolution_stoppage_debate.summary: Conflicting views on whether biological evolution in humans has ceased.

gould_stopped_hypothesis.label: Gould's Stopped Hypothesis
gould_stopped_hypothesis.summary: Stephen Jay Gould argued that biological change stopped 40-50k years ago as culture supplanted natural selection.

cochran_accelerated_hypothesis.label: Cochran & Harpending's Hypothesis
cochran_accelerated_hypothesis.summary: Argue that human evolution accelerated 100x in the last 10,000 years due to new selective pressures from agriculture.

recent_human_adaptations.label: Recent Human Adaptations
recent_human_adaptations.summary: Examples of adaptive evolution driven by cultural changes in the last 10,000 years.

fact_malaria_adaptation.label: Malaria and Agriculture
fact_malaria_adaptation.summary: Agricultural systems increased local population densities and mosquito habitats, favoring the sickle-cell allele and other antimalarial adaptations.

fact_thrifty_genotype.label: Thrifty Genotype Hypothesis
fact_thrifty_genotype.summary: Proposed by James V. Neel; suggests genes predisposing individuals to Type 2 diabetes were adaptive during periodic famines in early agricultural societies.

fact_lactase_persistence.label: Lactase Persistence
fact_lactase_persistence.summary: An adaptive trait resulting from the domestication of cattle and goats, allowing adults to digest milk.

gene_pool_definition.label: Gene Pool
gene_pool_definition.summary: The total set of genes collectively shared by a reproducing population.

adaptive_evolution.label: Adaptive Evolution
adaptive_evolution.summary: Evolutionary change that increases the fit between an organism and its environment.

non_adaptive_forces.label: Non-Adaptive Evolutionary Forces
non_adaptive_forces.summary: Factors that cause alterations in the gene pool independently of natural selection.

human_evolutionary_trends.label: Trends in Human Evolution
human_evolutionary_trends.summary: The specific application of evolutionary forces to the human lineage, heavily influenced by cultural innovation.

culture_induced_evolution.label: Culture-Induced Evolution
culture_induced_evolution.summary: The process where cultural innovations (agriculture, tools, fire) alter the selective environment, either shielding traits from selection or inducing new adaptations.

lactase_persistence.label: Lactase Persistence
lactase_persistence.summary: A trait determined by a single gene allowing the digestion of milk sugar, showing strong recent natural selection linked to agriculture (p. 812).

non_adaptive_human_evolution.label: Non-Adaptive Human Evolution
non_adaptive_human_evolution.summary: Evolutionary changes in humans that are not driven by direct selection but by correlations or the relaxation of selection.

craniofacial_evolution.label: Craniofacial Evolution
craniofacial_evolution.summary: The reduction of human jaws and teeth over the last 1.5 million years, not due to direct selection (eliminated by tools/fire), but as a correlated non-adaptive effect of increasing brain size (p. 812).

tooth_crowding.label: Tooth Crowding
tooth_crowding.summary: A result of the jaw becoming relatively smaller more rapidly than the teeth, leading to the cultural evolution of orthodontics (p. 812).

obstetric_dilemma.label: The Obstetric Dilemma
obstetric_dilemma.summary: The selective constraint on brain size caused by the difficulty of passing a large-brained baby through the birth canal; this constraint is being reduced by C-sections (p. 812).

adaptive_potential_via_neutrality.label: Adaptive Potential via Neutrality
adaptive_potential_via_neutrality.summary: The accumulation of functionally equivalent neutral alleles can allow a population to explore the mutational state space, facilitating future adaptive transitions that would otherwise be unlikely (p. 813).

population_demographics.label: Population Demographics
population_demographics.summary: The impact of human population growth on genetic variation.

superexponential_growth_effect.label: Superexponential Growth Effect
superexponential_growth_effect.summary: Large population sizes (6.8 billion) ensure that virtually every single-step mutational change occurs every generation, reducing evolutionary randomness and increasing responsiveness to environment (p. 813).

sickle_cell_example.label: Sickle-Cell Allele
sickle_cell_example.summary: Example of high responsiveness in large populations; the allele reached high frequency in sub-Saharan Africa via at least four independent mutations (p. 813).

deleterious_mutation_accumulation.label: Deleterious Mutation Accumulation
deleterious_mutation_accumulation.summary: In growing populations, the probability of losing deleterious mutations is reduced (to 53% for a 10% fitness reduction), leading to an excess of rare, harmful variants in the human gene pool (p. 813).

heterozygosity_trends.label: Heterozygosity Trends
heterozygosity_trends.summary: The shift toward increased individual heterozygosity due to decreased local genetic drift and increased global gene flow.

health_benefits_of_heterozygosity.label: Health Benefits of Heterozygosity
health_benefits_of_heterozygosity.summary: Increased heterozygosity is associated with beneficial clinical traits and a reduction in risks for schizophrenia and late-onset Alzheimer's disease (p. 814).

genetic_fusion.label: Genetic Fusion
genetic_fusion.summary: The process of fusing local gene pools into a single species-wide gene pool, leading to the loss of local adaptations, such as skin color (p. 814).

future_evolutionary_scenarios.label: Future Evolutionary Scenarios
future_evolutionary_scenarios.summary: Predictions of human evolution based on demographic trajectories.

optimistic_scenario.label: Optimistic Demographic Scenario
optimistic_scenario.summary: Stabilization at a large population size; results in high heterozygosity, a large reservoir of beneficial mutations, and a capacity for fine-tuning adaptations (p. 814).

pessimistic_scenario.label: Pessimistic Demographic Scenario
pessimistic_scenario.summary: Population crash and fragmentation; leads to local prevalence of deleterious variants, strong negative selection, but potential for major adaptive breakthroughs due to increased drift (p. 814).

eugenics_genetic_engineering.label: Eugenics and Genetic Engineering
eugenics_genetic_engineering.summary: The attempt to direct human evolution through selective breeding or molecular manipulation.

eugenic_limitations.label: Limitations of Human Genetic Engineering
eugenic_limitations.summary: Difficulties arise from genetic heterogeneity (different backgrounds produce different phenotypic effects for the same gene) and complex genotype-environment interactions (p. 815).

apoe_locus_example.label: ApoE Locus Example
apoe_locus_example.summary: The ApoE e4 allele correlates with coronary artery disease, but the highest incidence occurs in individuals with high cholesterol and the e2/e3 genotype, demonstrating that environmental and polygenic factors override single-locus predictions (p. 815).

evolution_and_religion.label: Evolution and Religion
evolution_and_religion.summary: The philosophical and theological dialogue regarding biological evolution and the existence of a Creator.

argument_from_design.label: The Argument from Design
argument_from_design.summary: The claim that the complexity and order of organisms necessitate an intelligent designer (e.g., Paley's Natural Theology, 1802).

darwinian_resolution.label: Darwinian Resolution
darwinian_resolution.summary: Darwin demonstrated that complexity and 'design' arise from natural processes (natural selection) rather than an external agent (p. 819-820).

problem_of_evil.label: The Problem of Evil
problem_of_evil.summary: The challenge of reconciling an omnipotent, benevolent God with the existence of suffering and cruelty.

moral_evil_explanation.label: Moral Evil Explanation
moral_evil_explanation.summary: Attributed to human free will and autonomy (p. 822).

physical_evil_explanation.label: Physical Evil Explanation
physical_evil_explanation.summary: Natural disasters (earthquakes, etc.) are attributed to the immanent laws of physics and natural processes (p. 822).

biological_evil_explanation.label: Biological Evil Explanation
biological_evil_explanation.summary: Cruelty in nature (predation, parasitism) is explained by evolutionary processes involving non-moral agents (p. 822).

imperfect_design.label: Imperfect Design
imperfect_design.summary: Evidence of incompetent design (e.g., human blind spot, narrow birth canal, tooth crowding) that contradicts intelligent design and supports evolutionary theory (p. 822-823).

creationism_and_intelligent_design.label: Creationism and Intelligent Design
creationism_and_intelligent_design.summary: Various beliefs that reject evolutionary biology in favor of special creation.

creation_evolution_continuum.label: The Creation-Evolution Continuum
creation_evolution_continuum.summary: A spectrum of beliefs ranging from extreme biblical literalism to materialism.

flat_earthism_geocentrism.label: Flat-Earthism and Geocentrism
flat_earthism_geocentrism.summary: Extreme literal interpretations asserting the earth is flat or the center of the solar system (p. 826).

young_earth_creationism.label: Young-Earth Creationism (YEC)
young_earth_creationism.summary: Belief that the universe was created in six 24-hour days thousands of years ago; often promotes 'creation science' (p. 826-827).

old_earth_creationism.label: Old-Earth Creationism (OEC)
old_earth_creationism.summary: Accepts an ancient universe but rejects biological evolution. Includes Gap creationism, Day-age creationism, and Progressive creationism (p. 827-828).

theistic_evolution.label: Theistic Evolution (TE)
theistic_evolution.summary: Belief that evolution is the natural process used by God to create life (p. 828).

materialism.label: Materialism
materialism.summary: The belief that matter and energy are sufficient to explain the universe, with no supernatural forces (p. 828).

intelligent_design_movement.label: Intelligent Design (ID)
intelligent_design_movement.summary: A form of special creationism claiming 'irreducible complexity' (e.g., bacterial flagellum) to argue that natural selection cannot account for certain biological structures (p. 829).

kitzmiller_v_dover.label: Kitzmiller v. Dover
kitzmiller_v_dover.summary: A 2005 court case that declared ID a religious rather than scientific view, making its teaching in public schools unconstitutional (p. 829).

evolution_and_media.label: Evolution and the Media
evolution_and_media.summary: The history and challenges of communicating evolutionary biology to the public.

science_communication_history.label: History of Science Communication
science_communication_history.summary: The rise of specialized science reporters in the 1970s and the popularization of challenges to the Modern Synthesis (e.g., punctuated equilibria) (p. 832-833).

journalistic_pitfalls.label: Journalistic Pitfalls
journalistic_pitfalls.summary: The tendency of media to seek conflict and employ 'false balance,' giving equal weight to scientific evidence and non-scientific beliefs (p. 834).

new_media_impact.label: New Media Impact
new_media_impact.summary: The shift from traditional print science sections to blogs, podcasts, and interactive websites, increasing access but also spreading misinformation (p. 834-835).

darwinius_case.label: The Darwinius Affair
darwinius_case.summary: A cautionary tale where media hype presented a fossil (Ida) as a 'missing link' to humans, whereas later scientific analysis placed it in the lemur lineage (p. 835-836).

directional_selection_fact.label: Directional Selection
directional_selection_fact.summary: Selection that favors one extreme phenotype over others, causing a shift in the population's mean trait value (pp. 206, 208, 225, 239, 240, 512, 513-514).

frequency_dependent_selection_fact.label: Frequency-Dependent Selection
frequency_dependent_selection_fact.summary: Selection where the fitness of a phenotype depends on its frequency relative to other phenotypes in the population (pp. 193, 211).

intrasexual_selection_fact.label: Intrasexual Selection
intrasexual_selection_fact.summary: Competition between members of the same sex for access to mates, often involving weapon evolution (pp. 641).

intersexual_selection_fact.label: Intersexual Selection
intersexual_selection_fact.summary: Selection based on mate choice, where one sex (usually females) chooses mates based on specific traits (pp. 641).

fisherian_runaway_fact.label: Fisherian Runaway
fisherian_runaway_fact.summary: A positive feedback loop where a female preference for a trait and the trait itself become genetically correlated, leading to extreme trait evolution (pp. 520, 523, 525-526).

good_genes_fact.label: Good Genes Hypothesis
good_genes_fact.summary: The theory that sexual traits are honest signals of a mate's genetic quality (pp. 520-521, 524-525, 652).

hamiltons_rule_fact.label: Hamilton's Rule
hamiltons_rule_fact.summary: A formal expression of kin selection: rb > c, where r is relatedness, b is the benefit to the recipient, and c is the cost to the actor (pp. 202, 215, 216, 219, 671, 698).

inclusive_fitness_fact.label: Inclusive Fitness
inclusive_fitness_fact.summary: The sum of an individual's own reproductive success plus the effects the individual has on the reproductive success of its relatives (pp. 196, 202-203, 215, 219, 656, 698).

fisher_fundamental_theorem.label: Fisher's Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection
fisher_fundamental_theorem.summary: The rate of increase in fitness of any organism at any time is equal to its genetic variance in fitness at that time (pp. 22, 208).

founder_effect_fact.label: Founder Effect
founder_effect_fact.summary: The loss of genetic variation that occurs when a new population is established by a very small number of individuals from a larger population (pp. 307, 507).

bottleneck_effect_fact.label: Genetic Bottleneck
bottleneck_effect_fact.summary: A sharp reduction in the size of a population due to environmental events or human activities, reducing genetic diversity (pp. 307, 308).

neutral_theory_fact.label: Neutral Theory of Molecular Evolution
neutral_theory_fact.summary: The theory that most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by genetic drift of mutant alleles that are selectively neutral (pp. 68, 307, 308, 312-313, 367, 370).

introgression_fact.label: Introgression
introgression_fact.summary: The movement of a gene from one species into the gene pool of another by the repeated backcrossing of an interspecific hybrid with one of its parent species (pp. 460, 491, 495, 529, 555, 563).

migration_load_fact.label: Migration Load
migration_load_fact.summary: The reduction in fitness of a local population caused by the influx of alleles from other populations that are not adapted to the local environment (pp. 321, 324, 337).

mutation_types_fact.label: Types of Mutations
mutation_types_fact.summary: Includes beneficial, deleterious, and neutral mutations, as well as indels and loss-of-function mutations (pp. 230, 316, 336-337, 339).

mutation_selection_balance_fact.label: Mutation-Selection Balance
mutation_selection_balance_fact.summary: The equilibrium where the rate at which a deleterious allele is produced by mutation equals the rate at which it is removed by selection (p. 317).

genetics_genomics.label: Genetics and Genomics
genetics_genomics.summary: The study of genes, genetic variation, and the structure and function of genomes.

molecular_components.label: Molecular Components
molecular_components.summary: The physical and chemical basis of heredity.

dna_structure_fact.label: DNA Structure
dna_structure_fact.summary: The double-helix structure composed of nucleotides; includes coding and non-coding regions (pp. 5, 7, 26, 40, 363).

rna_types_fact.label: RNA Types
rna_types_fact.summary: Includes messenger RNA (mRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), and transfer RNA (tRNA) (pp. 40, 41, 130, 132).

central_dogma_fact.label: Central Dogma of Molecular Biology
central_dogma_fact.summary: The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA (transcription) and from RNA to protein (translation) (p. 42).

c_value_paradox_fact.label: C-value Paradox
c_value_paradox_fact.summary: The observation that genome size does not correlate with the biological complexity of the organism (pp. 374, 380).

gene_evolution.label: Gene Evolution
gene_evolution.summary: The processes by which new genes arise and change over time.

neofunctionalization_fact.label: Neofunctionalization
neofunctionalization_fact.summary: The process where one duplicate gene acquires a completely new function while the other maintains the original function (pp. 397, 401, 406).

subfunctionalization_fact.label: Subfunctionalization
subfunctionalization_fact.summary: The process where the original functions of a ancestral gene are partitioned between two duplicate genes (pp. 397, 401).

pseudogenes_fact.label: Pseudogenes
pseudogenes_fact.summary: Non-functional segments of DNA that resemble functional genes but have lost their protein-coding ability (pp. 371, 380, 400).

hardy_weinberg_fact.label: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
hardy_weinberg_fact.summary: A principle stating that allele and genotype frequencies in a population will remain constant from generation to generation in the absence of evolutionary influences (pp. 40, 44).

effective_pop_size_fact.label: Effective Population Size (Ne)
effective_pop_size_fact.summary: The size of an ideal population that would show the same amount of genetic drift as the actual population (pp. 307, 310-311, 466).

linkage_disequilibrium_fact.label: Linkage Disequilibrium (LD)
linkage_disequilibrium_fact.summary: The non-random association of alleles at different loci in a given population (pp. 40, 44-45, 228, 307).

methylation_fact.label: DNA Methylation
methylation_fact.summary: A process of adding methyl groups to DNA molecules, which can change the activity of a DNA segment without changing the sequence (pp. 133, 422-423).

transgenerational_epigenetics_fact.label: Transgenerational Epigenetic Effects
transgenerational_epigenetics_fact.summary: Epigenetic marks that are passed from parents to offspring, affecting phenotype across generations (pp. 424-425).

prezygotic_barriers.label: Prezygotic Isolating Mechanisms
prezygotic_barriers.summary: Barriers that prevent mating or fertilization from occurring.

behavioral_isolation_fact.label: Behavioral Isolation
behavioral_isolation_fact.summary: Different mating rituals or signals that prevent different species from mating (p. 515).

temporal_isolation_fact.label: Temporal Isolation
temporal_isolation_fact.summary: Species that breed at different times of the day, season, or year (p. 493, 515).

mechanical_isolation_fact.label: Mechanical Isolation
mechanical_isolation_fact.summary: Morphological differences that prevent successful mating (p. 493).

gametic_isolation_fact.label: Gametic Isolation
gametic_isolation_fact.summary: Sperm of one species may not be able to fertilize eggs of another species (p. 210).

hybrid_inviability_fact.label: Hybrid Inviability
hybrid_inviability_fact.summary: Hybrids fail to develop properly or die before reaching reproductive age (p. 497).

hybrid_sterility_fact.label: Hybrid Sterility
hybrid_sterility_fact.summary: Hybrids reach adulthood but are unable to produce viable gametes (p. 498).

dobzhansky_muller_fact.label: Dobzhansky-Muller Incompatibilities
dobzhansky_muller_fact.summary: A model explaining how reproductive isolation evolves through the accumulation of incompatible mutations at different loci in diverging populations (pp. 543, 546-547).

speciation_modes.label: Modes of Speciation
speciation_modes.summary: Classification of speciation based on the geographic relationship between populations.

allopatric_speciation_fact.label: Allopatric Speciation
allopatric_speciation_fact.summary: Speciation that occurs when populations are geographically isolated (pp. 504, 506-507).

peripatric_speciation_fact.label: Peripatric Speciation
peripatric_speciation_fact.summary: A form of allopatric speciation where a small founder population becomes isolated at the edge of the parent population's range (pp. 504, 507).

parapatric_speciation_fact.label: Parapatric Speciation
parapatric_speciation_fact.summary: Speciation that occurs when populations are adjacent to each other but have limited gene flow, often across an environmental gradient (pp. 504, 509).

sympatric_speciation_fact.label: Sympatric Speciation
sympatric_speciation_fact.summary: Speciation that occurs without geographic isolation, often through polyploidy or strong disruptive selection (pp. 20, 21, 489, 496).

macroevolutionary_trends.label: Macroevolutionary Trends
macroevolutionary_trends.summary: Broad patterns of change across many species over long periods of time.

punctuated_equilibrium_fact.label: Punctuated Equilibrium
punctuated_equilibrium_fact.summary: The theory that evolutionary change occurs in rapid bursts of speciation separated by long periods of stasis (pp. 25, 91, 486, 571, 589).

copes_rule_fact.label: Cope's Rule
copes_rule_fact.summary: The tendency for lineages to evolve toward larger body sizes over time (p. 576).

key_innovations_fact.label: Key Innovations
key_innovations_fact.summary: New traits that allow a lineage to exploit previously unavailable resources, often leading to adaptive radiation (pp. 486, 563, 592).

extinction_processes.label: Extinction Processes
extinction_processes.summary: The loss of species from the earth, ranging from individual species loss to mass extinctions.

background_extinction_fact.label: Background Extinction
background_extinction_fact.summary: The standard rate of extinction that occurs continuously over geological time (p. 580).

mass_extinction_fact.label: Mass Extinction
mass_extinction_fact.summary: Events where a large percentage of the world's species go extinct in a short geological window, such as the 'Big Five' (pp. 118-119, 579, 581-583).

pseudoextinction_fact.label: Pseudoextinction
pseudoextinction_fact.summary: A term used when a species is considered 'extinct' but has actually evolved into a new species (pp. 579, 580).

paleontology_geology.label: Paleontology and Geology
paleontology_geology.summary: The study of prehistoric life through fossils and the geological context of the earth's history.

fossil_record.label: Fossil Record
fossil_record.summary: The totality of fossils and trace evidence of past life.

taphonomy_fact.label: Taphonomy
taphonomy_fact.summary: The study of how organisms decay and become fossilized (pp. 112, 576).

lagerstatten_fact.label: Lagerstätten
lagerstatten_fact.summary: Sedimentary deposits that exhibit extraordinary fossils with soft tissue preservation (p. 114).

stasis_paradox_fact.label: Paradox of Morphological Stasis
stasis_paradox_fact.summary: The observation that species often remain morphologically unchanged for millions of years despite environmental fluctuations (pp. 442-443).

geologic_time_scale.label: Geologic Time Scale
geologic_time_scale.summary: The chronological system used by geologists and paleontologists to describe the timing and relationships of events in Earth's history.

paleozoic_fact.label: Paleozoic Era
paleozoic_fact.summary: The first era of the Phanerozoic eon, characterized by the explosion of marine life and the colonization of land (pp. 117, 150).

mesozoic_fact.label: Mesozoic Era
mesozoic_fact.summary: Known as the 'Age of Reptiles,' including the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods (pp. 30, 116, 172).

cenozoic_fact.label: Cenozoic Era
cenozoic_fact.summary: The current era, characterized by the radiation of mammals and birds (p. 79).

ecology_behavior.label: Ecology and Behavior
ecology_behavior.summary: The study of how organisms interact with their environment and the evolutionary basis of their behaviors.

ecological_niches.label: Ecological Niches
ecological_niches.summary: The role and position a species has in its environment, including the resources it uses.

hutchinson_niche_fact.label: Hutchinson Niche
hutchinson_niche_fact.summary: The n-dimensional hypervolume where all environmental conditions allow a species to persist (pp. 288, 289, 292).

ecological_opportunity_fact.label: Ecological Opportunity
ecological_opportunity_fact.summary: The availability of unoccupied niches that can trigger adaptive radiation (pp. 561-562, 563, 594).

mating_systems.label: Mating Systems
mating_systems.summary: The patterns of mating and pairing in a population.

monogamy_fact.label: Monogamy
monogamy_fact.summary: A mating system where one male and one female form an exclusive pair bond (p. 357).

polygyny_fact.label: Polygyny
polygyny_fact.summary: A mating system where one male mates with multiple females (p. 357).

polyandry_fact.label: Polyandry
polyandry_fact.summary: A mating system where one female mates with multiple males (p. 357).

osr_fact.label: Operational Sex Ratio (OSR)
osr_fact.summary: The ratio of sexually competing males to sexually receptive females in a population (pp. 634, 637, 647, 653).

caste_differentiation_fact.label: Caste Differentiation
caste_differentiation_fact.summary: The specialization of individuals into reproductive (queens/kings) and non-reproductive (workers/soldiers) roles (p. 700).

haplodiploidy_hypothesis_fact.label: Haplodiploidy Hypothesis
haplodiploidy_hypothesis_fact.summary: The theory that the unique genetic relatedness in haplodiploid insects (like bees/ants) predisposes them to eusociality (p. 215).

symbiosis.label: Symbiosis
symbiosis.summary: Close and long-term biological interaction between two different biological organisms.

mutualism_fact.label: Mutualism
mutualism_fact.summary: A symbiotic relationship where both species benefit (pp. 19, 219, 671, 672).

commensalism_fact.label: Commensalism
commensalism_fact.summary: A symbiotic relationship where one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

parasitism_fact.label: Parasitism
parasitism_fact.summary: A symbiotic relationship where one species (the parasite) benefits at the expense of the other (the host) (pp. 139, 152).

hominin_lineages.label: Hominin Lineages
hominin_lineages.summary: The sequence of species leading to modern humans.

homo_erectus_fact.label: Homo erectus
homo_erectus_fact.summary: An early human species that first migrated out of Africa into Eurasia (pp. 185-186).

neanderthals_fact.label: Neanderthals
neanderthals_fact.summary: An extinct species of human that lived in Eurasia and may have interbred with early Homo sapiens (pp. 186-187, 480).

homo_habilis_fact.label: Homo habilis
homo_habilis_fact.summary: One of the earliest members of the genus Homo, known for tool use (p. 185).

eea_fact.label: Environment of Evolutionary Adaptedness (EEA)
eea_fact.summary: The set of selective pressures that shaped the evolution of a psychological trait (pp. 690, 694).

ep_models_fact.label: Models of Evolutionary Psychology
ep_models_fact.summary: Frameworks used to explain human behaviors like incest taboos and cooperation through an evolutionary lens (pp. 691-693).

history_philosophy_of_biology.label: History and Philosophy of Biology
history_philosophy_of_biology.summary: The evolution of biological thought and the intersection of science, philosophy, and religion.

origin_of_species_fact.label: On the Origin of Species
origin_of_species_fact.summary: The 1859 publication by Charles Darwin that laid the foundation for evolutionary biology (pp. 4, 18, 24, 29).

descent_with_modification_fact.label: Descent with Modification
descent_with_modification_fact.summary: The core idea that descendants inherit traits from ancestors, which change slightly over time (pp. 19, 29, 33, 36).

synthesis_phases_fact.label: Phases of the Modern Synthesis
synthesis_phases_fact.summary: The evolution of the synthesis through three distinct phases from 1930 to 1940 (pp. 22-26).

science_religion_conflict.label: Science and Religion
science_religion_conflict.summary: The philosophical and social tension between evolutionary science and religious belief systems.

intelligent_design_fact.label: Intelligent Design (ID)
intelligent_design_fact.summary: The belief that certain features of the universe and living things are best explained by an intelligent cause rather than undirected evolution (pp. 817, 819, 829-830).

creationism_fact.label: Creationism
creationism_fact.summary: Religious belief in the creation of the universe and life by a deity, often opposing evolutionary theory (pp. 827).

problem_of_evil_fact.label: The Problem of Evil
problem_of_evil_fact.summary: The philosophical question of how an all-powerful, all-good God can allow suffering and 'imperfect design' in nature (pp. 817, 821-823).
